title: Preservation of coffee baskets in the nursery
text: Since majority of coffee estates depend entirely on the supply of bamboo baskets for raising basket plants, the durability of these baskets has to be ensured as they are generally attacked by wetrot caused by saprophytic fungi and moulds etc. Copper sulphate is toxic to the moulds and other fungi. Hence a three year study was conducted in the Coffee Experiment Station to determine the economical strength of copper sulphate to be used with advantage. The experiments demonstrate the fact that boiling the baskets in at least 2% copper sulphate solution is essential to confer upon them immunity from the inroads of destructive moulds which cause delay and hasten rotting. Treating the baskets in the above manner has enhanced their lasting quality. The method of treatment is discussed in detail (Srinivasan, 1936).

title: Phytotoxicity of BHC
text: It was reported that the hydrocarbons such as Benzene and Toluene when used in sufficient amounts they became markedly toxic and act as cytolities to disrupt cellular organization. A preliminary study was undertaken to observe the effect of BHC on seedlings and germinating seeds. BHC treated plants showed marked intervenal chlorosis of new leaves. The control plants were normal. There was general stunting of linear growth of plants in BHC treatment. The percentage emergence was poor and recorded only 23%. Instead of normal, buttons of certain seedlings got stuck in the soil while their stubby roots were exposed. On examination various malformations of root were noticed in BHC treatment. Abnormal seedlings when shifted to the bed with normal soil appeared to give fresh roots. title: Polythene bags for raising coffee seedlings
text: The results ofa trial in the nursery to compare the growth of coffee seedlings in polythene bags with those grown in baskets or beds conducted during 1961 and 1963 revealed that seedlings in polythene bags were superior to those grown in baskets or secondary beds in terms of height of the seedlings, number of leaves produced, shoot and root weight. Since the seedlings in polythene bags developed better and balanced shoot and root, they will be able to withstand the transplanting shock better. In addition, they are cheaper by way of initial cost. They do not require any fungicidal treatment before use in the case of baskets. They also conserve more moisture and hence require less frequent watering. Though there was practically no difference in growth of seedlings among the 2 type of bags. black polythene bags appear to withstang weather conditions, wear and tear much bette than white bags, and therefore may be Preferred (Gopalakrishnan, 1964).

title: Studies on hastening of germination of
text: Arabica coffee seed and further growth of seedlings. 1. Hastening of germination Effect of pre-sowing of S.795 Arabica coffee seeds (with parchment) in aqueous solution of 22 different chemicals as also with various water soaking treatment (both under lab and nursery conditions) was studied and was consistently observed that about 50% of the total seeds soaked for 24 hours in Ascorbic acid (0.1%), Folic acid (0.1%) and Thiourea (1500 ppm) germinated earlier by about 5-7 days. The percentage of seed germination was generally better with these chemicals as compared to control seeds (Gopal and Ramaiah, 1971).

title: Studies on the physiology of germination of coffee seed. I. Observations on sprouting
text: Germination of Coffea arabica cultivar S.795 seeds was studied under natural conditions in nursery and laboratory. Seeds without parchment germinated much earlier than those with parchment intact. Possible causes for the delay in germination of seeds with parchment are discussed (Gopal and Ramaiah, 1972).

title: Seed germination in coffee
text: In Arabica 50%, 75% and fully ripened show higher germination than 25% ripened. In Canephora similar trends are seen in counts at 50" day. Observations on 50" and 100" day revealed that covering of beds with polythene chamber either alone or with paddy straw is superior to ordinary bed covered with paddy straw. Covering of sowing beds with polythene sheets likewise indicate higher percentage of germination by 50" day itself and 100° day onwards an increased percentage of germination. The failure of many sceds to germinate may have no relation to a need for pre-treatment but may be due to merely to requirement of specific conditions. Temperature is amongst the most important conditions. Use of chemicals or hormones or tepid water requires further probing with the use of polythene bags (Vishveshwara and Suryakantha Raju, 1972).

title: Effect of placement of seeds on germination
text: TA: Seed with groove downwards (embryo at the top of the surface) Seed with groove upwards (embryo at lower surface) TC: Seed with groove perpendicular to soil surface (embryo at the top of the surface) TD: Seed with groove perpendicular to soil surface (embryo at the bottom of the surface) TB: the Seed with embryo at bottom recorded the lowest value of soldier stage at 41*t day while seed with groove upwards recorded significantly high value over this and other 2 treatments. By 105" day the treatment differences are eliminated. Unfolding of cotyledons and initiation of first pair of leaves is significantly high in TB while these are affected and delayed in TD where loop formation is absent. Present study show that sowing seeds with embryo at the bottom is not conducive to good germination and sowing should be either flat-groove upward or downward or embryo at the top. With the parchment intact it is not possible to know the location of the embryo. Therefore, sowing as in TC embryo at the top is not practicable (Vishveshwara and Suryakantha Raju, 1973).

title: Effect of pesticides on coffee seedlings
text: The present study was undertaken to find out the effect of the commonly used pesticides on young coffee seedlings. When the seedling reached the first pair stage, the root system of each seedling was drenched with 10 ml of the insecticide or the fungicide solution. At the end of 2 months, visual observations on phytotoxicity, measurement of height of seedlings and count of number of leaves were made. There were no phytotoxicity symptoms on the foliage of treated and untreated (control) seedlings. Difference in the height and number of leaves were also not statistically significant. But the weight of root system showed significant difference between the control and treated seedlings. The seedlings in the control plot had heavier root system than all the treated seedlings. It is evident that the above pesticides used for the control of pests and diseases in the nursery had an adverse effect on the development of the young root system possibly by interfering with the mitotic division. Cytological studies did not show any malformations in the tip cells (Venkataramaiah and Deepak Singh, 1976).

title: Studies on the effect of some granular contact insecticides on the roots of coffee seedlings
text: Application of Ekalux 5G and Phendal 5G (up to 5g/bag) and Sevin 4G (up to 25g/bag) does not cause any injury to coffee roots. No toxic symptoms were noticed on the shoots either. Application of BHC in the nursery bags resulted in development of stubby roots and arrested the growth of root system. Therefore, these chemicals can be safely used in nursery for control of soil pests (Chacko et al., 1980).

title: Studies on the effect of pre-soaking treatments on seed germination and seedling growth of Coffea canephora
text: Effect of alternate pre-soaking and drying of C. canephora seeds in ash water solution on germination and seedling growth was studied. Periodical observations were made on_ the germination of the seeds and on the different growth stages of seedling development. title: Studies on the effect of Sevidol 4:4 G on roots of coffee seedlings
text: Investigations on the effect of Sevidol 4:4 G (Carbaryl+Linane) on the root system of coffee seedlings were carried out. No deleterious effect, were noticed. Thus, this granular insecticide at the rate of 10 g per seedling could be safely used for the control of root pests like cockchafers (Venkatesuly et al., 1981).

title: Studies on the effect of Nexagan 5G ang
text: Oftanol 5G on roots of coffee seedlings Two new granular insecticides, Nexagan (Bromophos-ethyl) 5 G and Oftanol (Isofenphos) 5G, have given effective control of white grubs in the nursery. A study was conducted to find out if the use of these has any deleterious effect on the roots of coffee seedlings. No phytotoxicity was observed up to the 30" day after the treatment, When the root system was examined after 15 and 30 days, no abnormal growth was noticed. There was little difference in the dry matter percentage of roots between the treated and untreated plants. The present study showed that the insecticides used do not cause any deleterious effect on coffee seedlings (Gokuldas Kumar et al., 1981).

title: Temperature control of physiological dwarfing in coffee seedlings
text: In the present study, endosperm present on the embryo of coffee seed was scraped to expose the embryo. Seeds started germinating within 48 hours. On 7" day these germlings were transplanted to pots. The growth was faster up to opening of ‘Seq 'dy, Cal "Ve “nt of Sal 0) o =- OO DB ¢ cotyledonary leaves and there after slowed down. Observations recorded after 20 months revealed reduction in height of the plant, length of the internode and size of the leaf. They had very poor root system (Purushotham and _ Sreenivasan, 1982).

title: Effect of Lindane 20 EC and BHC 50 WP on coffee seedlings
text: BHC at 0.5% and 1% and Lindane at 0.1% a.i. showed reduction in the dry matter percentage of roots. Lindane at 0.075% a.i. did not show any reduction in dry matter percentage of roots and so it could be used at this concentration for the control of root pests in nursery. Otherwise no visual phytotoxic symptoms were noticed (Vinod Kumar et al., 1983).

title: Seed borne fungi
text: Twenty six fungi representing different genera isolated from the seeds of Arabica. More number of fungi was isolated from the seeds with parchment than those removed of their parchment. Geotrichum candidum and _ Fusarium solani occurred in greater proportion than the other fungi. During seed germination on moist filter paper these fungi infected and killed the embryo and such seeds failed to germinate because of preemergence of rotting of embryo on the nursery beds (Muthappa, 1984).

title: Studies on the seed characters of some coffee species
text: The morphological differences of seed features in 12 species of Coffea available in gene bank were studied. The overlapping of different species in their center of origin perhaps has caused introgressive hybridization between some species of Liberica group resulting in broadening of genetical base that has manifested in this variability. It is possible that Arabica being selfpollinated species, tend to show narrow variation than other species who have predominantly crosspollinating reproductive mechanism. These limits offer good sources for exploitation in breeding programme in coffee and stresses the necessity of prior identification of plants possessing desirable seed features (Jamsheed Ahmed, 1984).

title: Bethel spray to overcome dormancy in coffee seedlings
text: Bethel (2-chloro ethyl phosphoric acid) @ 125, 250, 500 and 1000 ppm was sprayed to break the dormancy of seedlings (SIn.7.3) at button stage. The results showed that the seedlings sprayed with Bethel 250 ppm unfolded their cotyledonary leaves with the increase in plant height and number of leaves as compared to control (Shivarama et al., 1986).

title: Flower induction in juvenile coffee seedlings
text: Flower induction in juvenile coffee seedlings (S.274) was tried with different surgical and growth regulator treatments in pot culture experiment. Gibberlic acid (GA3) sprays were found to be effective in flower bursting while the other growth regulator sprays and surgical treatment like girdling, bark inversion and bending of main stem failed to induce flowering. The influence of each treatment on morphology of seedlings observed has been reported. Gibberlic acid induced flowering within 6 months after the spray, when the seedlings were at the stage of 24 months (Raghuramulu and Purushotham, 1987).

title: Seed germination and seedling growth as influenced by nursery soil mixture
text: Since good jungle soil is not easily accessible in every plantation and in many coffee plantations ordinary estate soils are being used in nursery soil mixture, studies were conducted to find out a suitable composition. Of the various compositions of soil, FYM and sand tried, the mixture of 5:3:1 ratio seemed to be more effective and conducive for early as well as higher seed germination of Robusta. Growth parameters also revealed that 5:3:1 mixture was more suitable for seedling growth (Veerendra Kumar and Raju, 1988).

title: Studies on the phytotoxic effect of systemic granular insecticides on coffee grown in polythene bags
text: Disystron 5G, Rogor 5G, Solvirex 5G and Thimet 10G caused phytotoxicity to coffee grown in polythene bags and that of Temik 10G is safe. No appreciable difference could be noticed in phytotoxic effect of plants in bags and those of sleeves. It is necessary to exercise caution in the use of these insecticides in nursery (Bhat et al., 1988).

title: Effect of pre-storage and mid- storage treatment on the germination of coffee seeds
text: Maximum germination (84%) of 6 month old stored Arabica seeds was obtained by soaking them either in Sodium phosphate (Dibasic) 250 ppm or in EDTA disodium salt for 48 hours before sowing. Cycocel and EDTA soaking treatment (for 24 hours) on freshly prepared Robusta seeds resulted in highest germination (91-97%) after 45 days of seed preparation (Raghuramulu and Purushotham, 1991).

title: Study on the effect of biofertilizers on the growth of CxR coffee seedlings
text: In a nursery study on the effect of different biofertilizers (Nitrogen fixing and Phosphorus mobilizing) on the growth of CxR coffee seedlings, it was observed that Azospirillum brasilense treatment significantly increased the plant height. There was also a significant increase in stem girth, tap root length and total root weight by combined application of Azospirillum brasilense + Phosphobacteria (Bacilus sp.) + VAM fungi (Gigaspora margarita). The results of this experiment indicated that application of biofertilizers could enhance the growth and vigour of CxR coffee seedlings (Glory Swarupa, 1996).

title: Seedling blight - A new disease of coffee seedlings
text: A new disease affecting 18 months old. Coffea arabica cv. Cauvery (Catimor) seedlings was observed for the first time from the Margolly estate, Consolidated Coffee Ltd., Pollibetta. Kodagu Dist., Karnataka during March 1996 caused by the fungus Alternaria alternata is reported here. In the initia] stage of infection a small necrotic spot seen in the nodal region is found to expand later becoming pale brown in colour followed by blightening and drooping of leaves leading to the gradual death of seedlings. 50-60 plants (2%) were affected during the month of March 1996 (Hanumantha et al., 1996).

title: Influence of commercial organic manures on the growth of coffee seedlings
text: A study was carried out at Central Coffee Research Institute for 2 years during 1995-96 with an objective of comparing the effectiveness of three commercial organic sources of coconut coir pith compost viz., Prajwala neem, Varanasi-cocompost-O (VCC-O, 100% organic), Varanasi-cocompost-F (VCC-F, enriched) and a vermicompost prepared at Central Coffee Research Institute using exotic earthworms Eudrilus euginiae with FYM and as a substitute for FYM in standard nursery mixture. These studies indicated that commercial coir pith compost namely Prajwala neem and vermicompost from exotic earthworms E. euginiae are superior to conventional FYM and could be used in preparation of nursery mixture for obtaining vigorous coffee seedlings in nursery (Muralidhara et al., 1996).

title: Effect of biofertilizers on germination of coffee seed
text: The studies conducted on the efficacy of seed treatment of coffee seeds with biofertilizers on percentage germination indicated that seed treatment with Phosphobacteria (at 10g/100 seeds) a day prior to sowing enhanced the germination compared to other treatments such as ash, Azospirillum, VAM, Azospirillum + Phosphobacteria, Azospirillum + WAM and Azospirillum + Phosphobacteria + VAM (Glory Swarupa et al., 1997).

Hybrids from Central Coffee Research Institute, Portugal and Arabica varieties of Ethiopian origin recorded predominance of race XXIII followed by III, XXIV, I, VITE and 1. C. bengalensis Heyne ex Roem and Shult and C. travencorensis White and Arn., established at Central Coffee Research Institute indicated races I, Ill, VIII, XVIII and XXIII. A few individual plants in diploids and tetraploids showed simultaneous occurrence of more than one race. The strategy of coffee selections to meet the challenges of any race/races prevalent in a locality is discussed. Since prevalence of race goes with suitable host for their manifestation, it is mecessary to collect spores from diverse lines given for cultivation in different zones and also to introduce indicator plants in each locality which can manifest the prevalence of unknown races and help in accelerated detection (Ramachandran et al., 1979).

title: Evaluation of horizontal resistance to leaf rust in Arabica coffee
text: Plants in varietal trials of Arabica coffee planted in 1967 (Trial 1) and 1974 (Trial 2) were scored for percentage of rust infected plants and intensity ofleaf rust, using 5 point scale for intensity (O=No_ infection. 0.25=few spots. 0.50 mild susceptibility. 0.75=high susceptibility, 1.00-high susceptibility followed by defoliation). Scoring was carried out during June, September and December of 1980. An increasing trend in rust build-up was noticed from the initial to the successive scoring periods. Rate of infection was faster on Kents in trial 1 and on San Ramon (selection 7.2) and S. 1934, in trial 2. Reduced rate of infection (horizontal resistance) was observed in the case of Tafarikela in trial 1 and in selections 5 and € uP in trinl 2. title: Coffee breeding - A retrospect
text: The screening of families started With sin gle plant selection (from 257 sources of Arabica ang 37 of Robusta) 80 cultivars of first Seneration intervarietal crosses. 54 cultures of secon d generation crosses, 37 of third generation CrOsses and from some promising 1* and 2™4 generation progeny of crosses between established families, It was interesting to note the wide variation among this material, in yield, vigour and to some extent in their resistance to disease. Further elimination was made which resulted in the selection of 36 Arabica and 17 Robusta plants. Such a screening has to be done periodically with the advent of newer generations so that still better yielders, better disease resisters and more flavourful coffee could be isolated. The easiest method of propagating, coffee are: by cleft grafting suckers, either in nursery or field and by rooting single nodded sucker cutting in a propagating frame (Thomas, 1954).

text: Introduction, brief description of the diploid species of coffee, the parent plants from those utilized for cross breeding. description of crosses, discussion and conclusions were discussed (Narasimhaswamy and Vishveshwara, 1961).

title: A note on the occurrence of three species of
text: Coffea indigenous to India The authors while presenting the distribution of three indigenous species namely Coffea bengalensis, Coffea travencorensis and Coffea wightiana have also dealt with ecological factors and description of the three species. It is also noted that these three species are indigenous to India found in tropical Himalayas and Eastern Ghats and Western Ghats and also these three species are reported to be susceptible to coffee leaf rust (Herileia vastatrix) (Narasimhaswamy and Vishveshwara, 1963).

title: Progress report on hybrids between diploid species of Coffea L
text: The write-up deals with studies on the hybrids between the diploid species, their progeny as well as on the occurrence of tetraploid plants in the latter quite a few of which show close resemblance in morphological features to Coffea arabica. The hybrids dealt by the authors include the F, of C. eugenioides x C. canephora, excelsa x eugenioides (S 1715) and C. liberica x C. eugenioides (S.1721) and their progeny (Narasimhaswamy and Vishveshwara, 1967).

title: Vegetative-floral balance in coffee. I. Effect of disturbing the floral phase on vegetative growth
text: In the present paper, the effect of moisture coupled with disturbing the flower buds and certain related plant organs in 2 varieties C. arabica (Cioccie and S.1934) is presented. The varieties and treatments showed significant difference for the number of vegetative buds produced. ‘The treatment removing all inflorescence showed the presence of highest number of vegetative buds followed by treatment of removing leaves on both sides. Least number was seen in control and treatment removing bracts. $.1934 showed more number of vegetative buds than Cioccie. Watered plants showed more number of vegetative buds than non-watered plants. The treatment x variety interactions was not significant. Probably due to the receipt of natural showers preceding the 2™! observation period, which usually induce growth and thus lower the treatment effect. A progressive increase in the number of vegetative buds initiated was observed from 1" to 3™ observations. title: Coffee breeding in India
text: A review of earlier work on collection of plant material from estates in South India, their exploitation through selection and hybridization, merits and demerits of cultivars and selections under large scale cultivation is presented. Clonal and seedling progeny trials undertaken during the initial years and the limitations in clonal propagation are dealt with. An assessment of variability in the germplasm collection of exotic and indigenous species, varieties, cultivars and selections and utilization of the same in breeding at the Central Coffee Research Institute is given along with an account of interspecific hybridization, haploid and polyploid breeding and mutation breeding (Vishveshwara, 1974).

title: Male sterility in Coffea liberica
text: A study of floral characters of the four male sterile plants indicated that the flowers were several times smaller than the normal hermaphrodite flowers. Anthers conformed to the description given already. It was, however, observed that in three of the four male sterile plants, there were two whorls of anthers, one originating from the corolla tube and the other from the rim of the disc. The majority of the pistils were normal with a straight style and bifid stigma. The style and stigma, however, showed variation in structure. Besides normal style, curved, bent or curled styles with bifid or trifid stigmas were found, in general. Split styles were also found to occur regularly in one plant (Santa Ram and Ramachandran, 1981).

Wide range of variability was observed for most of the characters, which confirmed the polymorphic nature of the species. From the breeding point of view, with moderate expression for most of the characters were capable of giving high yield (Srinivasan and Vishveshwara, 1981).

title: Physical characteristics of coffee beans as selection indices
text: Indian coffee is known world over for its quality. The planter is paid based on the visual assessment of his produce. Further, extra remuneration is based on the cup quality. The produce is graded into Peaberry and A, B, C and T grades based on the physical standards of measurement and appearance. At Central Coffee Research Institute, breeding is in progress since its inception. In the breeding programme importance is given for maximizing the production of A’ grade beans by eliminating the triage components. So far 12 Arabica and three Robusta genotypes have been released for commercial cultivation. In this article, procedures adopted to obtain the superior bean characteristics for commercial acceptance are discussed (Sreenivasan, 1988).

Empty locule formation is found to be due to the post fertilization abnormalities. A breeding scheme to evolve lines with reduced pea berry and empty locule production is suggested on the basis of data presented. This involves the selection of individual plants with low pea berry production and high self-compatibility from the F,, progeny and further testing for fertility and adaptability (Santa Ram et al., 1990).

title: Interspecific hybrid sterility in coffee
text: Various factors acting as barriers of reproduction among the sister plants of F, progenies of 6 interspecific hybrids involving 6 diploid species of the genus Coffea were studied. The osmotic concentration of the protoplasm of the pollen and stigmatic tissue and the reduced genetic variability of the hybrid population with regard to self-sterility alleles were proposed to be the possible barriers of reproduction and thus the cause of sterility in these hybrids. The possible model for increasing the productivity in these hybrids: F,’s of totally compatible parents would be exploited. A number of biparental F,, hybrids should be raised to have a large pool of self-sterility alleles. Natural crossing of these hybrids can be brought about by planting them in alternate rows (Santa Ram et al., 1992).

Percentage of bearing primaries, bearing nodes and berries per node with other growth characters were found to be the main attributes for total yield. BR.10, BR.9 and BR.5 were the good general combiners and BR.9 x BR.11 showed high SCA effects for yield. title: A putative natural hybrid in Palamalai estate
text: A plant with vigorous growth was noticed. Phenotypically the plant is intermediary to Robusta and Arabica genotypes and it used to bloom heavily, but the yield was poor with high percentage of pea berry. Hence the plant may be triploid originated from a natural cross between Canephora and Arabica, as crosses between the allotetraploid Arabica and diploid Canephora produced vigorously growing trees with profuse flowering and nevertheless completely sterile due to their triploid nature (Zwingly Premkumar and Ramanarayan, 1992).

title: Heterosis for yield in coffee.
text: The greater productivity of six F, hybrids of coffee over their respective parents was elucidated. Disease resistance pattern of the hybrids was also brought out. Transgressive yield increase in the hybrids was projected to be a probable utility model for increase in the coffee production in the context of declining/stagnating coffee productivity (Sreenivasan and Santa Ram, 1993).

While differences among hybrids from three parental cross groups were not significant, seasonal variations were highly significant, especially for fruit floats and yield. The Tall x Tall crosses showed the highest heritability and genetic advance, while Dwarf x Tall hybrids produced more fruits per cluster. Progenies from Cauvery x S.881 (Rume Sudan Wild Arabica) and interspecific C. arabica (Cauvery) x C. canephora (CxR) crosses exhibited lower fruit weight and volume, likely due to robusta genome integration (Anil Kumar et al., 2013).

title: Monohybrid Mendelian segregation in an interspecific hybrid population of tetraploid x diploid Coffea species- part 2
text: Coffee exhibits normal sexual propagation with significant variation, though its extent remains poorly understood. A study (2008-2011) at Coffee Research Sub Station, Chettalli, analyzed monohybrid segregation in the F, population of C. arabica cv. ‘Cauvery’ x (C. congensis x C. canephora var. robusta). The results showed that dependent and independent traits varied in expression, with independent traits following Mendelian segregation (3:1 and 1:2:1 ratios) at high confidence levels (P > 0.50 to 0.95). Dominant traits included dwarf bush, thin stem, and short primary branches, while tall bush, thick stem, and longer branches were recessive (Anil Kumar et al., 2014).

title: Balehonnur coffee selections
text: Breeding of coffee resistant to leaf disease with vigorous growth and fairly average to high yielding qualities commenced in the year 1962. A survey was conducted in all the coffee areas in South India and 267 plants from different zones was thus tapped and nearly.25,000 seedlings were raised. From these 80 mother plants that showed the desirable characters were selected in the first instance and were given serial numbers. At the same time self bred progeny of these mother plants as well as cross-breeds between these and the Kents and Coorgs were also raised. The procedure was continued until in the later generations the leaf disease susceptible segregates were either reduced to the minimum or altogether eliminated. By the year 1938, three mother plants had been finally fixed for further propagation. They are S.26, S.31 and S.44 whose progeny are known as the S.288 family including S.795 and S.333 family including S.645. It is gratifying to note that the performance of these selections in the field under different soil micro-climatic conditions has not belied the expectations. The majority of these selections are both disease resistant, good yielders and of vigorous growth (Narayanan, 1954).

title: Station selections
text: An attempt was made in 1949 in order to evaluate the relative yield of the selections (S.446 Kents, S.795, S.645 and S.288) in a manner, which would satisfy the eye of a statistician. Five harvest figures are recorded for 20 single plant selections, which are 100% resistant to leaf disease. If these plant selections continue to maintain their rank and do make good in other characters like bean z size, lower percentage of triage and quality in the cup, it would open up a new vista for the Indian coffee planter (Thomas, 1960).

title: Correlation studies in coffee selections.
text: I. Preliminary studies on correlation between stem girth and ripe cherry yield in some coffee selections The present write up relates to the correlation found between stem girth and ripe cherry yield of some Arabica and Robusta selections. The results showed that stem girth has a positive and significant correlation with mean cherry yield in 6 out of the 10 Robusta selections studied while one selection of the ‘t’ test value just fails to attain the 5% level of P. Both selections S.947 and S.948 show a highly significant positive correlation. The coefficient of variation for yield and stem girth is comparatively low in both these selections. This is probably attributable to the selections being advanced generation in straight line selection. This study however indicate that stem girth might be a useful character for purposes of selecting high yielding lines (Srinivasan, 1969).

title: Selection in coffee: Some criteria adopted and result obtained in India
text: In India 9 selections in Arabica and 3 selections in Robusta were evolved through pure line selection, mass selection, pedigree Selection and back cross breeding. The selection has helped to preserve and perpetuate genetic variability in this important perennial seed crop. The selection criteria have been for yield, resistance to leaf rust, low fruit and bean abnormalities, dwarf habit and good cup quality. Data on shifts in yield levels following advancement of selection at Central Coffee Research Institute are presented. Selection pressures being adopted in seed plots of these selections maintained in various zones are enumerated (Srinivasan and Vishveshwara, 1980).

title: A chemotaxonomic study of some species of Coffea
text: The chemistry often species and four varieties of Coffea L. viz. C. canephora Pierre ex Froehner, its varieties kKouilou, ugandae and laurentii, C. abeokutue Crammer. C. dewevrei De Wildet Durand. C. dewevrei var. aruwemiensis, C. excelsa Chev., C. arnoldiana De Wild. C. zanguebariae Lour., C. bengalensis (Roxb) ex Roem et Schult., C. khasiana Hook. C. wightiana Wall., and C. travencorensis W. et Arn. was studied by simple chemical tests. The reaction patterns indicate that the varieties and species are chemically distinct and the individual sub-sections of the genus Coffea: Erythrocoffea, Mazambicoffea, Pachycoffea and Paracoffea (Section/Genus) are relatively homogeneous in their chemical constitution. This study also suggests that Erythrocoffea and Pachycoffea are the oldest sub-sections of Eucoffea while Melanocoffea and Mozambicoffea are relatively recent evolutionarily. Paracoffea appears to be a very recent group. The possibility of elevating this gigantic genus to the family status is considered and rejected (Santa Ram, 1983).

title: Characters contributing to inter specific divergence in some species of coffee
text: Eleven Coffea species were studied for 15 morphological characters for 2 seasons: length and breadth of leaf; length of corolla lobe, tube: anther and style; length, breadth and thickness of fruit and seed and the ratio between fruit and seed. A simplified D2 analysis revealed that the species could be grouped into 4 clusters with cluster I containing 4 species: Arabica. Congensis, Eugenioids and Stenophylla. Cluster II and III having 3 species each: Arnoldiana, Aruwimiensis, Canephora and sie COFFEE SELECTIONS Abeokutae, Excelsa and Liberica respectively and cluster IV containing a single species: Dewevrei. This grouping vis-a-vis the classification proposed by other authors is compared and the importance of multivariate criteria in delineating species relationship in the genus is stressed (Jamsheed Ahmed and Sreenivasan, 1984).

title: Performance of Arabica varieties at 3 locations in Coorg
text: Mean yield and stability of yield of some C. arabica selections, trained on topped single stem under shade were studied at 3 locations in Coorg based on 6 annual yields. Significant differences were found between varieties at all the locations. The overall mean yields of S.795. S.1934, Sln.7 and 8 were superior to other varieties. Selection 5, 6 and 8 (HDT) were the best high yielding, stable genotypes (Srinivasan, 1984).

title: Newer station selections and crop improvement in coffee
text: Various important varieties/cultivars namely Sln.3, SIn.5, SIn.6, SIn.7, SIn.9 and SIn.10 in Arabica coffee and SIn.1R and SIn.3R in Robusta have been described by the author (Sreenivasan, 1985).

title: Adaptation of selections in traditional area
text: While touching upon the adaptation of different Arabica selections the author presents crop yields in Sln.4 and S1.5, 6, 7.2 and 9 at CCRI and in Kodagu and Tamil Nadu accordingly suitability of some of the selections to these areas is mentioned (Jamsheed Ahmed, 1985).

text: Nine selections of Arabica at eleven locations in Coorg were studied with respect to mean yield; coefficient of variation and stability bene co preernte gt ee ee mare COFFEE St ——— for yield based on yield records. In Robusta S.274 recorded high mean yield as compared to C x Rand BRIO (Srinivasan, 1985).

title: Adaptation of coffee selections in Andhra
text: Pradesh Studies on growth parameters and yield of different coffee selections revealed that Sln.7, SIn.7.2 (2491), Sin.4A (Agaro), Sln.11 (2464) and SIn.5 (2267-69) were found to be promising for large-scale cultivation under the eco-climatic and edaphic conditions of Andhra Pradesh. The fruit to clean coffee ratio of these selections also have been discussed (Dharmaraj, 1985).

title: Adaptation of selections in nontraditional areas
text: The paper discusses the introduction and systematic coffee cultivation in non-traditional areas like Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Orissa and Tripura. It also states that selections such as 795, 1934, Sln.4A, SIn.4C and Sln.7.2 in Arabica and S.274 in Robusta have adapted well to the northern and north-eastern climatic regions as it is reflected in their yields which ranged between 7591350 kg/ha (Reddy, 1985).

title: Station selections and their quality
text: The cup quality status of Arabica selections exotic Robusta and congensis x robusta, assessed by organoleptic method is described (Jamsheed Ahmed, 1985). ©

title: Studies on morphology and quality of
text: Ethiopian Arabica coffee Coffea arabica L. of Ethiopian origin possesses good quality, acidity, body and flavour and is considered to be the superior type. In order to find out the best cultivar. 54 accessions from Kaffa province were evaluated for cup quality characteristics. Cup grade accessions like S.2611, §.2618, S.2621, S$.2624, $.2632, S.2636, S.2638, S.2639, S.2642 and S.2677 were ranked from fine to good. These accessions have fruit with long pedicel, early ripening and tolerance to ‘Wet’ conditions of the soil. However, out-turn, grade percentages, yield, the extent of berry drop and tolerance to leaf rust disease varied among the accessions. The possibility of exploiting these qualitative characters of exotic Arabicas into the indigenous hybrids is being explored (Selvakumar and Sreenivasan, 1986).

title: Yield response of some new Arabica coffee selections to Bordeaux spray
text: 9 advanced generations of 5 Arabica selections (4, 5, 6, 7.2 and 8) evolved at Central Coffee Research Institute and private estates were ae studied. Fruit yield recorded for 5 years. One half of each plot was given 2 applications of Bordeaux (0.5%). From the results it may be said that although leaf rust is not a major problem in these selections, dhe profitability of Bordeaux is seen which can be taken advantage in 5 selections out of 9 evaluated, at the existing level of expenditure of spraying. The results also indicate that Bordeaux is not a prerequisite for high yield in at least 2 selections (S. 2499 dwarfs and S.2931) evaluated since they have recorded high yields even without Bordeaux. This finding can therefore be used by growing these selections without Bordeaux (Srinivasan, 1988).

title: Discriminating coffee varieties for early vigour and yield potential in North-East
text: Three year old plants in 8 selections of C. arabica and 6 of C. canephora were studied with reference to 7 morphological characters related to vegetative and reproductive vigour. A comparison of the varieties for percentage increase in growth, maximum increase in case of SIn.6 and old Robusta denoting faster growth rate in 2 varieties. However, the average percentage increase was more in Robusta than Arabica. Out of 8 discriminate functions fitted to the data, the one having 4 characters namely plant height, number of primaries, stem girth and flowers/node was found to give maximum discrimination indicating greater importance and reliability of these characters for selection for improvement of yield in coffee. The selections S.4345, S.4347 (both Cauvery) and $.795 in Arabica and CxR and S.274 were found to be promising based on their high total scores (Srinivasan and Anjana Saikia, 1990).

title: Growth performance of some coffee selections in Andhra Pradesh
text: Four years data on growth and yield of five selections of coffee (SIn. 3, 5, 6, 7 and 8) were subjected to analysis of variance to evaluate their performance at Regional Coffee Research Station, R.V. Nagar, Andhra Pradesh. The’ characters, number of primaries, number of nodes per primary, length of primary, brush spread and plant height show significant variation among the selections. Selection 7 produced maximum number of primaries and number of nodes per primary. Because of its dwarf and compact nature, the plant showed least height, length of primary and bush spread. Of the remaining selections, the order of performance is SIn. 5, 6, 3 and 8 respectively. Stem girth, bush spread, number of nodes per primary and yield per plant showed significant variations among the years during which they were studied (Santa Ram et al., 1992).

title: Performance of 5 Arabica Coffee selections in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu
text: Zone A survey was undertaken to assess the performance of 5 Arabica coffee cultivars viz., S.795, SIn.5, Sln.6, Sln.8, SIn.7 and Sln.9 in different agro-climatic zones of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. The survey showed varied performance of different cultivars in various zones. In Chikkamagaluru zone, S.795, SIn.5 (S.2931) and Sln.9 were the top performers compared to other selections whereas, in Aldur/Mudigere. Sakleshpur/Somwarpet and Coorg zones, SIn.5, 6 and 8 showed better performance. In Pulneys (Tamil Nadu). Sln.5, 6 and 9 were the best performers. In Shevaroys, S.795 and Sln.9 averaged higher than others. Considering the performance overall the zones, SIn.8 and S.795 indicated better yield responses to favorable environment while, Sln.5 showed marginal response. The differential performance of the cultivars is attributed to interaction between their genetic compliments and the environment (Jamsheed Ahmed et al., 1995).

title: Are there wild species of coffee in India
text: The genus Psilanthus is closely related to Coffea and the basic chromosome number, as in most other genera of Rubiaceae, is 11 for both the genera. However, intergeneric hybridization between Coffeaand Psilanthushasbeen unsuccessful so far. Palynological basis for differentiating Coffea and Psilanthus has been established. The pollen grains are 3-colporate in Coffea species, while in Psilanthus species they are 4-5-coloporate (Shetty, 1999).

title: Arabica selection: $.795 its origin and performance
text: With the object of improving the bean size and reducing CT content, S.288 was crossbred with Kents Arabica which is known to have comparatively bigger bean, less CT and less polyembryony but susceptible to leaf disease. One more plant with vigorous growth, resistant to leaf rust and fruits similar to Kents Arabica was selected in 1939 and its self-bred progeny consisting of 48 plants, planted in 1941. This family is S.795. It appears to maintain the vigorous and healthy growth with a profusion of cropping branches under widely ranging conditions of elevation, soil, rainfall and climate. It is definitely more resistant to the common race of leaf disease to which Coorgs and Kents are susceptible. In localities where blackrot is a menace and would very definitely require fungicidal application for effective control. Browneye-spot seems to be particularly severe when the young plants are in a weak state due to various causes. $.795 carries a comparatively heavier crown of leaf, it would require heavier blossom showers for successful blossom. It has a tendency to give abundant crops from the very first cropping yearthird to forth year from planting. In a comparative study with S.288, S.645 and S.446; S.795 leads the other three with its high crop. The CT content in the clean coffee of S.795 is reported to be of a higher order than Coorgs and Kents Arabica. The recorded CT ranges from 8-10% to 40-50% and over. There does not appears to be distinguishable difference in the cup quality of S.795 and it appears to be in no way inferior to that of Coorgs/ Kents Arabica under similar conditions of processing (Narasimhaswamy, 1960).

title: Root system of dwarf and tall plants in San
text: Ramon hybrid The root and shoot system of dwarf and tall types in dwarf x tall hybrids of Coffea arabica (F, of var. San Ramon x S.795) are described. Comparison between the two types indicated that girth of stem and primary branches in dwarf are smaller while that of secondary and tertiary did not differ much. Number of Primary and secondary branches were more in dwarf while tertiaries were more in tall type. Length of internodes in dwarf was smaller while the number of nodes was higher. The above characteristics give the plant type small size and compactness. Root and shoot ratio indicated that the root in dwarf is more for the size of the crown when compared with the tall type. Fresh and dry weights of root in the dwarf were more comparable with those of the tall type and indicated the superiority of the root system in the dwarf type (Vishveshwara and Suryakantha Raju, 1974). a ee ee ee dk ee ee ae

title: Cultivation of San Ramon (dwarf) hybrid coffee
text: San Ramon is a variety of Arabica introduced from Guatemala to India in 1953, San Ramon collection shows dwarfs as well as normal tall type of plants and hence is not a pure dwarf variety. A breeding programme was undertaken at Central Coffee Research Institute to improve the dwarf in this variety for leaf rust and at the same time to exploit the dwarf habit which can accommodate greater plant population per unit area. Three selections viz., 7.1, 7.2 and 7.3 under this have so far been found promising and the seeds of these are being given for cultivation (Srinivasan and Vishveshwara, 1979).

title: Variation in plant height in San Ramon dwarf hybrid (SIn.7.2) of Arabica coffee
text: Dwarf plants of San Ramon hybrid were studied for variation in 4 locations. A wide range of variation in height was observed at each location, which indicated the prominent interplay of genetic and environmental factors controlling this character. Analysis of variance of within location and between locations revealed the greater and significant magnitude of latter in relation to the former indicating the differential growth behaviour ‘of the same variety in different locations, which suggested the better adaptability of this hybrid to some locations (Srinivasan, 1981).

title: Flowering behaviour in San Ramon coffee
text: From the results it is evident that almost all hybrids of San Ramon have inherited the unique flowering character of San Ramon to certain extent, particularly the hybrids Sln.7.3 and San Ramon x Taffarikela. Among these two hybrids, Sln.7.3 is most popular because of certain desirable characters such as uniformity in growth, tolerance to leaf rust disease and drought. The bearing -of old nodes is certainly an added advantage in this hybrid (Raghuramulu et al., 1990). ss COFFEE SELECTIONS

title: Studies on collection
text: Hibrido de Timor coffee HDT has been in cultivation in some areas mostly used for renovation of old Arabica plantations. Variability appears to be very high especially in respect of productivity and bean characteristics. High content of aborted ovules and moka seeds have been recorded. Under nonshaded conditions susceptibility to leaf rust has been recorded. Morphological characters and general observations suggest a preponderance of Arabica phenotype. But some resemblance to Robusta is seen in fruit and seed characters. They are shy bearers. But some 10-11 year old plants are known to have recorded as high as 8 kg ripe cherry. Extent of selfing is highly variable (Vishveshwara and Govindarajan, 1970).

title: Cauvery- A new selection
text: Central Coffee Research Institute has released a new selection for commercial cultivation. This genotype was christened ‘Cauvery’ during 1985. This variety is the result of collaborative research work carried out by Central Coffee Research Institute, India and Coffee Rust Research Centre, Portugal, had higher number of primary branches, exhibited precocious flowering and have remained free from leaf rust so far. 40-82% ‘A’ beans and ‘C’ grade was absent. Spacing 5’x5’ and topping height 3-3.5 feet (Sreenivasan and Ramaiah, 1985).

title: Rooting pattern of Cauvery
text: The results indicated that the semi dwarf variety of Cauvery exhibits an almost identical growth rate of root system to the spread of shoot system. Cauvery is thus ideal plant type with inherent deep root system suited for row inter cropping system of plantation crops without any ee moe i i hiatal nen arm bane root interaction or antagonistic effects between the root system of plantation crops in order to increase the yield (Selvakumar, 1994).

title: Optimum plot size for field trials with
text: Coffea arabica cv. Cauvery Yield data were collected from the Coffee Research Substation during the 1987/88, 1988/89 and 1989/90 seasons for 2 lines of coffee cv. Cauvery; namely S. 4345 and S. 4347. The CV was calculated for plot sizes from 1 to 60 trees, arranged in plots of rows or columns. The Fairfield Smith equation (y= a x xt) and the generalized law (y = a x re! x c®) were fitted to the data for plot size (x), comprising rows (r) and columns (c), CV (y) and heterogeneity coefficient (g). Optimum plot size was determined using the maximum curvature method, graphical representation and minimum experimental cost. There was no consistent trend in row or column CV data, though the heterogeneity in rows tended to be higher than in columns. Hence blocks could be made in either rows or columns. The optimum was 8 plants/row (Srinivasan et al., 1994).

title: Relationship between morphological characters and yield in some Cauvery coffee (Coffea arabica L.)
text: Six F, genotypes of Cauvery-type coffee were evaluated during years 2-6 after planting. Stem girth, bush spread, length of primary nodes and number of bearing nodes were positively correlated with yield (Sadananda and Srinivasan, 1998). ee en EL ae ee aT ee ns Sr 3

title: Studies on polyploids of Coffea
text: The basic chromosome number of the genus Coffea is 11. The effects of ploidy on the organisms are varied. Though gigantism is a common feature in the higher ranges of ploidy, it is however, not a universal phenomenon. Observations recorded indicated the pentaploid and octoploid studied show a higher number of stomata than expected. Individuals in any particular population appear to show variation with regard to number of stomata. The stomatal number in the tetraploid’ plants of cultivar Kents and in S.288 ranges from 133.88 to 188.71/ sq.mm. The size of aperture is not correlated with chromosome number. From the present studies it may be concluded that in general the number of stomata in the leaf decreases from diploid to octoploid in coffee (Achyuta and Vishveshwara, 1960).

title: Occurrence of a haploid in Coffea arabica
text: During December 1959 two branches on the haploid were found with big sized leaves. An experimentation of shoot tip from these showed adjacent cells with 22 and 44 chromosomes. The leaves on these branches are broader, thicker and crinkled. This appears to be a case of spontaneous chromosome doubling and such phenomenon has been recorded in other crops like maize also (Vishveshwara, 1960).

title: A preliminary report on meioticirregularities in diploids and diploid interspecific hybrids in coffee
text: Studies on meiosis in F,, of Coffea excelsa x C. eugenioides and C. liberica x C. eugenioides and the parent plants are presented in the paper. 39 - ens ey Parent plant in C. liberica is highly regular. Plants in F,, show irregularitics such as failure of pairing, unequal distribution of chromosomes chromatin bridges and precocious cytokinesis whereas the parent plants in C. excelsa and C. eugenioides show only chromatin bridges occasionally. The irregularities in F, are considered as the probable cause for the gametic sterility and sterility in fruitset. The formation of chromatin bridges in the parent plants of two diploid species indicate that detailed studies of these and other species-in the genus Coffea are important and may throw more light on the full significance of this phenomenon (Vishveshwara, 1963).

title: Induced auto-tetraploid in Coffea canephora
text: Pierre Ex Froehner The technique employed to induce tetraploidy in the shoot portion of seedlings and the subsequent growth of these gigas characters and flowering showed the success of the colchicine used technique. The colchicine induced auto-tetraploid in Coffea canephora (2n=22) showed the highest association of chromosomes was quadrivalents. Bivalents are considerably more and univalents and trivalents are fewer. Meiotic irregularities are also very few. The sterility of the induced auto-tetraploid is attributed to meiotic, genetic and physiological imbalances. However, self incompatibility is maintained at the tetraploid level as there was no fruit set on selfing (Vishveshwara and Chinnappa, 1965).

title: Embryological studies in Coffea arabica L.
text: Information on fruit development from lower bud initiation in C. arabica (var. Kents and Station Selections, $.288 and S.795) under SouthWest monsoon conditions is presented. Ovary is generally bilocular and each locule may show one or more ovules. Mature ovule is anatropous, subpeltately attached to the middle septum by a short flat funicle, is tenninucellate, unitegmic with a distinct micropyle. title: Effect of maleic hydrazide on meiosis in coffee
text: In the present experiment it is seen that in case of Coffea canephora the divisions started 24 hours after placing the cut twigs in distilled water, while in case of Coffea arabica it was after 46 hours. Different concentrations of Maleic hydrazide have effected delay in the commencement and have also prolonged the duration of meiotic divisions. At higher concentration from 5000 ppm both delay in commencement as well as prolonged duration of meiosis were more prominent. It is interesting to note that Maleic hydrazide at a concentration of 10000 ppm had no adverse effect on the divisions except that the duration was more i.e., 8 hours in Cc. canephora and 10 hours in C. arabica as against the control 4 hours and 5 hours respectively. C. canephora seems to be affected more than C. arabica. From this it is quite evident that the chemicals also act as a meiotic depressors in coffee (Chinnappa, 1968).

title: Observations on the effect of moisture on microsporogenesis in coffee
text: Coffee is known to blossom after pre- blossom rains. Irrigation also induces blossom. However blossom is also induced when twigs with welldeveloped flower-buds are cut and kept in moist chambers. This indicates that surface absorption of adequate moisture induces flower opening. Several factors like plant condition, its foliage, flower bud size, drought and quantity of water are known to influence blossom. In the present study observations on the effect of moisture on meiosis under different atmospheric temperature and humidity conditions are presented. After the receipt of water microsporogenesis leading to pollen formation and megasporogenesis leading to the organization of the embryo-sac are initiated. Atmospheric humidity seems to influence the rapidity of meiotic divisions both in C. arabica as ee CYTOLOGY and C. canephora. The initiation and duration of meiotic divisions are earlier and shorter in C. canephara. Factors affecting the blossom are discussed (Chinnappa, 1969).

title: Octoploidy in Coffea arabica
text: Morphology and cytology of three octoploid forms of Coffea arabica were studied. A comparison of the morphological characters of natural allotetraploids and the derived octoploids indicates that there is a reduction in size from tetraploidy to octoploidy. The inferiority in vegetative vigour and high sterility of the octoploids suggests that the optimum chromosome number has been reached in nature at the tetraploid level. Occurrence of a high frequency of quadrivalents in meiosis of the octoploids presently studied is contrary to the reports of earlier workers where quadrivalents were not observed. The significance of quadrivalent formation is discussed (Chinnappa, 1969).

title: Interspecific hybrids of Coffea canephora and C. liberica
text: Plant morphology and metaphase 1 chromosome association of six hybrids between C. canephora (subsection Erythrocoffea of section Eucoffea) and C. liberica (subsection Pachycoffea of section Eucoffea) are described. Between plants, variation in the expression of parental characters was observed and attributed to heterozygosity especially in the liberica parent. Bivalent frequency was high, but comparable to that of earlier reports. Trivalents and quadrivalents, indicating structural hybridity, were observed here for the first time in such hybrids. In spite of their classification in different subsections and apparent hybridization barrier, the two species have considerable chromosomal homology (Chinnappa, 1970).

title: Meiosis in the pollen mother cells of Coffea eugenioides S. Moore
text: The authors record for the first time the periodicity of microsporogenesis leading to pollen formation immediately following rain in ee oy ELLEN EOE Te oe, CYTOLOGY the diploid species. C. cugenioides (2n=22). It is stated that under South Indian conditions, the flower buds in many species of coffee including the present one under report overcome the drought by remaining dormant before the initiation of microsporogencsis. The different stages of meiosis reported to have been found between 41 and 45 hours following rain. The meiotic behaviour of the chromosomes was normal in the species studied (Narayan and Reddy, 1972).

title: Dormancy break and meiotic division in flower buds of Liberica coffee
text: In C. liberica the mature flower buds of the size of 10-13 mm containing fully formed PMCs remained dormant till they were exposed to rain. Once exposed to rain, meiosis was initiated in the PMCs at 40 and % h after rain and was found to be completed by 48 h. i.e., within 8 and % hours. The tetrads were however found to persist until at least 16 h. after completion of meiosis. Water and possibly temperature have an effective role on dormancy break, initiation and progress of meiosis. The diploid C. liberica 2n=22 formed eleven regular bivalents at diakinesis and at metaphase I. Further the accompanying stages of meiosis were regular giving rise to four daughter nuclei at the end of telophase II. Various phases of meiosis from prediakinesis to tetrad formation are illustrated in the photomicrographs (Reddy and Narayan, 1974).

title: B chromosomes in C. arabica
text: The meiotic behaviour of B chromosomes observed in Arabica is described. 2 B chromosomes were noticed in about 50% of the pollen mother cells and 39% pollen sterility was observed in the plant. This is the first report of the occurrence of such B chromosomes in the genus. It is likely that they are the by-products of structural rearrangements and chromosomal instability associated with hybridity in this tetraploid species (Chinnappa, 1974).

title: Note on 2n-3n incompatibility in Coffea canephora
text: The authors found that diallelic crosses involving clone BR 11 as female parent yielded not only low set compared to its reciprocal crosses but also that the seeds failed to germinate. title: A trisomic Coffea canephora
text: The cytology of a trisomic in C. canephora is reported. The plant has several morphological differences from normal C. canephora. Cytology of the plant indicated the presence of an extra chromosome 2n + 1 = 23 which is a trisomic form. Meiosis was regular in the plant with occasional laggards at anaphase I. Eighty two per cent of the pollen grains were stainable (Sreenivasan, 1980).

In the cross C. dewevrei ‘excelsd X C. eugenioides several maternal types occurred, attributed to parthenogenesis. The hybrids are selfsterile and set few seeds on open pollination, again partly involving parthenogenesis, and participation of some unreduced gametes in hybridization. Subdivision of the section Eucoffea into different subsections (C. dewevrei and C. liberica belonging to subsection, Pachycoffea, C. eugenioides to Erythrocoffea) has no cytological basis (Reddy and Narayan, 1981).

title: Cyto-chemistry of pollen development in
text: Erythrocoffea Developmental characters of anther and male gametophyte in Arabica and Canephora are described and their evolutionary significance is discussed. Cyto-chemical aspects of pollen development are brought out_in detail and their evolutionary and physiological significance is elucidated. A primitive evolutionary status is suggested for these taxa on the basis of this study (Santa Ram et al., 1987).

title: A trisomic Coffea arabica
text: Cytological behaviour and morphological characters ofa trisomic of C..arabica were described. Importance of this trisomic in gene mapping, on the basis of cytological behaviour was indicated. Origin of the trisomic was proposed to be due to the union of a normal gamete and a gamete with extra chromosome derived through non-disjunction of a chromosome pair (Sreenivasan and Santa Ram, 1985).

title: Cyto-chemistry of pollen development in
text: Paracoffea Cyto-chemical aspects of pollen development in a few species of the selection Paracoffea of the genus Coffea L. were out in detail. Anther development in these species confirms to the basic type. Tapetum is secretory. Endothecium completely surrounds the anther locule. Meiosis and simultaneous cytokinesis in the microscope mother cell give rise to tetrahedral, isobilateral and decussate pollen tetrads. Coupled with these primitive ontogenetic features is the presence of starch less pollen in C. travencorensis indicating a relatively advanced evolutionary status of carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids provided a preliminary insight into the developmental physiology of pollen (Santa Ram et al., 1991).

title: Relationship of stomatal length and frequency to ploidy level in coffee
text: There was a positive correlation between stomatal length and ploidy level but expected increase was not observed at triploid and octoploid level and no overlapping occurred among different ploidies. The frequency of stomata could be used as an indirect ploidy indicator. Since stomatal density has been reported to be influenced by environmental factors, consideration of the number of stomatal chloroplasts as an additional parameter is likely to enhance the reliability of the method (Mishra et al., 1991). 4,33. Evaluation of some indicators in Coffea L. indirect ploidy Several indirect ploidy indicators viz., stomatal plastid number, stomatal length, stomatal frequency, leaf area and pollen grain diameter were evaluated for their usefulness in coffee. A positive correlation is observed between the ploidy level and the characters studied except for stomatal frequency, which is negatively correlated. The stomatal plastid number and stomatal frequency were found the most suitable characters as they manifested regular and distinct differences in relation to ploidy level. They can therefore be recommended to screen coffee populations for ploidy at any stage of plant growth (Sreenivasan et al., 1992). i! ec eer aay

Increase in ploidy status was associated with the increase in thickness of lamina, epidermis, palisade tissue, spongy tissue and diameter of spongy cells and the relationship observed is discussed in detail. The study in general supports the common concept of regular correlation between the ploidy status and various characters of the plant including the anatomical ones and could be attributed to the different levels of gene dosage in ploidy variants ’ (Prakash et al., 1993).

title: Cytomorphological studies of two polyploid forms of Coffea arabica L.
text: Cytomorphological features of two spontaneous polyploid plants of Coffea arabica var. Cauvery/Catimor have been studied. Morphologically the plants exhibited reduced phenotype and there were marked differences with respect to stomatal features and pollen characteristics in comparison to their tetraploid counterparts. Meiosis was irregular due to asynaptic behaviour of the constituent genomes resulting in high sterility. The polyploids manifested field resistance to leaf rust disease. The differences observed among the ploidy variants could be attributed to the nature of expressing of genes at different levels of genetic make up (Prakash et al., 1993).

text: The genetical studies in C. arabica L. regarding young leaf colour and ripe pericarp colour showed that the colour of pericarp of ripe fruits appears to be linked with leaf colour: plants with copper and brown leaves have red pericarp; and plants with light green leaves have golden- yellow pericarp. Plants homozygous for copper and light green leaves have been met with; whereas, all the plants with brown leaves appear to be heterozygous. Copper colour of leaves combining with light green colour in the crosses between the two have produced some plants with brown leaves. Segregation in the progeny of plants with (a) copper and, (b) light green leaves into (a) copper and brown classes, and, (b) brown * and light green classes respectively, seems to be not inconsistent with a monohybrid ratio. text: Observations on flower number in relation to final fruit set were made for two years between exotic varieties of Coffea arabica L. In general, all the varieties were capable of producing average to high flower number. The final fruit set was, however, determined by variable weather conditions and physiological factors. After formation of crop initials, fruit drop was more from June to October in all the varieties. S.12 Kaffa and Tafarikela exhibited same tendency for flower production and fruit retention (Thimma and Srinivasan, 1979).

text: 5.1 0. Genetic convergence and divergence among selected cultivars of Arabica coffee (Coffea arabica L.) Genetic relations were studied among seventeen Coffea arabica selections of Indian and exotic origin using Mahalanobi’s D” statistic involving 11 morphological characters. The selection could be grouped into five clusters with cluster I consisting of nine varieties, cluster II with three varieties, cluster III and IV with two varieties each and cluster V with single variety. Divergence between clusters I, II, IV and V were maximum and hence the varieties in these were suggested for hybridization. The characters internodal length, number of nodes and total length of primary, leaf area, fruit volume and weight were found to be more important for distinguishing (Srinivasan and Subbalakshmi, 1984).

title: Quantitative genetics of flower number in coffee
text: Inheritance of flower per node, inflorescence er node and flowers per inflorescence were studied in the cross C. congensis x Robusta based on gencration means. Robusta showed higher values for all 3 characters. Inflorescence per node and flowers per inflorescence were found to be mainly governed by influence of both additive and non-additive gene effects. Reciprocal recurrent selection was suggested for upgrading this important character in coffee (Srinivasan, 1985).

title: Studies on morphology and anatomy of certain abnormal growth in Arabica coffee
text: Considerable variation is noticed with regard to these abnormalities in an affected patch. Shoot growth resumed after blossom showers on such affected twigs showed usually a combination of following features in morphology and anatomy. Growth especially continuing on the short internodal terminals was vigorous, stout and very succulent. When the terminal growth ceased, multiple buds became active or fasciation developed in few cases. Leaves were either extra ordinarily fresh, long and broad or longer than broad or small and brittle. Sometime showed cupping inward. Shape of some of the leaves entirely altered. Yellowing and browning of terminal shoot leaves necrosis and premature defoliation. Internally endocarp and developing endosperm showed discoloration. Vegetative growth produced at the end of the South-West monsoon and till October did not show any high degree of abnormalities. On yellow leaves sporulation was meagre and on green leaves leaf rust sporulation was profuse. Symptoms in morphology and anatomy described earlier became more pronounced on bushes that suffered defoliation/defoliation and die-back. It can perhaps be concluded that functional and physiological disorders play a major role in bringing about these abnormalities (Vishveshwara, 1960).

title: Male sterility in coffee.
text: In some varieties of C. arabica like polysperma and anomala, deviations in floral characters are reported to be associated with certain types of growth and vegetative characters and are said to be controlled by single pair of genes with pleiotropic effects. In the present study however, the data are meagre and it is difficult to estimate the pattern Poa 51 ne anes Were ams - oy of inheritance. Morphological studies showed a gradation in the abnormal type. Here opening ix retarded and at times flowers do not respond even to heavy rains. Extreme cases with petaloid anthers and abnormal pistils show poor set and produce highly abnormal seeds and are therefore, commercially undesirable. Most of the plants with abnormal flowers showed very vigorous growth and comparative freedom from leaf disease in field. Male sterile types have been usefully employed in several crops in hybrid seed production. However, use of male sterility for this purpose requires a thorough knowledge of combining ability and inheritance of. sterile and restorer genes (Vishveshwara, 1967).

title: Aerial roots in Coffea canephora
text: Aerial roots were observed hanging in clusters from the apex of the main stem ina 41- year old C. canephora Pierre, plant in the estate of the Central Coffee Research Institute. These roots were seen at about 136 cm from the ground level where there was no chance of getting either soil or any other favorable medium to induce root formation. This was an unusual phenomenon not recorded so far. Attempts were made to induce rooting at the apex of the main stem and side branches in the same plant at the same height by making injury and then covering the injured portion with soil and moss. Only callus formation was noticed even after four months (Suryakantha Raju, 1972).

title: A mutant for pericarp colour in C. canephora leaf sh
text: The present note records the first case of changes in pericarp colour from fruit set to ripening. The plant with the unusual type of pericarp was noticed at Central Coffee Research Institute. It is similar in all taxonomic characters to C. canephora excepting for pericarp colour. The colour of the developing fruit skin was studied from the pepper stage to fully ripened berry using Munsell colour charts for plant tissue. The colour of the pericarp gradually underwent the following changes: from red red-yellow 3/6 to red 4/6 to red yellow-red 6/6 to yellow 7/4 to yellowish green yellow 7/6 to red 5/10, whereas in normal plants the pericarp colour just changed from green to red. Cytological studies revealed that the plant is diploid (2n=22) (Sreenivasan et al., 1980).

title: Aerial roots in Coffee
text: This phenomenon of occurrence of accessory buds (adventitious buds) changing their potential was noticed in four plants in a plot planted in 1932 to Coffea canephora Pierre ex Froehner, and in one plant of S. 905 (C. arabica Linnaeus cv. Kents x S.274 robusta) at the Central Coffee Research Institute. The roots were seen scattered or in lumps on the main trunk and main branches (Fig. 1). The plants were in healthy condition with normal bearing as others in the same plot. The diameter of the trunk was about 42 cm while that of branches averaged 6.5cm. Some of the roots showed a maximum growth of 3.0 cm. Death of root tip due to necrosis was seen in most of the roots. The fourth plant had innumerable roots, but only at 220 cm from ground level. The high humidity prevailing during monsoon period appears to have favoured such adventitious root formation. This phenomenon is not noticed in pure Arabica coffee and it is possible that there is an inherent tendency in Robusta for such behaviour (Purushotham, 1981).

title: A chlorophyll deficient mutant in coffee
text: The present note deals about a spontaneous bud mutation spotted on one plant on F, of C. congensis x C. canephora. The self sheltered leaves were yellowish green in colour. The flower bud number at the nodes of the mutant sucker was significantly lower than that of the normal branches. The chlorophyll contents of normal, pale yellowish green and white leaves were 1.23, 0.39 and 0.00 mg/g respectively. It is inferred that the mutation is located within the chloroplasts and that the normal plastids are left in the midrib portion of the leaf by a rapid sorting mechanism. Further, the efficiency of this sorting mechanism seems to be restricted to the leaf blade alone since the stem remains green throughout the growth period. Development of pale yellowish green colour in the leaves in shade indicates the light sensitivity of this mutant (Santa Ram and Sreenivasan, 1982).

title: Effect of chemical mutagens of coffee
text: Three mutagenic chemicals viz., Diehtyl sulphate (DES), Dimethyl sulphate (DMS) and Ethyl methane sulphonate (EMS) were tried on coffee using 3 cultivars in C. arabica and one in C. canephora. Concentrations used were 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5% aqueous solution on dormant and activated seeds for 24, 28 and 72 hours duration. In all the treatments, percentage of seed germination was reduced and abnormalities in growth of seedlings were noticed. The chemical action was severe on activated seeds. In C. canephora seedling a % 6 Te ony abnormalities were not noticed but percentage germination was reduced. All the varieties had shown good response to mutagenic chemicals. Increased duration of treatment reduced the fermination percentage in many cases. The favorable concentration of chemical appeared to be at 50% L.D. (Sreenivasan and Vishveshwara, 1982).

title: Acrial roots in C. arabica
text: Acrial roots were observed on the main stem of a 48 year old C. arabica cv. Kents. This is an unusual phenomenon in Arabica not recorded so far. The roots were seen at about 96 cm above the ground level. Maximum length was 2.5 cm. Root tips were dry due to the temperature. The high humidity prevailing during the monsoon appeared favorable for formation of such adventitious roots. The accessory buds can alter their potentiality in Arabica in some environments (Zwingly Premkumar, 1982).

title: Abnormal flowering in Robusta
text: The phenomenon of conversion of accessory buds to flower buds on the trunk of Robusta was noticed which was planted in 1932. Coffee. berries were noticed on this 50 year old trunk and on branches. A few fruits were on the knots and many were on the branches. This plant had -a few inflorescence also on the trunk and these were made open by irrigation. Fruit set found to be normal, followed by uniform ripening but all were pea berries. As this plant was able to bear on the old wood for last few years consecutively, the conversion of buds may not be due to environmental change as opined by Harrer (1962) as in Arabica plants (Purushotham and Sreenivasan, 1983).

title: Mechanism of male sterility in some species of Coffea
text: Cytochemical and developmental mechanisms involved in the expression of male sterility in 4 species of genus Coffea viz, C congensis, C. liberica, C. kapakata and C. khasiana were studied and compared with the normal development. It was found that the supply of basic nutrients suchas proteinsand lipids to the generativé tissue was hampered at early developmental stag over production of primaries is possible by - mnen anor rarrntnra or wewee (sporogenous cells and pollen mother cell stages) in the male sterile matcrials of C. congensis and sterile anthers of C. libcrica. Suppression of androecium was resulting in male sterility in C. kapakata and C. liberica. Insome plants of C. libcrica a differentiation of generative tissuc was the cause of male-sterility. Tapetal hypertrophy leading to the breakdown of sporogenous tissue and resulting in male sterility was found in C. congensis and C. liberica. In the anthers C. khasiana the tapetal differentiation would not take place leading to the degeneration of sporogenous tissuc and manifestation of male sterility. title: A flower mutant in C. canephora
text: The characters were observed on a whole plant and in a particular branch on another plant. These plants can be grown for ornamental purpose as blossom looks attractive and lasts over a month. Some of these mutations are coded by the chloroplastic genome. Chloroplast pigmentation inheritance cannot be determined where the mutant plants are sterile (Sreenivasan et al., 1987).

title: Petaloidy - A floral abnormality in Arabica coffee
text: Flower abnormalities such as star flowering occurring due to some external and internal factors are found to effect the normal fruit set and thereby reduce the yields. Some plants in older selections of Arabica were found to show the incidence of petaloidy in which the stamen is transferred into petal like structures. Fruit set and retention was found to be quite low under this condition. In the present article, the distinct morphological features of petaloid flowers are described and their influence on fruit set and retention is reported. From the results it could be seen that petaloidy would greatly affect the coffee yields. Normal vegetative growth is seen in these plants. Possible conclusion seems to be these plants may be genetically predisposed to this abnormality (Raghuramulu and Sreenivasan, 1988).

title: Comparative study of the natural and induced purpurascence mutants in Coffea arabica
text: The expression of colour in young and matured le aves was found to be uniform incase of induced mutants compared to natural ones and the light intensity had no notable impact on the expression of leaf colour. From the results it can be inferred that the spectrum of genetic change in induced mutants is slightly differing from that of natural mutants resulting in more stability and uniformity in expression of the mutant characters. Hence, although the present induced mutant is of no utility in coffee improvement it gives clear evidence that the approach for induction of variability in coffee especially in self compatible Arabicas was correct and encouraging to induce variability for rust resistance for Cattura type of mutants (Prakash et al., 1990).

text: Coffea The pollen morphology of 38 representative species and varieties with in the genus Coffea L. (Rubiaceac) are described. title: Influence of certain chemicals on coffee pollen
text: Pollen studies were carried out in vitro using the solutions of Thiourea, 2,4-D, NAA, Planofix and Plantvax as media at three concentrations. Pollen tube growth of S.274 was at maximum in Thiourea while NAA increased the same in bulk Robusta. Medium and low concentrations of chemicals recorded maximum germination of pollen in S.274 and bulk Robusta respectively. In general Thiourea at 0.01% gave the maximum percentage of germination both in S.274 and bulk Robusta and the tube growth was also enhanced by the same treatment in S.274 (Zwingly Premkumar et al., 1981).
