title: Indian coffee (Coffea arabica L.) cultivars and their adaptive significance
text: Leaf architecture including venation pattern was studied in ten different Indian arabica (Coffea arabica L.) cultivars. The leaf size, areole size, number of vein endings entering the areole and vein islets termination number showed variation in different cultivars and is attributed to their origin involving different parents and selection pressure. The adaptive significance of leaf architecture is discussed. The study further indicated that the cultivars, Sln.7.3, SIn.9, SIn.11 and Sin.5 have inherent structural advantage over other arabica cultivars to cope with the water distribution during stress conditions (Mishra et al., 2010).

title: Evaluation of coffee varieties derived from diverse genetic sources of resistance for prospective exploitation - An International cooperative effort
text: Coffee leaf rust (CLR) caused by the obligate parasitic fungus Hemileia vastatrix Berk & Br. and Coffee berry disease (CBD) caused by Colletotrichum kahawe are the two most important diseases of coffee (Coffea arabica L.) causing considerable economic damage. In order to address the problem of CLR and CBD, there is an urgent need to focus research efforts on searching for new sources of resistance, exploitation of the available genetic resources for development of new varieties and to provide resistant and resilient coffee cultivars to farmers. It is imperative to test the potential varieties under realistic conditions to assess their performance (Prakash et al., 2010).

title: Morphological proportions for detection of genetic inheritance in F, progenies of arabica (Coffea arabica L.)
text: Plant architecture is composed of several morphological components combined in a certain proportion to produce the phenotype of the particular species. Consequent to the breeding protocols, this proportion changes from one generation to the other and the offspring possess a new proportion dissimilar to their parents. To identify the genetic traits transmitted by the parents, an attempt was made to measure the morphological ratios between the various components of the F, progenies of dwarf and tall coffee cultivars. The ratios between the changeable characters and within non-changeable characters were separately calculated in the hybrids and the parents and compared (Anil Kumar et al., 2012). 7.11 Screening of Coffea arabica germplasm for Caffeine level A total of 76 collections of coffee bean (Coffea arabica) are being maintained in the germplasm bank at Coffee Research Sub Station in North Kodagu, Karnataka, India. Following evaluation of caffeine level in 34 collections, a wide variability ranging from 1.18% (Misan Taferikala) to 2.07% (Sumatra) with an overall mean value of 1.84%, was observed (Gopinandhan et al., 2015).

title: Assessment of Genetic Divergence for Bean

title: Investigations on propagation of coffee the vegetative
text: Earlier work has given indications of the usefulness of cow’s urine extract in promoting rooting of cuttings. Later on studies favouring rooting of coffee sucker cuttings stressed the importance of adequate reserves of food material in the cuttings or their supply followed by treatment with B-Indolyl butyric acid for optimum results. Propagation studies with Arabica sucker cuttings showed that treating cuttings in lower concentration of Gibberellic acid for a period of 3 minutes resulted in better rooting and production of thin, well spread primary roots and profuse branching. Hardier cuttings required a relatively higher concentration of the chemical (Kuppu Swami, 1958).

title: An unusual phenomenon Noticed vegetative propagation in coffee
text: Fifty percent of the semi-hard ang hard wood cuttings in Robusta showed unusual formation of suckers from the top cut surface e the internode in addition to those, which sprout in the axil of the leaves. These 5 uckers Tanged from 3-10, were small in size and crowded. The differentiated from the meristematic activity of tk. cambium at the cut surface of internode. These cuttings however have not rooted even after three months from planting. This phenomenon of sucker formation from the cut surface in the internodal region is unusual and does not seem to have been recorded in coffee as seen from available literature (Vishveshwara, 1968).

A study on Robusta propagation: Clone vs. seedling Seventeen Robusta selections tested in two clonal progeny trials and 12 in seedling progeny trial were evaluated for their relative variation for yield and mean yields based on 8 years data. Clonal progeny trials had lower levels of variations for individual plant yield than seedling progeny trial and the variation was further reduced when plots of three plants available in the clonal progeny trails considered. Mean yield of the clones was in general higher than that of seedling progenies. Crossing between specific mother plants based on their mean performance in these trails is suggested (Srinivasan and Vishveshwara, 1980). Clonal versus seedling performance in Robusta coffee: An evaluation of morphological characters related to yield 8.1.5. Seventeen clonal and 12 seedling progenies in Robusta coffee (Coffea canephora) were evaluated for five morphological characters related to yield. Clonal progenies showed higher means and lower coefficients of variation compared to seedling progenies for most of the characters. Number of primaries was the most variable character in both kinds of progenies. Heritability estimates were higher in clonal trial I compared to clonal trial II and seedling trial for all the characters, presumably because of the better stand of plants in this trial. Mean yield per se showed higher heritability than any of the characters studied. Stem girth, mean diameter of primaries and bush radius were significantly correlated with mean yield of progénies. Path analysis revealed that stem girth and mean diameter of primaries and leaf size exerted high direct effects on mean yield (Subbalakshmi et al., 1981).

title: Vegetative propagation as practiced in certain other countries
text: The paper gives an account of vegetative propagation that is practiced in Togo and Ivory Coast where it is undertaken mainly for distribution of clonal planting material for use by the growers. The superior stock clones maintained under daybook system of planting. While the planters are provided with rooted cuttings, they in turn have to bring filled poly bags to take delivery of the rooted material. However in India such an extensive vegetative propagation is not taking place to establish Robusta plantations (Sreenivasan, 1985).

title: Studies on rooting ability of Cauvery cuttings
text: The rooting response of coffec stem cuttings to the basal treatment involving Sucrose + IBA and also to the foliar dip treatment in IBA solution is tried. From the results, it is apparent the addition of 5% sucrose to the usual dose of IBA 5000 ppm for basal treatment; or a foliar dip treatment with IBA 7000 ppm alone have given better results. Commercial sugar may also be tried in place of sucrose for more practical purposes (Anuradha and Sreenivasan, 1993).

title: Response of different growth regulators on rooting of mallet cuttings in coffee
text: A study on rooting ability of mallet cuttings with different growth regulators viz., IBA, Planofix, Alar at varying concentrations (1000, 2000, 3000 and 4000 ppm) was conducted. Result showed 90% rooting in IBA, 80% in Planofix and 70% in Alar at 100 ppm concentration level. Highest number of primary and secondary roots were obtained with lowest concentration of IBA (1000 ppm). Control cuttings showed lowest rooting of 30% (Anil Kumar and Srinivasan, 1993).

title: Factors favouring rooting of coffee sucker cutlings
text: The results of the trial have proved that three substances, Auxins, Carbohydrate and Nitrate in combination are capable of inducing greater root production and earliness in rooting. Deficiency of one or more of these would appear to have been the cause for the varying success obtained in rooting in the earlier trials. Standing the basal ends of the cuttings first in a mixture of 0.2% Ammonium nitrate and 3% Dextrose for 12 hours and then in a solution of B-Indolyl acetic acid at 100g/L for a similar period gave the best results. Response of the more woody fourth internode was comparatively less. Hence it is desirable to collect sucker growths when four internodes are formed, as many further growth is bound to produce in the lowest internode refractory material not suited for quick vegetative propagation (Sundaram, 1953).

title: Root suckers in coffee
text: Occurrence of typical cases of suckers from roots in Coffea canephora, Coffea excelsa and Coffea liberica have been noticed in Central Coffee Research Institute and on some private estates. Canephora, excelsa and liberica generally showed typical orthotropic types of suckers all along the thick roots and horizontal or gourmondizer type at the cut end of the root either exposed or submerged in soil. While horizontal or gourmondizer type of suckers were observed all along the thick roots in a few plants in canephora collection s from Ceylon (CCRI No. 240). Orthotropic suckers showed vigorous growth. They formed secondary and tertiary branches with flowers and fruits similar to water sprouts. Formation of new roots was seen at the point of sucker sprouting in case of canephora and excelsa. The horizontal suckers in canephora (CCRI 240) were less vigour and were more than one per point (Suryakantha Raju, 1971).

title: Rooting of sucker cuttings in coffee rooting experiments on the basis of starch reserve
text: Statistical analysis showed a__ positive correlation (r = +0.23580 between starch status In cuttings and rooting percentage. In Coffea arabica there is a negative correlation (o = -0.01 18) between starch status and rooting percentage (statistically not significant at 5% level). No marked difference in rooting percentage between ringed and nonringed cuttings was observed in both the species (Suryakantha Raju, 1972).

title: Rooting of root suckers in indigenous species of coffee
text: Occurrence of plageotropic and orthotropic root suckers was observed on the exposed/ submerged primary and lateral roots of the mother plant of C. canephora, C. excelsa and C. liberica. Rooting of root suckers of the three species was studied. The data revealed that rooting of root suckers in all the three species was very high and in the order of 72-100%. The primary, lateral and feeder roots were also in greater number (Shivaram and Ramachandran, 1982).

title: Rapid multiplication of suckers in vegetative propagation of coffee
text: Forty, one year old C. canephora seedlings were cut at their internodal region about 20-30 cm from the base of the plant. RH was maintained between 90 and 100%. The sprouting of suckers from the internodal cut surface was noticed in 50% of the plants after three months. These sprouts were allowed to grow for two more months under same conditions. They were then severed and planted in sand medium. Rooting was observed in 76% of the suckers two months after planting. The average number of primary roots/cutting was 2.8. Meristematic activity of the cambium initiated at the internodal cut surface is capable of differentiating into a shoot comparable to the main suckers. This potentially unlimited system of proliferation of such multiple shoots in turn can develop into individual plants (Shivaram and Vishveshwara, 1982). Ty

title: Studies on the rooting of invigorated sucker cuttings of coffee
text: Studies on the rooting capacity of invigorated sucker cuttings of $.274 carried out indicated the superiority of invigorated shoots in rooting. Plants beheaded at 0-45 cm from ground level produced sucker which recorded 90.37% rooting. Besides, planting of cuttings during August obtained from plants beheaded during April recorded highest percentage (71.47%) of success. ‘The rooting capacity of invigorated shoots was attributed to high content of sugars, auxins and rooting cofactors present in the shoot (Purushotham and Sulladmath, 1985).

title: Propagation of Robusta coffee through sucker slips
text: When single nodal cuttings are vertically divided into two equal parts, these could give rise to sucker slips. To find out the rooting ability of sucker slips under Indian climatic conditions this study was taken up. A rooting success of 73% with an average number of 2.2 primary roots and 39.1 secondary roots was recorded. Slow shoot growth on the rooted slips was observed. But the shoots were stick and sturdy with short internodes. This method offers the possibilities of producing more number of true to type plants from a limited source of high performing superior clones of Robusta (Anil Kumar, 1994).

title: Propagation of coffee by sucker cuttings
text: Experimental results indicated that planting of cuttings during rainy season (June-Aug) gives a good percentage of success (above 95%) in rooting (Anonymous, 1997).

title: Rejuvenation of old coffee with newe selections by cleft grafting A preliminary report
text: Unproductive and moribund coffee, either of Arabica or Robusta could be rejuvenated into newer lines like Cauvery and CxR hybrids by adopting wedge-cleft method of grafting. Uniformity of the population is achieved by this method. Grafting advances blossom and bearing. Cauvery on old Robusta produced better shoot growth than that on San Ramon. The stock scion establishment was highest in Cauvery/San Ramon and it was 88% in CxR on old Robusta. The wood of both the stoa and scion should be in the unlignified cota The graft union was completed in 60 days in he, bow Robusta, 50 days in Cauvery/San Ramon and it was 60-80 days in Cauvery/Robusta. Whe cost worked out to be only Rs.60/- per 100 grafts i.c., 60 praise/graft. By conversion bean quality of Arabica fetches higher points besides overall market price. By conversion to CxR, compactness of the bush with percentage ‘A’ grade beans is enhanced (Ramachandran ct al., 1993).

title: Top working of C. canephora cv. §.274 with
text: C. arabica cv. Cauvery 72% of the scions survived of the 100 plants grafted. The graft union was completed in 45-60 days. The Cauvery scion began to yield in the very next cropping season with profuse flowering and set. The scions of Cauvery maintained usual genetic differences in time of flowering on the tenth day after rains save one scion, which coincide with Robusta on the eighth day. Grafting was effective during the month of July. Thus, top-working of old Robusta was successfully carried out thus both Robusta as well as Arabica crops can be harvested from same plant (Ramachandran et al., 1993).

title: Preference of growth regulators on graft union success in coffee
text: A field trial to investigate the role of growth regulators on the early union of grafts in coffee was laid out in two locations viz., Regional Coffee Research Station, Chundale and Cherunchal estate in Wayanad. The results have revealed that treating the cut end of the scions in different concentrations of plant growth regulators have no significant effect on early graft union. Under normal circumstances the union of stock-scion takes place in 45 days time, but the treatments have not hastened the union as per the observations made in the trial (Suresh Kumar et al., 1996).

title: Influence of canopy retention on suckers, success and growth of grafts in coffee
text: An investigation was carried out during 1993-94 to study the influence of canopy retention on success of grafting and growth of grafts in the rejuvenation of undesirable Robusta coffee. Results VEGETATIVE PROPAGATION revealed that collar pruning of plants in the early summer would lead to mortality of stump up to 17%. The success of grafting was not influenced by the amount of canopy retained at the time of grafting. Growth of grafts on stumps with 50% of canopy retained was on par with those on collar pruned stumps. The grafts on plants with full canopy had desirable growth characteristics like long internodes and poor stem girth. Thus it is observed that p artial canopy retention while grafting coffee helps in reducing the mortality, enhance sucker production and successful graft union (Suresh Kumar et al., 1998).

title: Grafting and its practical utility in coffee plantations
text: Grafting is an art of inserting a part of one plant into another in such a way that both will fuse together and continue their growth and yield satisfactorily. As per records available on grafting in coffee, the graft combination of CxR, Catimor, SIn.6, SIn.8 and SlIn.9 scions on Robusta and San Ramon root stocks were found most promising to get higher early yields. A maiden crop of 200 to 500 g of ripe fruit is harvested after 18 months of grafting. An yield of 5-15 Kg of ripe fruit per plant can be obtained after 28-30 months after grafting on a Robusta stock aged 15-20 years with Arabica or CxR scion (Anil Kumar and Srinivasan, 1999).

title: Rejuvenating coffee by grafting
text: Studies made on the effect of grafting to rejuvenate the coffee in the Wayanad coffee tracts is discussed in this paper. The investigations revealed that (1) grafted plants start to bear from the second year (2) treatment with hormones does not improve the graft take. Further it is also found that collar pruning results in the mortality (17%) of stumps. Partial retention of canopy helps to minimize the crop loss as well as mortality of the stumps. title: Bamboo cages for temporary shade hutting of coffee in North East region
text: A type of cage prepared out of bamboo are being tried. This is an inverted version of the khang or bamboo basket used locally. These cages are dipped in 1% Copper sulphate solution to prevent fungus attack. The cages are placed on coffee plants in the field. Coffee plants covered with khangs are found to grow faster compared to control. Weed growth under the khang is also checked and grass mulch applied round the coffee plant after weeding is retained in place much better compared to control. The cages are expected to last at least for two seasons (Srinivasan et al., 1987).

title: Successful establishment of Dadaps in coffee clearings
text: The Dadap branches are to be ringed at their bases, about a month prior to the proposed planting time. It is recommended that on the top cut end of the stakes a cap ofsome cattle dung mixed with urine is put on and covered with leaves or waxed paper. To minimize the bad effect of sun scorching, white washing is the best method. Retaining suckers all along the stem for 1 or 2 years will ensure a proper flow of sap even on the side of stem exposed to Western sun and there by minimize the scorching effect. If the stakes are planted in slant manner, the upper side of the stakes exposed to mid-day sun, resulting in more severe injury. The cuttings were 1 to 1.5 inches in diameter, 8 feet in length and 1.5 feet being underground (Pattabhiraman, 1953).

title: Propagation of Bischofia javanica by cuttings
text: Cuttings collected from collar pruned tree, rooted better than that of girdled tree. Rooting percentage was further enhanced by treating with IBA 500 ppm. Cuttings treated with IBA produced more number of sprouts and leaves (Zwingly Premkumar and Purushotham, 1982).

title: Root spread of Ficus retusa
text: The network of root growth was observed on Robusta planted in the vicinity of the shade tree for a distance of 19.5 m from trunk. Root spread was up to a plant height of 1778.8 cm from ground level. Length of these roots varied from 132 to 300cm. ‘The girth of this tree was >350 cm. The congenial atmosphere prevailed in this plot might have enhanced the root spread of Ficus retusa (Sreenivasan and Purushotham, 1983).

title: Boosting the growth of Dadap by using shorter stakes
text: The best results were obtained by planting shorter Dadap stakes, drenching the soil with dilute solution of Hormonal and applying about 25g of Superphosphate after the Dadap stakes have sprouted well after establishing a good root system. Probably the Phosphorus and Calcium in Superphosphate is responsible for boosting the vegetative growth and also for better development of root system (Vasudeva, 1984).

title: Embryo culture of three interspecific crosses in coffee
text: Immature embryos _ resulting from three interspecific crosses involving Coffea canephora cv. Robusta (selection no.274) as the common female parent and three indigenous wild species, C. travencorensis, C. bengalensis and C. wightiana as different make parents were cultured on modified MS medium. Both direct and indirect pathways regenerated plants. In the former pathway, the embryos matured and germinated directly into single plantlets. In the latter pathway, many plantlets were regenerated from single hybrid embryos, through callous and subsequent somatic embryogenesis (embryoidogenesis). Many hybrid plantlets rescued by the above methods are established in the soil and are being evaluated. These studies were taken up with a view to combining the agronomic properties of C. canephora with some useful characters of the wild species, especially the low caffeine content (Sreenath et al., 1992).

title: Somaticembryogenesisand plantregeneray: from cultured immature zygotic embryos of
text: Coffea canephora Pierre Direct somatic embryogenesis was obtaineg ; cultured embryos in a cultivar of Coffea canephoy, (Robusta). In this cultivar, somatic embryoids ws formed directly on cultured zygotic embryos oan or no callus when cultured on half strength Ms medium supplemented with 0.1 mg/L of IAA ang 0.1 mg/ L of 2 iP. The direct somatic embryos were formed by one of the following two ways. In the first somatic embryos are formed on ungerminated zygotic embryos, and in the second the zygotic embryos first germinated into 1 to 2 cm long individual plantlets and then the somatic embryos were formed on these plantlets. In both the cases the embryoids were formed on the hypocotyl or cotyledonary leaves of the zygotic embryos or zygotic embryo-derived plantlets. Initially the direct somatic embryos formed were few in number (low frequency embryogenesis) with little or no callus. However, within increasing number of passages in sub culture, proliferation of the embryoids continued and after a few sub cultures resulted in high frequency embryogenesis. The somatic embryos thus obtained were germinal into plantlets on half strength MS medium with 0.1mg/L of BAAP. Significance of the results are discussed (Muniswamy et al., 1993). es OS ee ee SS ee er ee g. Plant Regeneration through high frequency eomatic embryogenesis from leaf tissues in gvo cultivars of coffee Planilets were regenerated through high frequency somatic embryogenesis in two coffee cultivars viz. §.2790 (Coffea arabica) and BR11 (Cc. canephora) from the leaf tissues. In all the experiments, MS agar medium supplemented with L-Cystein HCl (50 mg/l) and 3% sucrose was used, which was modified in various ways for experimentation. The calli were subcultured at 45-60 days interval to fresh medium of same or different composition. In §.2790, calli were induced from the leaf explants on MS medium supplemented with Kn (5 mg/l) and 2,4-D (1 mg/l). After 22 weeks of culture with 3 subcultures, the calli turned embryogenic on the medium of same composition. In BR-11, the calli were induced from the leaf explants on MS medium containing gamborg's-b-5 vitamins but supplemented with the same growth regulators as stated above. Calli were subcultured on the medium of same composition and after 18 weeks they were transferred to MS medium with 2 iP (2-5 mg/l) and 2, 4-D (0.2 mg/l). In this clone, the calli turned embryogenic after 9 weeks of culture on this medium. In both the cultivars, further proliferation of the embryogenic calli as well as maturation of the somatic embryos (embryoids) were obtained by culturing for 6 weeks on MS medium supplemented with IAA (0.1 mg/l) and BAP (0.1 mg/1). Germination of embryoids into plantlets was achieved on half strength MS medium with 0.1 mg/1 kn. Differences were observed between the two cultivars in respect of multiplication rate, maturation and germination of somatic embryos into plantlets. The frequency of embryogenesis and multiplication as well as germination of embryoids into plantlets was substantially higher in BR-11 as compared to S.2790 (Harinath et al., 1993).

title: Comparative efficacy of four disinfectants for
text: raising aseptic leaf cultures of coffee (Coffea canephora Pierre ex. Froehner) Efficacy of four sterilants viz., Benzylkonium Ciloride, = Calcium ~~ Hypochlorite, Sodium Hypochlorite and Mercuric Chloride for surface sterilization of BR-10 (Coffea canephora) \eaf explants was evaluated by monitoring microbial contamination, browning and callus induction. It was found that the three parameters varied from sterilant to. sterilant, depending on the concentration as well as duration of treatment. Mercuric Chloride and Sodium Hypochlorite were effective in eliminating microbial contamination without affecting callus proliferation within a specific range of concentrations and duration of treatment. In the cultured leaf explants, only fungal contamination was noticed and there was no bacterial contamination (Madhava et al., 1993).

title: Hardening of in vitro raised plantlets
text: This note reports the simple procedure for hardening the plantlets of $.274 raised from stem culture through somatic embryogenesis. The experiment clearly indicated the importance of high humidity in hardening of coffee plantlets. Hence beaker covering was adopted. By adopting the procedure described here, around 90% of in vitro plantlets could be successfully hardened. Two points are important for good survival. 1. The in vitro plantlets should have reached the right stage with good root and shoot system. Provision for high humidity and low temperature and light intensity during the first 2-3 months of exvitro stage (Muniswamy et al., 1994).

title: Somatic embryogenesis from integument culture of coffee
text: Somatic embryogenesis was induced in the integument (perisperm) cultures of CxR hybrid cultivar of coffee after a culture period of 15 months using a sequence of three different modifications of MS medium. Vigorously growing white, soft, crystalline calli were obtained on MS+TIBA (1 mg/1). After 45 days, the calli were subcultured EEE A eS aN PIRkUE CULTU to MS 4 IAA (0.5 mg/1) 4 2,4-1) (0.05 mg/1) + kn (8.6 mp/)) and maintained for the next 9 months without any transfer. On this medium, the callus proliferation slowed down after 5-6 months and then the calli turned light brown and compact. Later the calli were subcultured to MS + 2,4-D (0.2 mg/1) + 2iP (2.5 mg/1) and after 2 months the calli turned darker, more compact and the proliferation almost stopped. This calli were subcultured once again on to the medium of same composition. After another 2 months of culture a cream coloured friable embryogenic callus appeared, which in turn produced clearly identifiable somatic embroys (SEs) in another 1 month. Further proliferation and maturation of SEs was achieved by culturing the embryogenic calli on MS + ABA (1 mg/1) (Sreenath et al., 1995).

title: Effect of Tyrosine, Abscissic acid and
text: Ethephon Experiments were conducted on callus induction in integument tissues of C. canephora. The results revealed that vigorous callus proliferation occurs in the integument tissue on basal medium without any growth regulators, indicating that this tissue produces sufficient quantities of endogenous growth regulators required for callus. proliferation. Tyrosine increased the activity of IAA oxidase in tissue culture. Low concentration of Ethephon stimulated embryo formation and higher levels were inhibitory in orange cultures. Somatic embryogenesis can be achieved from these tissues using growth inhibitors like TIBA. The integument tissue of coffee has high callusing ability and phytohormone autotrophy. This tissue can be used for basic studies on cell proliferation and regeneration (Madhava, 1995).

title: High frequency somatic embryogenesis from cultured leaf explants of Coffea canephora on a single medium
text: High frequency of somatic embryogenesis from cultured leaf explants of C. canephora on 2 single medium has been reported. The protocol has been discussed (Muniswamy and Sreenath, 1995).

title: Haploidy in Coffee
text: Various aspects of haploidy in coffee such as significance of haploids in coffee improvement programmes, frequency of occurrence of natural haploids among the coffee species, morphological and anatomical features and leaf rust tolerance of (di) haploids of Arabica, are dealt with. In vivo and in vitro approaches for production of haploids in coffee and the progress achieved in the coffee anther culture are also discussed (Raghuramulu and Prakash, 1995).

title: Somatic embryogenesis from cultured zygotic embryos of Coffea bengalensis
text: Coffea bengalensis is a wild indigenous species. It is wide spread and more adaptable to varied soil and climatic conditions and is characterized by low caffeine content or no caffeine. This note deals with the somatic embryo genesis and plant regeneration from the cultured zygotic embryos of C. bengalensis. In the present study, somatic embryogenesis and plant regeneration is achieved from the zygotic embryos of C. bengalensis. This will be useful for producing aseptic plants which in turn can be used in advanced studies like somatic hybridization for transferring the useful characters into commercial cultivars. This is the first report of inducing somatic embryogenesis and plant regeneration from cultured zygotic embryos of C. bengalensis (Muniswamy and Sreenath, 1996).

title: Effect of Kanamycin on callus induction and somatic embryogenesis in cultured leaf tissues of Coffea canephora Pierre (Robusta)
text: The effect of kanamycin at 0, 50, 100 and 400 mg/l in MS medium supplemented with NAA (0.1 mg/l) + BAP (1 mg/l) + L-cysteine HCl (50 mg/l) + sucrose (3%) on callus proliferation and somatic embryogenesis was studied using aseptic leaf tissues of Coffea canephora. Proliferation of callus subsequent embryogenesis was observed in a nearly all the explants cultured on kanamycin free medium. Callus development was reduced at 50 mg/l of kanamycin, while the callus induction was almost completely suppressed at 100 mg/I and higher concentrations. The results elucidated the sensitivity of coffee leaf tissues to kanamycin. As kanamycin resistance is widely used as a selectable marker in genetic transformation studies in plants, the possible utility of the present results in coffee transformation studies indicated (Muniswamy and Sreenath, 1996).

title: Callus proliferation from cultured roots in coffee (Brief Note)
text: The cotyledonary stage zygotic embryos were cultured initially on MS medium supplemented with ABA (1 mg/1) for 30 days for embryo maturation. The mature zygotic embryos of Coffee arabica cv. San Ramon and Cauvery (S.4348), C. bengalensis and C. canephora (S.274) were germinated by culturing on half strength MS medium (Murashige and Skoog, 1962) supplemented with 0.1 mg/1 of Kn. Roots from these aseptic plantlets were excised and cut into pieces of about 5-6 mm long and cultured on MS medium with NAA (1 mg/1), Kn (5 mg/1) and 3% sucrose. The pH of the medium was adjusted between 5.6 and 5.8 and solidified by adding 0.7% of bacteriological agar. The medium was sterilised at 121°C for 20 minutes and cultures were incubated at room temperature. All the four materials tested showed varying degrees of callusing response on MS medium with NAA and Kn. All the callused explants produced roots ranging from 1.4 to 2.6 cm in length (Muniswamy et al., 1996)

title: Effect of TIBA and BAP on Integument
text: Cultures of C x R cultivar of robusta coffee (Coffea canephora) Micropylar and chalazal sections ofintegument of CxR cultivar of Robusta coffee (Coffea canephora) were cultured on MS medium supplemented with different concentrations of TIBA and BAP (up to 10 mg/1) individually and in combinations. Microbial contamination was very low. The response was dependent on the maturity of the tissue as well as concentrations of TIBA and BAP. On the basal medium itself (without any growth regulator) vigorous callus proliferation was obtained in both micropylar and chalazal sections. Lower levels of TIBA appeared to promote callus proliferation, especially when young integument tissues were cultured. When the medium was supplemented with higher levels of TIBA and BAP (10 mg/1) callus proliferation was reduced substantially. When both TIBA and BAP were supplemented in the medium, there was progressive decrease in proliferation of the callus with the increasing concentrations of one or both of these growth regulators. Integument tissue of coffee with its aseptic nature, high, callusing ability and phytohormone autotrophy could be an excellent system for basic studies in cell proliferation and regeneration in addition to its physiological role (Harinath et al., 1997).

title: Biotechnology approaches for coffee improvement
text: The author while narrating biotechnology as a powerful tool, describes micro-propagation, anther culture, embryo rescue, somaclonal variation and cell line selection and protoplast fusion as various approaches for coffee improvement (Sreenath, 1998).

title: Tissue culture studies in coffee and _ its applications
text: In coffee, overall success in the tissue culture studies is quite encouraging. Plants are successfully produced from different tissues like embryo, anther, endosperm, stem and leaf. Tissue culture helps to overcome the limitations of the conventional breeding techniques. Several tissue culture methods can be extremely valuable in the improvement programme like disease resistance. Integration of these technologies will also reduce the time for varietal development and preserve haterozygosity and plasticity in coffee plantations (Muniswamy and Sreenath, 1999).

title: Direct shoot induction from cultured root explants of Coffea arabica
text: The procedure of obtaining direct shoot induction from cultured root explants of Coffea arabica is presented. Root explants were selected from aseptic plantlets regenerated from leaf tissue through callus and subsequent somatic embryogenesis. The root explants were cultured on MS (Murashige and Skoog) medium supplemented with 3% sucrose and different concentrations of NAA, 2,4-D, kinetin and BAP (benzyl adenine). All combinations produced callus but only halfstrength MS + 0.1 mg/l kinetin produced direct adventitious shoot buds after 4-5 weeks of culture. Multiple shoots were isolated from original root explants and cultured on MS + BAP (1 mg/litre) + kinetin (1 mg/litre). The shoots grew to 3-4 cm after 45-60 days. Some of the shoots produced roots simultaneously (Muniswamy & Sreenath, 1999).

title: Embryo culture in coffee techniques and applications
text: In coffee breeding programmes, embryo abortion is normally encountered in the seeds of unsuccessful crosses. The most useful and a rISSUE CULTURE popular application of zygotic embryo culture is rescuing incompatible hybrid crosses. In breeding programmes, inter- specific and_intergeneric crosses are frequently carried out to transfer valuable genes from wild species to cultivated Incompatibility is often encountered species. in such crosses and results in shriveled seeds containing aborted embryos (Muniswamy and Sreenath, 1999).

title: Preservation of coffee (Coffea arabica L.) by in vitro culture of zygotic embryos under slow growth conditions
text: Preservation of coffee (Coffea arabica L) by in vitro culture of zygotic embryos under slow growth conditions is reported. Zygotic embryos of Coffea arabica L. cv. Cauvery (Catimor) were cultured on MS based medium and on medium supplemented with different concentrations of abscissic acid. Cultures were maintained in dark at room temperature (25°C). The embryos were taken out at 5-6 months interval from above said culture conditions and transferred to germination medium containing BAP. The type of response depended on the different cultural conditions in which embryos were cultured and on concentrations of ABA in the medium. It was found that a higher concentration of ABA is effective for induction of embryo dormancy. Effective embryo germination was achieved on MS medium supplemented with BAP. The results confirm that embryos can be preserved without the loss of viability in presence of ABA even at room temperature up to two years without any subculture. The application of this technique to the germsplasm preservation of coffee discussed (Madhava and Sreenath, 1999).

title: Improved method of explant preparation for micro propagation of coffee through node culture
text: Disinfection of nodal explants of mature, field-grown coffee (cv. Catimor/Cauvery S. 4347) with different concentrations of NaOCl (0.05, 0.5 or 1%) or HgCl, (0.05, 0.1 or 1%) for 0, 5, 10 or 15 min resulted in the identification of conditions for efficient disinfection of explants. Nodal explants treated with 1% NaOCl for 15 min and 0.19% HgCl, for 5 min yielded best results among all the treatments tested. Foliar application of an antibiotic and fungicide mixture to orthotropous branches of mother plants improved the recovery of explants. Presence of stipules in the nodal explant was one of the factors responsible for poor recovery of explants. Treatment of nodal explants with very low concentration of HgCl, after the removal of stipules improved recovery, although the exposed axillary buds were sensitive to HgCl.. Removal of stipules in the nodal explant as well as pretreatment of the explant with sterile fungicide before inoculation on the nutrient media improved the recovery of explants (Samuel Ganesh, D. and Sreenath, 1999).

title: Plant regeneration through somatic embryogenesis from anther cultures of CxR cultivar of coffee
text: Plant regeneration through embryogenesis has been achieved from cultured anthers of C x R cultivar of coffee (an interspecific hybrid derivative of C. Congensis and C. canephora) (Robusta). Initially, flower buds were pretreated at different temperatures (5-25°C) for 24-72 h in dark. The anthers of uninucleate microscope stage where cultured on MS medium supplemented with different concentration of auxins, cytokinins and L-cysteine HC]. Anthers excised from the floral buds were pretreated at 5°C for 48 h followed by 10°C for another 24 h and cultured on MS medium with IBA and BAP (1 g/l each) for 90 days. After one more subculture on the same medium, they developed 1-2 mm wide, brown calli. After subculturing for another 90 days on MS medium with 2, 4-D (0.05 mg/l), IAA (0.5 mg/l) and Kinetin (8.6 mg/l), the calli grew further to 3-4 mm thickness. When these calli were transferred subsequently onto half-strength MS medium supplemented with NAA (0.05 mg/l), Kn (0.5 mg/l) and 2 x KNO,, nodular, friable embryogenic calli were produced after two months from the original brown callus. The embryogenic calli in turn differentiated into 3-4 white somatic embryos in another month. These embryogenic calli and embryos were further multiplied on MS medium with ABA (1 mg/l). The embryos were converted into plantlets on half-strength MS medium with 0.1 mg/l of Kn. Subsequently, these plantlets were hardened in net-pots and polybags (Muniswamy and Sreenath, 2000).

title: Embryogenesis and plant regeneration from endosperm tissues of Coffea arabica L.
text: Embryogenesis and plant regeneration were achieved from cultured endosperm tissue in the S.2803 genotype of Coffea arabica, a tetraploid and self-pollinated species. Endosperm was taken from green fruits and cultured on MS medium supplemented with 2, 4 - D (0.5 mg/L) and Kn (5 mg/L) with 50 mg/L of L-cysteine HCI, for about 60 days. A meagre brown callus 1-2 mm wide was obtained from the cut edges. When sub-cultured on half-strength MS medium with KNO, (3800 mgL?) + NAA (0.1 mg/L) + Kn (0.5 mg/L) for 70-80 days, the calli grew further and produced nodular, friable calli. On these calli, embryogenic masses were induced after culturing for one more month on the same medium. Miultiplication and maturation of the embryos was achieved by culturing the embryogenic calli on MS medium with 1 mg/L of ABA for 30-40 days. The mature embryos germinated into plantlets after 3-4 subcultures at monthly intervals on half-strength MS medium supplemented with 0.1 mg/L of Kn. After producing 2-3 pairs of leaves and a good root system, these plantlets were planted in net pots containing soilrite mixture and hardened, with a good survival rate (Muniswamy and Sreenath, 2001). ee ee ae ee ee ee ee, 1 tt _

text: and plant regencration from leaf explants of Coffea bengalensis Roxb. : A wild coffee species In vitro adventitious shoot formation from foliar explants of Coffea bengalensis Roxb. was achieved. Among various combinations of growth regulators tested, N6 benzyl adenine (BA) was found to be the most effective in inducing shoot buds. Shoot buds are induced from the cut surface of foliar explants incubated on Murashige and Skoog (MS) medium supplemented with either BA alone (2.5 - 10 mg/l) or the combination of Indole -3-Acetic Acid (IAA, 0.1 - 1.0 mg/l) and BA (0.5 -5.0 mg/l). The frequency of shoot regeneration was positively correlated with the concentration of BA .The presence of IAA increased plant responsiveness to lower concentration of BA. The regenerated shoots were morphologically normal and successfully rooted on half strength MS medium supplemented with Indole - 3 butyric acid (IBA) (0.5 - 1.0 mg/l). This is the first report of plant regeneration through direct adventitious shoot formation from the leaf explants ofa wild coffee species (Mishra & Sreenath, 2003).

title: Development of caffeine free coffee varieties
text: While dealing the scope of biotechnology the author envisages ‘creation’ of caffeine free coffee plant, through different approaches like introduction of genes that block caffeine synthesis de novo. Caffeine synthesis may also be inhibited by producing plants with a regulated copy of a gene which expresses, for example a ribosome to the mRNA for the methyl transferase gene responsible for the methylation of xanthosine to 7-methyl xanthosine etc. Further possibilities of development of caffeine free coffee varieties have been discussed (Sreenath, 1997).

title: Coffee genetic resources - mapping and management
text: Genetic resource conservation and management is discussed along with brief consideration of methods to assess levels of genetic diversity ; coffee. Examples given include the use of ee and isoenzymes (Mishra, 1998). ;

title: Procedure for generating silver stained AFp markers in coffee
text: Despite its economic and agricultural importance, coffee has not been _ benefited extensively from the technological developments, which have been applied for genetic analysis of other cash crops. There are only a few reports on the use of DNA based molecular techniques like RFLPs, RAPD and PCR for coffee genome analysis. Recently developed AFLP technique has tremendous potential in the marker assisted genetic improvement and genetic analysis and biodiversity evaluation of this commercially important crop. However, there is no report on AFLP analysis of coffee. Hence, studies were undertaken to optimize the procedure to generate silver stained AELP markers in coffee. Five selections of Coffea arabica, Coffea canephora and Psilanthus bengalensis (previously C. bengalensis were used a the study. DNA was isolated by SDS method. ‘AFLP procedure was performed as per the product anual supplied by M/s. Life Technologies Inc. with Se modifications. The amplified products were ov on a sequencing type vertical electrophoresis stem using 6% denaturing polyacrylamide gel. the amplified DNA bands were visualized by silver staining. In the five materials tested, AFLP technique could produce 20-50 amplified DNA bands, ranging in size from less than 200 pb to more than 2 kb. Many of the bands were polymorphic indicating the usefulness of the technique for genetic analysis of coffee. P bengalensis generated maximum polymorphic bands (Sreenath et al., 1999). 4. A method for isolation and amplification of coffee DNA using random octamer and decamer primers Standardization of a method for the isolation of high mol. wt. DNA from the young leaves of 3 different species of Coffea L. (C. arabica L. (Rume Sudan), C. racemosa and C. congensis) is described. Optimization of components and conditions for PCR amplification using the DNA of C. arabica as template are also described. It is suggested that the standardized method may be used to generate fingerprint profiles of coffee physiologic types to show distinctions at the DNA level (Santa Ram and Sreenath, 1999).

title: AFLP analysis of introgression in coffee cultivars (Coffea arabica L.) derived from a natural interspecific hybrid
text: S.288 an offspring of a putative spontaneous interspecific hybrid between tetraploid Coffea arabica (2n = 4x = 44) and diploid C. liberica (2n = 2x = 22) and 17 arabica coffee introgression lines (representing F2 and F4) derived from the 9 id e cross S.288 x Kent arabica were evaluated for introgression of C. liberica genetic material. In all analyte, een cpbinations were used in the analysis. -P profiles of introgressed lines were compared to five accessions each of C. arabica and C, liberica. A total of 137 polymorphic bands were scored among the 29 accessions analysed. The introgressed genotypes exhibited 102 marker bands consisting of 65 additional bands and 37 missing bands associated with introgression of C. liberica genetic material. C. liberica accessions of EA group (C. liberica var liberica of Guinean origin) seemed to be the likely progenitor in the origin of natural hybrid. Analysis of genetic relationships in the introgressed lines suggested that introgression was limited to few fragments. Segregation and wide variation in number of marker fragments in the F, and F, progenies were attributed to chromosome recombinations. The differences in the level of introgression between introgressed parent, F, and F, groups was not pronounced. Therefore the alien genetic material appeared to be fixed and there was no elimination or counter-selection over generations, from introgressed parent to F,. In C. arabica accessions, only 35 polymorphic bands were seen confirming _ the low genetic diversity. On the contrary, although representing a small amount of alien genome introgression, the Liberica-introgressed genotypes provided notable genetic diversity. Considering the fact that the diploid species of Coffea constitute a valuable source of genetic diversity, the potential implications of variability generated by Libericaintrogressed genotypes in C. arabica breeding are discussed (Prakash et al., 2002).

title: Fingerprinting of Indian Coffee selections and development of reference DNA polymorphism panels for creating molecular
text: IDs for variety identification 2004 There are two main cultivated species of coffee namely, tetraploid C. arabica and diploid C. canephora (also called Robusta coffee). A number of breeding programs were initiated in India at Central Coftee Research Institute, Chikkamagaluru, with main thrust being building resistance coupled with productivity without affecting quality in Arabica and improvement of bean quality and yield in Robusta. Such efforts spread over many decades resulted in the development of 16 superior selections of coffee (14 Arabica and 2 Robusta selections). The present study was undertaken to fingerprint these station-bred selections using high-resolution DNA marker approaches for their individualization and to ascertain their genetic base. DNA typing was performed using fluorescence-AFLPs; RAPDs and a large number of in-house developed coffeespecific microsatellite markers. The data revealed very limited variability in Arabica genotypes, which could be visualized for their discrimination only by employing a very large number of DNA markers. The fingerprinting data were analyzed to create reference’ DNA polymorphism panels’ (Microsatellite, AFLP, RAPD-based) which can readily be used for: a) generating ‘Molecular IDs’ needed for genotype individualization/ registration/IPR protection; b) selecting genetically diverse genotypes and suitable/efficient marker approaches for breeding programs; and c) other genetic studies. In our opinion, this study involving DNA fingerprinting of Indian coffee selections, in perspective strongly suggests the need for creation of molecular data banks (enumerating DNA marker efficiencies and DNA polymorphism status) for globally available elite coffee germplasm for use as reference resources. title: Morphological, biochemical and molecular characterization of ploidy variants in coffee for genetic improvement
text: The genus Coffea consists of more than hundred species of which only C. arabica (known as arabica coffee) and C. canephora (known as robusta coffee) are commercially cultivated. All the species of the genus Coffea are diploids and self-incompatible except C. arabica, which is an allotetraploid and selfcompatible species. In C. arabica, a series of ploidy variants of spontaneous origin were recovered and documented. In C. canephora, which is a diploid species, colchicine was used successfully to induce tetraploidy. In addition, a few spontaneous triploid plants conforming to either arabica or robusta Phenotype were also recovered. All the ploidy variants were studied for morphological characters such as leaf shape, leaf venation pattern, leaf anatomy, and stomatal features. The biochemical characters such as chlorophyll starch carbohydrate, phenol, sugar, amino acid cGnfent and flavonoid profile pattern also have been investigated. Molecular characterization of all the ploidy variants was carried out by using RAPD and PCR-RFLP and polymorphism was recorded. These results along with the utilization of the ploidy variants in coffee breeding program is discussed (Mishra et al., 2006)

title: Genome organization in coffee as revealed by
text: " EST PCR-RELP, SNPs and SSR analysis An EST-based PCR-RFLP method was employed to gain insight into genome organization in eight allopolyploid Coffea arabica cultivars and seven diploid coffee species. The PCRamplified products at 19 EST loci were digested with 46 different restriction enzymes and size fractioned in agarose gels. Most often, the sum of the fragments length was double or more than the PCR product. In arabica, this condition could be explained by assuming the presence of duplicated loci in paralogous chromosomes and this was supported by considerable evidence of multiple loci SSR amplification. Based on the RFLP analysis, 12 EST loci were polymorphic. The level of polymorphism was higher in different species ‘compared to the arabica varieties. Sequencing of the amplified products revealed a SNP frequency of 0.021 among diploid species and of 0.007 among arabica varieties. We propose that the involvement of two genomes in C. arabica maintains a residual level of heterozygosity in the form of paralogous chromosomes, while the self-fertilization in this species tends to drive of homozygosity. The heterozygosity of paralogous chromosomes in arabica creates valuable polymorphism essential for species diversity and survival in various ecological niches, while self-fertility tends to preserve in homozygosity many genes of functional significance (Mishra et al., 2011).

title: Genetic molecular analysis of Coffea arabica
text: (Rubiaceae) hybrids using SRAP markers In Coffea arabica (arabica coffee), the phenotypic as well as genetic variability has been found low because of the narrow genetic basis and self-fertile nature of the species. Because of high similarity in Phenotypic appearance among the majority of arabica collections, selection of parental lines for inter-varictals hybridization and identification of resultant hybrids at an carly stage of plant growth is difficult. DNA markers are known to be reliable in identifying closely related cultivars and hybrids. Sequence Related Amplified Polymorphism (SRAP) is a new molecular marker technology developed based on PCR. In this Paper, sixty arabica-hybrid progenies belonging to six crosses were analyzed using 31 highly polymorphic SRAP markers. The analysis revealed seven types of SRAP marker profiles which are useful in discriminating the parents and hybrids. The number of bands amplified per primer pair ranges from 6.13 to 8.58 with average number of seven bands. Among six hybrid combinations, percentage of bands shared between hybrids and their parents ranged from 66.29% to 85.71% with polymorphic bands varied from 27.64% to 60.0%. Percentage of hybrid specific fragments obtained in various hybrid combinations ranged from 0.71% to 10.86% and ascribed to the consequence of meiotic recombination. Based on the similarity index calculation, it was observed that F, hybrids share maximum number of bands with the female parent compared to male parent. The results obtained in the present study revealed the effectiveness of SRAP technique in cultivar identification and hybrid analysis in this coffee species (Mishra et al., 2011).

title: Molecular genetic analysis of arabica coffee hybrids using SRAP marker approach
text: In Coffea arabica the phenotypic as well as genetic variability has been found low due to narrow genetic base and self-fertile nature of the species. Because of high similarity in phenotypic appearance among majority of arabica collections, selection of parental lines for inter-varietal hybridization and _ identification of resultant hybrids at an early stage of plant growth is difficult. Application of DNA markers provides a promising alternative for quick and reliable assessment of hybrid genotype. Sequence Related Amplified Polymorphism (SRAP) is a new molecular marker based on PCR technology. In this study, we evaluated the effectiveness of SRAP for molecular genetic analysis of selected arabica hybrids (F) and their parents. Forty arabica hybrid progenies belong to four crosses were analyzed using 27 highly polymorphic SRAP markers. These 27 primer pairs generated seven different types of marker profiles, which are useful for discriminating the parents and hybrids. The number of bands amplified per primer pair ranged from 5.56 to 7.81 with average number of 6.42 bands. The polymorphic bands varied from 28.07 to 44.57% among different hybrids. The percent bands shared between hybrids and their parents ranged from 80.0 to 91.87%. Percentage of hybrid specific fragments obtained in various hybrid combinations ranged from 2.70 to 4.49% and ascribed to the consequence of recombination. Analysis of the SRAP marker profiles revealed that two hybrid progenies are closer to maternal parent, and other two are closer to paternal parent in banding pattern. The results obtained in present study revealed the effectiveness of SRAP technique in cultivar identification and hybrid analysis in coffee (Mishra et al., 2011).

title: Field performance and genetic fidelity. of micropropagated plants of Coffea canephora
text: (Pierre ex A. Froehner) This study was conducted to compare the growth and yield of one of the commercial hybrid coffee cultivars (Coffea congensis x Coffea canephora) of robusta coffee established from somatic embryogenesis as well as conventional seedlings. Results indicated no _ statistically significant differences in the growth pattern or the cumulative yield between the somatic embryogenesis derived plants and the seedlings. The genetic fidelity of somatic embryogenesis derived plants and the mother plant was tested using Sequence Related Amplified Polymorphism (SRAP) markers. A total of 24 SRAP primers were employed for DNA analysis which produced a total of 153 clear, distinct and reproducible amplicons of variable size. Out of 24 SRAP primers, 9 primers produced amplification patterns which are identical between the mother plants and plants derived from somatic embryogenesis. Cluster analysis revealed more than 95% genetic similarity between the somatic embryogenesis derived plants and the mother plants indicating a high degree of genetic fidelity. The present study clearly demonstrates the usefulness of SRAP markers in genetic fidelity analysis of coffee (Muniswamy et al., 2017).

Although the rust fungus exists in different physiological races, the genetic difference between them is meagerly understood. In this study, genetic diversity of 14 identified and two unidentified leaf rust races was determined by sequence-related amplified polymorphism (SRAP) markers. In the present study, four commercially important species of Trichoderma isolated from coffee ecosystem were screened with sequence related amplified polymorphism (SRAP) markers. The highest homology (83.0%) was observed between T. viride and T. harzianum and the lowest homology (74.0%) was observed between T: harzianum and T. konangii. Further, among 29 polymorphic SRAP markers screened, four primer pairs (ME1-EM3, ME1-EM20, ME1EM22 and ME2-EM4) produced unique fragments specific to each species. title: Molecular and physiological characterization of a natural interspecific coffee hybrid
text: Natural hybridization is a common phenomenon in plants and considered to be a driving force of biodiversity and evolution. In coffee spontaneous hybridization between two different species is earlier documented. title: Diversity genotyping of Indian coffee (Coffea arabica L.) germplasm accessions by using
text: SRAP markers Coffea arabica L. is the only cultivated tetraploid species in the genus Coffea and it contributes more than 61% to the total world coffee production. Arabica produces superior beverage quality compared to robusta coffee but is susceptible to a number of pests and diseases. Improved varieties of arabica coupled with durable disease resistance can be achieved by incorporating novel sources of genetic variation from diverse germplasm sources. Assessment of genetic diversity within the germplasm pool is a prerequisite for estimating its true breeding potential. In the present study, 42 world germplasm accession of arabica were screened with co-dominant sequence-related amplified polymorphism (SRAP) markers. Twenty-one SRAP combinations amplified a total of 171 fragments of which 116 (67.83%) were polymorphic and 5.47% were rare alleles. A total of 171 alleles with 8.14 alleles per marker were identified and the average polymorphism information content (PIC) value was 0.28. Based on the Jaccard’s similarity coefficient the UPGMA dendrogram differentiated all the 42 accessions, with genetic similarity estimates ranging from 0.59 to 0.98. The model-based Bayesian analysis of population structure using the admixture model grouped the 42 arabica germplasm accessions into two ancestral groups. The diversity and structural analysis of 42 arabica world collections identified 11 arabica diverse germplasm accessions and clearly demonstrated the suitability of SRAP markers for coffee genetic diversity studies. These accessions should be analyzed for agronomic and quality parameters, and the same can be utilized in arabica improvement programs. Further, these accessions need to be conserved to enrich arabica diversity (Jingade et al., 2019).

title: Genetic resources and breeding of Coffee
text: (Coffea spp.) Coffee is an important agricultural export commodity in many Asian, African and Latin American countries. It provides a livelihood for more than 125 million people worldwide: The genus Coffea comprises more than 125 species of which only 2 species Coffea arabica (arabica coffee) and C. canephora (robusta coffee) are commercially cultivated for beverage production. Climate change present sun precedented challenges to sustainable coffee cultivation on a global scale. Besides, both arabica and robusta coffee are subjected to biotic and abiotic stress conditions that limit their production and _ productivity. Although conventional breeding approaches are followed to attenuate some of these problems, they were slow and time-consuming. Furthermore, arabica coffee has a narrow genetic base and needs to be addressed immediately by incorporating diverse germplasm with potential agronomic values, using focused breeding programs. In both arabica and robusta, the full potential of germplasm has not been exploited. Recent progress in the biotechnological field particularly on molecular markers and new generation sequencing platform hold great promise to discover new genes and eee <<< accelerate coffee breeding programs. The progress achieved in coffee transgenic technology also has unparalleled opportunities to develop new cultivars with improved agronomic traits. Recent progress in gene editing techniques has a significant impact on the genetic improvement of coffee. This chapter provides current and innovative information about coffee’s origin and distribution, genetic resource diversity and conventional breeding strategies and application. Current advances in the field of tissue culture, genetic transformation, gene editing and molecular breeding are also discussed (Mishra, 2019).

title: Gene expression analysis of Coffea arabica seeds processed under different post-harvest processing methods
text: The mode of coffee processing, either the wet or dry method, determines the characteristic flavour and establishes the differences in quality of the final green coffee produced. The present study focused mainly on identifying the differential gene expression in green coffee seeds of Brazilian arabica coffee (Coffea arabica L.) among samples prepared under three different post-harvest treatments (natural, washed and semi washed method) and grown in two different locations. Expression levels of 16 genes of interest were measured. These genes are involved in various cellular, metabolic and biochemical activities influencing levels of certain compounds, such as lipids, carbohydrates, caffeine and chlorogenic acid, associated with quality characteristics of the beverage. Microarray experiments were designed with cDNA probe sequences. Microarray data was analyzed to identify the differences in gene expression between two altitudes and between two variables; location and post-harvest treatment. Cluster analysis was carried out with samples showing similar patterns, which are characteristic to the group. With this approach, it was possible to identify the important genes in C. arabica seeds that have differential (increased or decreased) expression levels. It was also seen that between the location and treatments, location profoundly impacts the levels of gene expression in samples (Pallavicini and et al., 2019). f f i i

title: First report on genome size and ploidy determination of fivé indigenous coffee species using flow cytometry and stomatal analysis
text: The nuclear 2C DNA content and ploidy level determination of five indigenous coffee species from India was carried out using flow cytometry and by assessing the stomatal characteristics. The nuclear DNA content (2C/pg) analyzed varied from 1.29 pg in Coffea wightiana Wall. ex Wight & Arn. to 1.48 pg in Coffea jenkinsii Hook.f. Based on the genome size, all five species were divided into two groups. The first group comprises Coffea travancorensis Wight & Arn and C. wightiana with lower genome size (2C DNA 1.29-1.30 pg), and the second group consists of Coffea bengalensis Roxb. ex Schult, Coffea khasiana (Korth.) Hook.f and C. jenkinsii with larger genome size (2C DNA 1.451.48 pg). The species included in the first group were inhabited in dry environmental conditions in contrast to the species included in the second group which was predominantly from mesic habitat. Among the stomatal characteristics, no significant variation in stomatal density was observed among the species, although stomatal guard cell 99 (Abstracts of Research Pzpers) ee length and stomatal chloroplast number recorded significant variation among some species. Based on flow cytometry and stomatal characteristics, all five endangered coffee species analyzed in the study were identified as diploids. The study revealed that stomatal guard cell length and stomatal chloroplast number could be fast, inexpensive, and reliable methods for determining the ploidy status of indigenous coffee species (Jingade, 2021).

title: Applications of omics technologies in Coffea
text: The omics platform in coffee is full of promise, and much advancement in omics technologies is expected in the future. The combination of transcriptomics and metabolomics _ research along with phenomics will provide important information on the regulatory functions of genes linked to various agronomic traits. Some of the areas that will prominently feature in the coming years include the identification of key genes and regulatory mechanisms and pathways responsible for enhanced biotic and abiotic stress tolerance, understanding the complex mechanism of coffee quality, and flavor and the development of climate- resilient coffee (Mishra et al., 2022).

title: RAPD marker analysis reveals high genetic stability in high frequency somatic embryogenesis-derived plants of Robusta coffee (Coffea canephora)
text: This paper reports high frequency somatic embryogenesis, plant regeneration and _ high genetic stability in somatic embryo-derived plants (SEPs) of CR cultivar of robusta coffee (Coffea canephora Pierre) as assessed by RAPD markers. High frequency embryogenic calli were induced from the leaf explants from a 15 year-old superior plant (TL1) on MS medium supplemented with IAA (1 mg/l) and kinetin (5 mg/l). Somatic embryos were matured on MS medium with ABA (1 mg/l) and germinated on half strength MS medium supplemented with kinetin (0.1-1 mg/l). After hardening in net pots in a polytunnel and further growth in polybags in nursery, the SEPs were planted in the field. There was no detectable morphological variation in the SEPs. Fourteen SEPs established in the field were used for RAPD analysis. Genomic DNA was isolated from the fresh leaves of the mother plant (TL1) and one year-old SEPs by a modified SDS method. After initial screening of 25 arbitrary 10-base primers, 16 primers that gave distinct RAPD bands were used for further study. In total, 121 RAPD markers were obtained from 16 primers, out of which 120 markers were monomorphic across all the SEPs and the mother plant. One polymorphic marker of 1.4 kb size was obtained with the primer OPA- 14 in one SEP (Sreenath and Naidu, 2004).

title: Somatic embryogenesis and __ genetic homogeneity assessment in Coffea - Recent approaches
text: Coffee is one of the most preferred beverages consumed by millions of people throughout the world. It is cultivated in more than 80 countries in tropical and subtropical zones of Asia, Africa, and Latin America and provides livelihood to 125 million people worldwide. Among 125 coffee species known so far, only two coffee species, Coffea arabica (arabica coffee) and Coffea canephora (robusta coffee), are commercially cultivated for beverage production. Coffee is a perennial plant and therefore subjected to constant environmental Stress. However, during the last few decades, o _TISSUE CULTURE & MOLECULAR BIOLOGY sustainable coffee cultivation has been threatened by unprecedented climate change. This calls for unified efforts, including cutting-edge research and modified management practices. Although conventional breeding efforts have been developed to address some issues, emerging biotechnology research, especially in-vitro propagation technology, could augment the coffee cultivation landscape. Despite the tangible progress made in coffee tissue culture, there were some grey areas, such as the level of somaclonal variation and the genomic changes associated with somatic embryogenesis in coffee, which needs to be addressed imminently. This chapter provides detailed progress on coffee tissue culture and addresses some of the critical issues associated with the genetic homogeneity of tissue culture plants (Mishra et al., 2023).

title: Comparative genetic assessment of somatic embryo and seed derived plants of two arabica hybrid coffee cultivars using SRAP and SCoT molecular markers and organellar and nuclear genes sequencing
text: Traditionally, coffee is propagated by seed. However, in recent years, the propagation of plants derived from somatic embryos has become increasingly important. The genetic homogeneity of plants derived from somatic embryos must be assessed before large-scale propagation. In this study, the genetic uniformity of somatic embryoderived and seed-derived plants obtained from the same mother plant in two arabica hybrid coffee cultivars was examined using sequence-related amplified polymorphism (SRAP) and start codontargeted (SCoT) markers, as well as the sequencing of seven functional genes. In both cultivars, the analysis of molecular markers revealed a remarkable genetic similarity of 93 to 98% between the plants derived from somatic embryos and those derived from seeds compared to the mother plant. Sequence analysis confirmed that the large subunit of ribulose-1,5-biphosphate carboxylase and mitochondrial ribosomal protein had the highest sequence similarity of all the genes studied. title: Agrobacterium-mediated transformation of coffee: An assessment of factors affecting gene transfer efficiency
text: Experimental conditions influencing Agrobacterium t-DNA delivery to coffee tissue were investigated using plasmid vector containing gusA (b-glucuronidase) intron reporter gene. Leaf explants, hypocotyls, zygotic and somatic embryos were used for co-cultivation experiments and transfer of t-DNA was assessed by analyzing the transient gusA gene expression. The study revealed that t-DNA delivery is preferentially targeted to distinct anatomical regions in different target tissues. In co-cultivated leaf explants, cut ends of the veins are the preferential target sites where as in zygotic and somatic embryos, hypocotyl and its adjacent region are the main target sites. Pre culture of recipient tissue and manipulation ofco cultivation conditions affected gene transfer efficiency and this is evident from transient gene expression assay. Two aminoglycoside antibiotics, kanamycin and hygromycin were tested at different concentrations and it was observed that hygromycin could be more effective in transformants selection at lower concentration. It is concluded that an interactive selection protocol is essential for eliminating the escapes and recovering stable transformants in coffee (Mishra et ali, 2002).

title: High-Efficiency Agrobacterium—Mediated
text: Transformation of Coffee (Coffea canephora Pierre ex. Frohner) Using Hypocotyl Explants An efficient regeneration and Agrobacterium mediated transformation system was developed 107° 4 2 arr e ¢ for two commercially important: cultivars (cv 6.274 and CxR) of robusta coffee. Hypocotyl explants obtained from the in vitro grown seedlings and embryogenic calli gathered from the hypocotyl explants were co-cultivated with Agrobacterium tumefaciens strain EHA 101/p BECKS that harbored genes for B-glucuronidase (GUS), kanamycin (npt II) and hygromycin (hpt) resistance. Prior to co-cultivation the target explants were incubated on MS medium containing 0.1 mg/l 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid, 1 mg/l Indole-3 Acetic Acid and 4 mg/l Kinetin for 3 days in darkness. Several factors which significantly affected the t-DNA transfer were evaluated and optimized co-cultivation was performed at 22 °C in an acidic medium (pH 5.5) in the presence of 50 4M acetosyringone for 3 days. After 2-3 months of culture on hygromycin (30 mg/l) supplemented selection medium, hygromycin resistant somatic embryos were isolated and separately cultured on germination medium containing 0.5 mg/l IAA and 2 mg/I kinetin and 50mg/l hygromycin. Putative transformed plantlets of two cultivars were obtained after rooting on half strength MS medium supplemented with 0.5 mg/l kinetin and 40 mg/l hygromycin and subsequently hardened in the polybags containing soil mixture. Stable transformation of the recovered plants was verified by histochemical GUS assay and molecular analysis (Mishra and Sreenath, 2004).

title: Recent advances in the genetic transformation of Coffee
text: Coffee is one of the most important plantation crops, grown in about 80 countries across the world. The genus Coffea comprises approximately 100 species of which only two species that is Coffea arabica (commonly known as arabica coffee) and Coffea canephora (known as robusta coffee), are commercially cultivated. Genetic improvement of coffee through traditional breeding is slow due to the perennial nature of the plant. Genetic transformation has tremendous potential in developing improved coffee varieties with desired agronomic traits, which are otherwise difficult to achieve through traditional breeding. During the last twenty years, significant progress has been made in coffee biotechnology, particularly in the area of transgenic technology. This paper provides a detailed account of the advances made in the genetic transformation of coffee and their potential applications (Mishra and Slater, 2012).

title: Effect of rain on coffee blossom
text: A field trial was laid out on young Arabica coffee (S. 1934) to elucidate information on the effect of rain on blossom. Rain in the morning hours affected the blossom-berry ratio adversely during all the 3 years of trial. No such adverse effect was noticed with afternoon rain. If rain came down on the open flowers, the pollen was largely lost. The stigma was more resistant and could still be fertilized the following day if there was some fresh pollen. Since pollination is over in the forenoon itself no adverse effect of afternoon rain was noticed (Awatramani and Satyanarayana, 1973).

title: Rainfall pattern
text: Rainfall data collected from 13 coffee districts of South India were analysed statistically. Those due to months and months x years were highly significant. This indicated that differences in the mean annual rainfall were small. Differences in the amount of rain received during various months of the years very large. Quantum of rain received during any particular month was not uniform during different years. Therefore, while annual rainfall was predictable, monthly rainfall was not (Awatramani et al., 1975). (Abstracts of Research §

text: An analysis has been carried out to study the rainfall pattern its quantum, distribution, variability or stability during the 40 year period (1950-89) in 5 coffee growing zones of Karnataka viz., Chikkamagaluru, North Coorg, South Coorg, Hassan and Biligiris. Excepting Biligiris, all other zones exhibit similar characters in monthly distribution and seasonal contribution. The variability as indicated by co-efficient of variation, is high ranging from 103-332% during January to March and December, depending upon the zone and month. During April and May, the rainfall is more stable with C.V. ranging from 39-68% together with a better chance of getting more than 25 mm rainfall normally required for blossoming and fruit setting in coffee in any given year. The stability has been found to be good during June to November. Among the four seasons, South West monsoon season was the least variable while winter season rainfall was highly unstable. In Chikkamagaluru and North Coorg, a steady decline in the quantum of rainfall could be observed from first decade (1950-59) to fourth decade (1980-89). The decline was apparent only in fourth decade in the case of South Coorg and Biligiris while it was negligible in Hassan (Radhakrishnan et al., 1990).

text: : and rainfall trends in CRSS-Chettalli of N-KODAGU, Western Ghat, India This study examines recent changes in monthly mean of maximum temperature (M-MAX), relative humidity (M-RH) and total rainfall (TMREF) of Coffee Research Sub Station (CRSS), Chettalli, North Coorg, Karnataka, India over approximately Jast four decades stretching between years 1975 to 2012. The increasing trend in mean of maximum (M-MAX) temperature and relative humidity and decreasing trend in total mean annual rainfall (TMRF) is confirmed by MannKendall trend test. It is observed that monthly mean of maximum (M-MAX) temperatures have increased significantly for all the months and for annual. While monthly mean of TMRF have increased significantly for the months of March, April, July, September, October, November and December _ whereas it shows decreasing trend in January, _ February, May, June and August for the station. title: Influence of soil cultivation methods in young coffee on soil moisture, weed suppression and organic matter
text: A field experiment was conducted on the CCRI farm for three consecutive years in a randomized block design with ten soil cultivation practices and three replications. Significantly higher stem girth, number of primary branches and bush spread were recorded in deep digging, scuffling, mulching with coir pith and green manure crop incorporation practices in all the years compared to control. Mulching with cherry husk and paddy straw did not improve the growth parameters of coffee. All mulches were found better than green manure crop, digging, scuffling and control in conserving the soil moisture during February. Whereas, weed suppression (as indicated by weed population, fresh and dry weed biomass) was higher in green manure treatments followed by mulch application compared to rest of the practices. Mulching, green manure crop incorporation, digging and scuffling Were found to improve the soil organic carbon content over the years. Control recorded the lowest soil moisture and organic carbon and the highest weed bio-mass which smothered the growth of young coffee variety C x R (Shivaprasad et al., 2005).

title: Effect of cultivation practices and green manure crops on soil moisture conservation and growth of coffee
text: A field experiment was conducted at the Research Farm of Central Coffee Research Institute, Chikkamagaluru during 2000-01 to 2003-04 to find out the effect of cultivation practices and green manuring on growth of coffee, soil moisture conservation, weed population and soil fertility. Results showed that significantly higher stem girth, number of primary branches and length of longest primary branch and bush spread were recorded with deep digging, scuffling, coir pith mulching and green manuring than control. Cherry husk and paddy straw mulching did not improve the growth parameters of coffee. Mulches were found better than green manure crops, digging, scuffling and control in conserving soil moisture during blossom period (March-April). Whereas, weed suppression was highest in green manure treatments followed by mulches as compared to other treatments. Mulches, green manure crops, digging and scuffling improved the soil organic matter (SOM) and available phosphorus in soil. Control recorded the lowest soil moisture, SOM, available phosphorus and the highest weed biomass which affected the vigour of young coffee (Shivaprasad et al., 2007).
