text: Fertile jungle soil is a primary ingredient of potting mixture used in coffee nursery to raise healthy, vigorous seedlings and in recent times its availability has diminished due to the receding forest lands in traditional coffee cultivating areas. Hence a nursery trial was conducted with the objective of exploring the possibility of utilizing marginal or less fertile soils enriched with bio-inoculants in ee ee a i eee ee < . alll sO, Cul TTVATION PRA NICES » mixture. Two soils, (soil-1 and soil-2), Se ee euiinttir and marginal in eh Gin compared to the jungle soil enriched with ne inoculants consortia of Azosprillum, Pseudomonas fluorescence, Phosphate Solubilising Bacteria (PSB) and Vesicular Arbuscular Mycorrihiza (VAM) were employed in the secondary nursery to raise coffee seedlings and monitored for growth parameters, nutrient uptake, soil nutrient status and colony forming units for about 200 days after sowing. The results of the study indicated that the recommended Standard Package of Practice (SPP) with jungle soil, Farm Yard Manure (FYM) and sand in the 6:2:1 proportion is a best suited potting mixture to raise the coffee nursery. But in absence of the fertile jungle soil, the marginal soils also can be utilized as an ingredient of potting mixture with due care to incorporate adequate quantity of farm yard manure and the microbial consortia is not a substitute for FYM in the potting mixture (Shivaprasad et al., 2015).

title: Soil health management for Plantation,
text: (Coffea spp.), recent advances and "obs paradigms ew Coffee farming regions on the globe along th equatorial zone between the Tropic of Cancer - the Tropic of Capricorn are generally calleg as th. “Bean Belt.” Coffee plant prospers well in Voleanj . red-lateritic, alluvial and colluvial soils. Acidic Pa reaction, high organic matter content, ang better potassium status are the general characterigt; of coffee soils. The productivity Potentia] of coffee plantations depends on the timely Cultural operations and soil health. Soil erosion, soil acidity and low nutrient availability are some of the Major constraints. Soil conservation measures such ag contour planting, opening of cradle pits, Scuffin mulching and terracing in steep slopes to avoid erosion are important cultural practices. Time} application of liming materials and fertilizers jn two to three splits based on the soil test is required for nutrient management under sustainable coffee production. Nitrogen is essential for coffee plants in all seasons and it has to be provided three to four times a year. The phosphorus requirement is higher for the coffee plants at the time of blossom season, Similarly, the potassium requirement is higher at the time of post-monsoon season. Coffee in India has been cultivated under the canopy of two-tier different shade trees. Leaf litter from different shade trees, periodical pruning practices for coffee plants add considerable amount of biomass to the coffee soil. This type of coffee cultivation practice will help to improve organic carbon status in the coffee soil. Hence, technological options to improve soil health including farm biomass recycling, application of bio-fertilizers, cover cropping, integrated nutrient management, agro-forestry systems for higher carbon sequestration, and opportunities for organic farming are attractive options for sustainable coffee farming (Nadaf et al., 2024).

title: Methods ofreplanting coffee- Abrief study
text: There are four simple methods for replanting. Replanting - This is the best method so far as the new plants are concerned. They will not stand any competition from established coffee and being young they are likely to get better attention. Interplanting - This consists of planting the seedlings of the selected plant material in between rows of existing old coffee. Competition from old coffee is severe in this method. Interlining-Simple - Alternate rows of old coffee are eliminated and new plants are planted in the row. The spacing within the row becomes flexible but the rigid spacing of the old lines will have to be maintained between the two rows. However, yield from the old coffee cannot be good as it is already exhausted. Interlining-Complex - In this case, while the rejuvenation is being attempted, old coffee also gets a fresh lease of life. This appears to be the best method as, although there would be any crop in the first year, the sucker from the collar pruned plants will bear better crops from second year onwards thus maintaining the plot while a portion of it getting rejuvenated (Hanumantha, 1964). j

title: Cover crops for weed control and improving soil fertility in established coffee plantations
text: In coffee plantations, weeds pose a severe problem particularly during early stages of establishment. Hence, trials were conducted to decide the right cover crop. The highest fresh biomass of 5508 Kg/ha was produced in Cowpea Highest numbers of root nodules were found in case of Cowpea (26.8/plant) and weighed 206 mg per plant. Significantly lowest monocot (10.6/sq.m.), dicot (7.0/sq.m.) weed count and total dry weight (9.9 g/sq.m.) was observed in Cowpea compared to control. title: Shade cum fruit yielding avocado under coffee ecosystem
text: Avocado is one of the most commonly preferred shades grown tree crop under Coffee ecosystem. In view of that, Peninsula of Nicoya and Cost Rica farmer was rated avocado (Persea americana L. Mill) is a primary shade tree crop under coffee plantation at the level of 66.3 per cent and it ranked as a fourth position after the Inga spp., Guazuma ulmifolia and Cordia alliodoara. Hence, the avocado is a commercially important shade cum fruit yielding tree under coffee ecosystem which has cultivating both in humid tropic as well as subtropical climates of throughout the world. The tree is basically grown as the forest species but later on as a shade growing tree under coffee cultivation because of high nutritional and medicinal values of fruit and it makes for wider diversity. Thereafter it was entered into the other parts of the world from Central America and Mexico. The tree is of multipurpose in nature and also helps to avoid the soil and water erosion by way of its wider spread canopy. Generally, Avocado leafs reduce the beating action of rain drops which in-turn minimize the soil erosion. The soil enrichment by adding the leaf litter continuously is an advantage in the coffee plantations. It yields in the additional economic returns after three to five years of establishment. Maximum density giving maximum yield is the density at which yield per unit area due to addition of extra plants is offset by loss due to decrease in weight per bush. Spacing in coffee depends on more than one factor. There is a strong genotype -density fertility interaction. The species /cultivars of coffee used, pruning /training system adopted, type of soil, rainfall pattern - whether irrigated or not etc. However under Indian conditions spacing of 1.8 x 2.7 m is the best for Arabica var. S.795 grown on single stem topped at 137 to 165 cm. This could perhaps be initially planted at 1.8 x 1.37m and brought to final spacing of 1.8 x 2.7m after 1 or 2 initial years but before overcrowding has become serious enough to reduce yield. title: Pruning practices
text: A perennial crop like coffee, requires a strong frame work on which to maintain healthy cropping wood, for profitable production each year. Balanced wood production and thereby crop, without impairing the efficiency or economic longevity of plants are important aspects. title: The effect of modified pruning and planting
text: Systems on growth, yleld, labour use efliciency and economics of Arabica coffee — The economics of colfee plantations is onal linked to pruning, which can improve the canopy architecture and thereby increase use efficiency. However, in India, recommended pruning methods viz., light, medium and hard pruning on Arabica coffee plantations have been highly labour intensive. The labour constitutes about 60 % towards cost of cultivation of coffee. In this study, the modified pruning and planting systems were investigated on Arabica coffee cv. Chandragiri and assessed for growth, yield and labour productivity at Central Coffee Research Institute, India over a period of nine consecutive years (2010-2018). Experimental results revealed that all the growth attributes and clean coffee yield were significantly influenced by modified planting systems (hedge row and paired row) and pruning methods (cyclic and rock-n-roll). Correlation coefficient data indicated that growth parameters had shown positive and significant correlation with clean coffee yield (CC) due to effect of modified pruning and planting systems except plant height. Mean data showed that adoption of modified pruning and planting systems helped to get higher clean coffee yield (1316 kg/ha), about 22-55 % of labour savings and maximum cost:benefit ratio of 1:2 could be achieved over traditional system of pruning and planting system. These results suggest that modified pruning methods facilitate vertical growth of coffee plants and thereby provide huge scope for high density planting system without compromising the yield. Further, an efficient labour force and adequate supply of human labour is the basic requirement for successful commercial cultivation of coffee. Hence, modified pruning methods such as cyclic and rock-n-roll pruning could be an option for improving the labour productivity of Indian coffee plantation (Gokavi et al., 2021). title: Drip irrigation
text: A study on the impact of drip irrigation on 4 year old S.274 was carried out for 2 years to find out its effect on flowering, fruit set, retention and crop yield. Five different types of emitters viz., oneway dripper (2.28 LPH), two-way dripper (8.09 LPH), micro tube (6.35 LPH), micro sprinklers (14.60 LPH) and pitcher with a discharge rate of 1 L/day were used for irrigation during December to March-April. The effect of these irrigation treatments was discernible as reflected on the average fruit set, retention and crop yields. A highest yield increase of 146% was obtained from micro sprinkler irrigation, followed by two-way dripper irrigation (58.9%) over the unirrigated control. These results appeared highly promising, considering the age of the bushes (Sopal Ram et al., 1992).

A long- ‘erm experiment was conducted to study the impact of different fertigation levels on the yield, nutrient use efficiency and quality of Robusta coffee. The present experiment was conducted on a randomized block design consisting of six treatments with four replications over a period of 5 years from 2017 to 2021 at the Central Coffee Research Institute (CCRI), Balehonnuru, India. The results revealed that among different fertigation levels, fertigation with 75% and 100% of the recommended dose of fertilizer resulted in significantly higher yields (2117 kg/ha , 1821 kg/ ha) and yield attributing parameters, namely, total number of nodes/branches (49.1, 44.1), number of bearing nodes/branches (35.0, 29.4) and number of fruits/branches (758, 679) in Robusta coffee, based on the pooled mean (2017-2021). Therefore, adoption of the fertigation level with 75% of the recommended dose of fertilizers not only increased the productivity of Robusta coffee but also ensured a higher efficiency of nutrients (25%-30%) and cost-benefit ratio (1:2.48) (Kishor et al., 2024).

title: Influence of fertigation on soil-plant nutrition and crop productivity of shade grown Robusta coffee (Coffea canephora) in India
text: Coffee in Western Ghats grown under shade, soils are enriched with all the nutrients except phosphorus. The areas receive high rainfall, which leads to leaching loss and surface runoff of applied nutrients causing low fertilizer use efficiency. Improved agronomic practices are essential to address these issues. Fertigation is one such practice, having the potential to reduce extra chemical load by improving nutrient use efficiency. title: Particular reference to grass
text: Control usually involves reduction of the weed stand sufficiently to prevent competition with coffee. The quantum of control is generally a balance between its economy and injury or loss weeds may cause to coffee. Dowpon appears effective against the common grasses when applied at 10 Ib/acre either in one or two applications. It has to be sprayed when grasses are in active growth phase. The treated plots continue to remain free of grass weeds anywhere from 4 to 12 months. Combination with other weedicides having selective action can achieve kill of grasses and other weedsdicots. In this case extra care is essential to ensure that spray drift does not affect coffee or young shade trees. Dowpon applied at 5 lb. and above per acre affects dadaps. This is noticed generally 2 to 4 months after application and the effect persists for a considerable time. Regarding persistence of Dalapon the chemical could last much longer under dry conditions. Dadaps commenced to show phytotoxic symptoms from September-November onwards though it was applied during May-August. Dowpon, which may enter into dadap trees by root absorption, may continue to exert the toxic effects for a long period. On account of the bad effects seen on dadaps large scale use of Dowpon for suppression of grass in coffee fields is not recommended (Narasimhaswamy et al., 1962).

title: Herbicidal control of weeds
text: Application of Gramoxone and its combination with Simarazine and Karmex did not produce any adverse effect on mean number of nodes and primaries per plant, girth of main stem, spread of bush, yield and fruit weight. On the contrary, they produced beneficial effect when compared to manual weeding due to more efficient weed control. Karmex + SNID, however, affected the girth, spread of bush and yield of coffee due to persistence of lawn grass (Awatramani and Mathew, 1973).

title: Use of weedicides
text: Among various weedicides tried. Gramoxone 0.5 L in 180 L water per acre was found to be the best. It was found cheaper than manual control. It improved the growth and yield of coffee because of more efficient weed control than manual weeding. It is essential to ensure that spray solution does not fall on coffee foliage. Application has to be drift free. To achieve this, a hand operated low pressure Knap Sac sprayer fitted with pressure gauge and flood jet nozzle can be used. Soil acting herbicides should be used at minimum effective dose. Repeated application may lead to phytotoxic symptoms on coffee and shade trees (Awatramani, 1976).

Biology and Distribution of the Invasive Alien Weed Mikania micrantha-A review Invasion by alien perennial weed Mikania created a serious problem in micrantha has i Southeast Asia. This climbing vine possesses very fast growth rate and could multiply from seed and vegetative parts. It climbs on other plants, create a dense cover and block sunlight thereby damage or kill the other plant. It compete for water, soil nutrient and release allele-chemicals inhibiting growth of plants. The weed creates economic loss to plantation, horticultural crops, displaces and kills native vegetation. It is designated as one of the worst invasive plants of the world. M. micrantha is native to Central and South America and is a harmless plant in its native range. It was widely distributed by man to tropical areas of Africa, Asia, Australia and many different countries. The growth of the weed depends on availability of sunlight and soil moisture. M. Micrantha flowers during cool dry season and produces large number of viable seeds. The seed losses its viability with time. Temperature, light, soil moisture content effect the germination of seed and the seed may persist for about seven years in soil seed bank. The vegetative reproduction of the weed occurs through stem sections and its success depends upon maturity, length and orientation of the stem sections in soil as well as soil moisture content (Bora and Babou, 2021). einai . title: Conjunctive use of coffee effluent and pond water on the performance of Robusta
text: "Coffee and soil properties A field experiment was conducted to study the influence of coffee effluent irrigation on performance of established Robusta coffee, nutrient contribution and microbial activities in the soil. The results revealed that the field irrigated with coffee effluent from aerobic tank having COD of 1009 ppm, did not affect the yield of clean coffee (1309 kg/ha) and it was on par with the plots irrigated with pond water (1310 kg/ ha) (Shivaprasad et al., 2010).

title: Characterization of coffee effluent with environmental perspective and possible treatment using zeolites
text: The results obtained from the study carried out to understand the possible utility of Zeolites in coffee effluent abatement were encouraging as they indicated effective lowering of chemical and biological oxygen demands of the effluent by treatment with small quantities of Zeolites in combination with agricultural lime. High CEC of Zeolites and their lower contribution to the conductivity are also beneficial characteristics which can be useful in containing the pollution levels of the effluents. More detailed studies are necessary to recommend the use of Zeolites for pollution abatement (Shivaprasad et al., 2013). eR os a eee 0, 143

text: ae ced was conducted at the Coffee Research nn sad ne Chettalli, during the years 2002an ii wen for two planting seasons, to thine a leacy of different bio-fertilizers and oe ek ant Growth Promoting Rhizobacteria (N-PGPR) on growth, vigour and development of coffee seedlings. The results revealed that the combined inoculation of Azospirillum + Vesicular Arbuscular Mycorrhiza (VAM) + Phosphate Solubilising Bacteria (PSB)+N-PGPR increased the plant height, tap root length, stem girth and dry matter content of seedlings significantly at field planting stage (150 days after transplanting) when compared to un-inoculated control and individual inoculation treatments. Results also indicated a significant increase in plant height, tap root length and dry weight of seedlings at all the stages of growth when VAM was used in combination with other bio-fertilizers when compared to individual inoculations and un-inoculated control. text: Indian Coffee Plantations: Evaluation of different machineries to improve labor use efficiency and to reduce drudgery Field evaluation of different machineries was carried at Central Coffee Research Institute (CCRI) and Coffee Research Sub Station (CRSS), Chettalli during the year 2012-16. Results of field evaluation on different spaying system indicated that significantly higher field efficiency was observed with Multi Utility Track Vehicle spraying with 4 spray lance (0.557 ha/hour) and it was on par with Centralized Spraying System with 14 spray lance (0.510 ha/hour). Lower field efficiency was observed with power tiller spray system (0.410 ha/ hour) with 8 lance. Similarly, the labor requirement for Multi Utility Track Vehicle system was less (9 labors/day) as compared to Centralized Spraying System (28 labors/day) and PT (16 labors/day), which resulted in labor cost savings to the extent of 211% as compared to Centralized Spraying System. Mechanical weed cutter was found to be more efficient and economic in terms of cost (Rs.829 per acre) over manual weeding (Rs.2800 per acre) and chemical weeding (Rs.1075). Man days utilized for mechanical weed cutter was also much lesser (1.5 per acre) than manual weeding (10 per/acre) and chemical weeding (3.3 per/acre) respectively. Under the same trial, regeneration of weeds was more in manual weeding compared to mechanically per 147) i QV weeding. title: Trends in area, production and productivity of coffee across the major coffee growing states in India
text: India has been ranking among top seven producers of coffee in the world, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu being the major coffee producing states in the country. However, there has been a consistent fluctuation in the production in the recent years across the states due to changing climate conditions. The paper aims to examine the trends in planted area under coffee, bearing area under coffee, production and productivity of coffee in India by using compound growth rate analysis with the 18 years time series data. It also analyses the area and productivity effect as preliminary determinants of coffee production. The major issues and challenges relating to production and productivity of coffee have also been dealt with. Concluding remarks includes some of the initiatives taken by the Coffee Board (a nodal agency for coffee sector in India) - COFFS {Abstracts of Research Pzpers) 149 OTHERS for augmenting the overall coffee production and its consistency (Babou ct al., 2019).

title: Liquid bio-fertilizer formulated oe coconut and its effect on growth an root characteristics of Robusta coffee seedlings under drought conditions
text: A nursery trial was carried out at Regional Coffee Research Station, Chundale, Wayanad district, Kerala during 2018 to study the effects of concentration levels of liquid organic nutrient mixture (20 ml, 30 ml and 40 ml dissolved in 4.5 L of water square meter of nursery area of area) prepared from coconut, cow byproducts and naturally available organic materials against standard nursery nutrient management practices like application of inorganic fertilizer (20g of urea dissolved in 4.5 L of water for square meter of nursery area) and supernatant solution of fermented cow dung slurry on growth and root characteristics of robusta coffee seedling. There were significant differences (p>0.05) in growth parameters (plant height and numbers of leaves) and root parameters (root length and average root diameter) due to the different nutrient management options. Significant differences were observed in organic treatment resulted in tallest plant height (48.25 cm) and maximum numbers of leaves (16.50) where seedlings received Coconut mixture nutrient spray @ 40 ml and which is on par with the treatment received Coconut mixture nutrient spray @ 30 ml and shortest plant height (31.85 cm) and lesser numbers of leaves (9.15) were noticed in the control without nutrient spray. Similar trend were observed in root parameters and resulted in lengthiest root (39.50 cm) and maximum root diameter (2.45 mm) in the treatment received Coconut mixture nutrient spray @ 40 ml. This preliminary result indicate that liquid organic nutrient mixture prepared from coconut, cow byproducts and naturally available organic materials is an effective bio-fertilizer and are most effective at high levels compared to conventional methods followed by the planters under the moisture stress condition (Babou and Lisna, 2019). aie Ar tenet

Arabica coffee is being cultivated in Karnataka in an area of 1.1 lakh ha and Robusta coffee in 1.2 lakh ha. Coffee growing soils are deep, friable, rich in organic matter, high in potassium content, well drained and slightly acidic in reaction. These soils contain large quantities of aluminium and iron oxides. Hence, phosphorus (P) availability in the Indian coffee growing soils is a constraint as the aluminium and iron oxides fix the applied phosphorus. Soil testing laboratories (STLs) of Coffee Board are rendering advisory service to the growers based on soil analysis and classify the data into low, medium and high category. In order to know the impact of the lime and fertilizer management on the soil available P status of the coffee growing soils of Karnataka, the soil-P data were compiled and Synchronized adsorption studies with Pb, Cu, Zn and Cd were attempted for coffee growing soils of south India with graded doses of the metals. Among the four soils from different agro-climatic regions the affinity sequence was in the order Pb> Cu > Zn > Cd except in one where preferential adsorption of Cu exceeded that of Pb. Among the metals Pb and Cu were strongly immobilized, while Zn and Cd were least adsorbed. The incumbent toxicity of Pb and Cu were effectively nullified, whereas free Zn and Cd in the vadose zone pose the problems concerned to nutrition and pollution, respectively upon leaching and runoff losses (D’Souza et al., 2013).

Ninety four percent of samples representing the three states in South India were acidic in reaction and among them 52 percent were strongly acidic (pH: < 5.5). The phosphorus nutrient management also needs attention to improve the deficiency of the nutrient found in 19 percent of the samples representing three states. Kerala is found to contain higher (31 %) number of samples deficient in available P while Tamil Nadu (27 %) and Karnataka (12 %) soils are deficient to lesser extent. title: Lime requirement of coffee soils
text: The lime requirement of 33 high-level laterite soils of West Coast where coffee is being grown was investigated. The lime requirement of these soils varied from 0.5 to as high as 5.4 tons per acre as Calcium carbonate depending upon the soil acidity, exchangeable bases and exchangeable Hydrogen and Aluminium contents. A prediction equation has been established between pH and lime requirement to calculate the quantity of lime to be applied to similar acidic soils (Biddappa, 1973).

title: Lime-Zinc interactions
text: In a laboratory trial addition of Calcium carbonate @ 2.5-20.0 tons per ha significantly raised the soil pH with simultaneous decrease in DTPA extractable Zinc. Increases in exchangeable Calcium, consequent to liming resulted in higher leaf calcium, in C. arabica seedlings grown in differentially limed soils, application of lime, boosted the growth of seedlingsin spite of decreasing extractable Zinc, possibly due to the nutritional effect of Calcium in promoting abundant root growth. title: Evaluation of liming materials and Rock phosphate of different particle size at varying soil moisture regimes
text: A laboratory incubation study was conducted for a period of 6 months to find out the efficacy of few liming materials and Rock phosphate of different particle size at varying soil moisture levels to raise the pH of soil grown to coffee to 6.5. The study indicated that soil moisture played a dominant role in raising the pH, the moisture level of 60% water-holding capacity being necessary for complete reaction. Particles, which passed through 80 mesh, were found more effective than the coarser ones even at lower moisture levels. It was further observed that most of the lime-soil reaction resulting in the pH change occurred in a week's time. Finely ground Rock phosphate also effected a pH change and was found on par with basic slag. title: Fertilizer Practices in Kerala
text: The soil fertility levels of various coffee growing zones of Kerala is evaluated by the MSTL. Majority of the soils (70.3%) were acidic in soil reaction. Available P ranged from 1.36-2.29 and available K from 1.20-2.35, 43.6% of the estates of less than 5 acres did not apply any fertilizer and liming was not done in 68.9%. Yield was less than 100kg/acre in 36.0% and between 101-250 kg/acre in 42.4% of these holdings. In next category (5-10 acres), 60.8% received fertilizer ranging from 31120 kg NPK/acre. 57.3% of estates were not limed in this group. In the holding of 10-25 acres, 74.8% applied fertilizer ranging from 46-150 kg/acre. Liming was done in many of these holdings. Yield was 251-500 kg/acre in 34.2% and 500 kg/acre in 21.6% of these holdings. This investigation revealed a higher degree of fertility consciousness among the large growers (Raju and Kandaswamy, 1987).

title: Fertilizer usage in Tamil Nadu

title: Foliar sprays of Urea to Arabica coffee in
text: South India An exploratory trial to determine the absorption pattern of Nitrogen from Urea sprays, the optimum concentration of Urea at which considerable quantities of Nitrogen can be supplied to coffee as foliar sprays was conducted at the Central Coffee Research Institute. The maximum 173, By MATIOR NUTRII NTS ws absorption of Nitrogen sprayed as Urea occurred within 48 hours of the spray. The study also indicated that Urea could be applied through the foliage at concentration up to 5%, without causing any injury. Slight scorching was observed in young foliage (Krishnamurthy ct al., 1976).

title: Biurct toxicity in Arabica coffee
text: Effect of foliar sprays and soil applications of Urea containing concentrations of Biuret was studied using 15 month old Coffea arabica Cv. Kents seedlings. This was compared with foliar sprays and soil applications of pure Biuret and available samples of Urea. Foliar applications of Urea containing Biuret at 2.5% and above and soil applications of Urea with 10% Biuret and above resulted in Biuret toxicity. The symptoms of toxicity and the sequence of its development have been described. While for foliar sprays, coffee was found to be tolerant to Biuret contents of up to about 2% in Urea, that for soil applications an accumulation of about 1.5 g of Biuret in the soil appeared critical. The present study showed coffee to be more sensitive to Biuret toxicity than Citrus, Tea and vegetable crops (Iyengar et al., 1976).

title: Continuous heavy application of fertilizers on various forms of Nitrogen in the soil
text: Pot culture studies using field soil samples collected from the trial plots on the effect of continuous heavy application of fertilizers indicated that there was considerable buildup of all forms of Nitrogen as a result of considerable heavy application of Nitrogenous fertilizers. title: Effect of Biuret
text: Effect of different concentrations of biuret on seed germination and growth of seedlings was studied in sand culture and nursery. Addition of Urea solution containing biuret >2.5% delayed and reduced the germination. Soaking seeds in solution of biuret of different concentrations also delayed germination. Increased biuret concentration in Urea caused a progressive reduction in seedling growth and dry matter and slightly decreased Nitrogen content of leaf. text: Soil incu bation st j i Studies with varying rates of Phosphorus ke: at different fixed levels of Zinc revealed that Phosphorus even at 2400 ppm, did not alter the extractable soil Zinc appreciably, Possibly due to the presence of Zinc mostly as Organically bound or occluded Zinc in the soil under experimentation. However, growth studies with Arabica seedlings on the differentially treated incubated soils showed that leaf Zinc reduced with increasing amounts of added Phosphorus, suggesting a possible interaction of P-Zn within the plant system. Application of heavy doses of Phosphorus enhanced the leaf Phosphorus and growth of coffee seedlings despite its depressing effect of leaf Zinc. Increments of leaf Zinc and extractable soil Zinc upon the addition of ZnSo,. 7H,O indicated the possibility of soil application of Zinc-salts to improve the Zinc status of soil and plant (Raju and Deshpande, 1986).

title: Efficacy of Mussoriephos
text: Soils of different pH were incubated with Dicalcium phosphate, Superphosphate and Mussoriephos to test the extent of release of available Phosphate from MRP as compared ‘to DCP and SP under laboratory conditions. It was inferred from the experimental data that MRP performs very well at a soil pH level of 4.76 even at higher dosage levels (90 and 120 kg/ha) of fertilizer. MRP releases P in slow and steady rate behaving like a slow releasing P fertilizer. The rate and level of available Phosphate from MRP was initially low but gradually increased till it reaches the maximum after a month of incubation (Haricharan et al., 1988). :

title: Long term application of Phosphorus
text: Phosphorus fractionation studies conducted on coffee soils which received high doses of MRP over 30 years and lime once in 2 years was found to contain Ca-P in dominant proportion followed by Al-Fe bound Phosphorus and reductant soluble Phosphorus. Correlation studies revealed that Bray-I and Al-Fe bound Phosphorus fractions positively and significantly correlated with dry matter yield and Phosphorus uptake by Robusta coffee (Thimma Reddy et al., 1991).

title: Effective citric acid on the solubility of phosphorus in coffee soils
text: The effect of citric acid on residual phosphate and phosphate from applied sources in red lateritic coffee soils has been studied. Addition of citric acid increases the soil available Phosphorus. Uptake of Phosphorus both in the presence and absence of applied Phosphatic fertilizer was increased at 5.7 and 6.4 soil pH. It was noted that complexation of Al*** by citric acid competes with the conversion of absorbed Al*** to an exchangeable form thereby increasing orthophosphate solubility in these soils. text: Phosphorus use efficiency by coffee pl is very poor, due to fixation of phosphorus the soil by metallic elements. The effects of cit mn acid amendments on phosphorus availabilix are discussed with reference to the results of culture, soil solution and soil incubation stadia and field experiments. Stability of Al- and Mn. citric acid complexes was high compared with that of the Zn-citric acid complex. In soil incubation studies, the solubility of Al and Mn were reduced in the presence of citric acid, but solubility of 7, increased. This was reflected in the higher leaf Zp concentration in citric acid-treated plants. Thus citricacid could help to reduce phosphorus-induced Zn deficiency. Citric acid increased the release of P from applied P sources and soil P reserves. In field trials over a 4-year period at Chikkamagaluru, India, with arabica coffee (cv. Sln.6), citric acid increased the soil P availability and coffee yield and reduced the fertilizer requirement of coffee plants. It is concluded that citric acid amendments could reduce the required P application rate and number of fertilizer doses for coffee cultivation. (Jayarama et al., 1998).

title: Forms of Potassium in coffee soils of
text: Chikkamagaluru 60 soil samples in Chikkamagaluru under coffee cultivation were studied for different forms of Potassium and other related characteristics. The results reveal that the available form of Potassium is positively and significantly correlated with water soluble, exchangeable and total Potassium. Among the soil characteristics studied, all the forms of Potassium correlated positively and significantly with clay + silt content whereas negative correlation was observed with sand content (Aseef ef al., 1995).

title: Availability of Sulphur
text: Application of Ammonium _ sulphate, Superphosphate and Muriate of potash mixture containing sufficiently higher S component increased the availability of heat soluble and available soil Sulphur fractions of soil and leaf Sulphur content. Heat soluble Sulphur, a reliable index for assessing soil availability was found to be well above the critical limits of 15-20 ppm proposed by several workers. Leaf Sulphur status was well above the critical values of 200 ppm represents adequate supply. The data indicated that Sulphur deficiency could not manifest even under the conditions of continuous use of fertilizers containing low or no Sulphur component in them (Krishnamurthy and Ananda, 1982).

title: Sulphur status of soils cropped to coffee
text: (Koppa and Mudigere) Survey of Sulphur status through soil analysis in 2 coffee growing sub-zones revealed Ta that 70% of the soil samples tested had available Sulphur determined as heat soluble Sulphur well above the critical limit revealing that there was no immediate possibility of Sulphur being a limiting factor under the present day use of high analysis fertilizers. This could perhaps be due to high organic matter status of coffee soils as revealed by the data and incidental uses of sulphates of Copper and Zinc (Krishnamurthy and Ananda, 1984).

title: Evaluation of extractants to assess the availability of soil Sulphur
text: Evaluation of some of the commonly used extractants to predict the availability of soil Sulphur to Arabica vis-a-vis heat soluble Sulphur indicated that heat soluble Sulphur was present in higher amounts followed by Ammonium acetate or Ammonium acetate- Acetic acid extractable Sulphur. Sulphur extracted by Bray- I reagent, 0.15% Calcium chloride or cold water was comparatively less. Correlation co-efficient worked out revealed that heat soluble Sulphur and Sulphur extractable by Ammonium acetate- Acetic acid, cold water and Ammonium acetate had significant correlation with plant Sulphur. Bray-I extracted Sulphur had poor correlation. This study suggested that Ammonium acetate - Acetic acid or Ammonium acetate could be employed to assess the availability of soil Sulphur to C. arabica in routine soil testing programme (Ramamurthy and Raju, 1987).

title: Micronutrient disorders in Arabica coffee
text: The requirement of any micronutrient js in the order of 2-3 kg/ha or less whereas the micronutrients are to be supplied almost 100 times as much. The importance of inclusion of the micronutrient elements in the nutritional rogramme of the plant, the distress symptoms exhibited by Arabica coffee due to lack of adequate supply of the micronutrients, the causes leading to inadequate supply of the trace elements resulting in the manifestation of deficiency symptoms and the ameliorative measures are discussed (Raju, 1981).

title: Influence of long-term application of NPK to coffee on some micronutrient contents
text: ‘Analysis of soil samples collected from a long-term fertilizer trial receiving graded amounts of NPK ranging from 0:0:0 to 495:374:495 kg/ ha over a period of years revealed that continuous application of fertilizer brought down the soil pH significantly with concomitant increase in available Iron and Manganese. Extractable Zinc and Copper were not appreciably affected, possibly due to the presence of higher content of organic matter resulting in the complexation of these elements. Plant analysis indicated that leaf Manganese increased considerably due to continuous manuring; no perceptible variations were noticed my MICRONUTIUENTS in leaf Jron and Copper, Leaf Zine gradually decreased with increasing doses of fertilizer (Raju and Deshpande, 1985).

title: Effect of organic acids on the uptake of
text: Zinc, Aluminium and Manganese by coffee The occurrence of zinc deficiency of coffee in India is widespread and the most effective current means of correcting the disorder is the foliar spray of zinc sulphate neutralized with lime. The soil application of ZnSO,, was found to be ineffective. Application of ZnSO,, along with oxalic, citric or tartaric acids into soil was found to increase the zinc content in plant tissues considerably. On the other hand aluminum and manganese uptake by plants decreased when soils were amended with organic acids (Jayarama et al., 1988).

title: Effect of micronutrient sprays on Arabica coffee
text: Two micronutrient formulations were evaluated in the field trial to find their effect on the yield and cup quality of Arabica coffee. Statistical analysis of the data collected over 3 seasons indicated no significant difference between the treated and the control plots. Cup quality also revealed no apparent difference in overall quality between the treated and the control (Jayarama et al., 1992).

title: Factors associated with little leaf syndrome
text: It was noticed that the soil samples from plantations manifesting little leaf symptoms contained low amounts of total as well as available Zinc. The soil test data further revealed that higher Phosphorus, Potassium, Calcium, pH and low Organic Carbon and Nitrogen in the soils of affected plantations than in. soils of unaffected plantations without any. appreciable differences in the values of available and total concentration of Iron, Manganese and Copper. Analysis of leaf samples from diseased and healthy plants indicated that the malformed leaves invariably contained less Zinc, while Phosphorus and Potassium were found to be in higher concentration. The concentration of Calcium, Iron and Copper were low in leaves of diseased plants compared to the values in healthy plants. Leaf Manganese was found to be erratic (Raju et al., 1987).

title: Suitable extractant to determine the available Manganese status of soils cropped to coffee
text: A pot culture experiment using seven soils representing different coffee growing zones, to standardize a suitable extractant for assessing available Manganese content in soils cropped to coffee was carried out. Out of 6 extractants tried, Neutral normal Ammonium acetate (NH,OAc) and neutral normal Sodium acetate (NaOAc) were found suitable. There was a significant correlation between soil Manganese extractant by these two reagents and total uptake of Manganese by coffee plants at 5% level (r= 0.4834 and 0.5248 respectively). 0.2% Hydroquinone in neutral normal ammonium acetate extracted more of Manganese and was highly correlated with that of total soil Manganese. title: Foliar nutrition of Arabica coffee
text: In general it is observed that young leaves absorbed more of plant nutrients than old leaves. Hence to obtain maximum response to foliar Sprays it would be advisable to time the sprays during the rapidly flushing periods. Dilute solutions of plant nutrients are better accepted as foliar spray than concentrated solution, as the later cause severe scorching of leaves. An initial low Phosphorus status in the leaf produces greater absorption of Phosphorus. Nitrogen and Phosphorus appeared to be better absorbed when an NPK spray is applied, there being a very little absorption of Potassium. This would appear to indicate that Potassium aids in the better absorption of NPK. Nitrogen appears to produce better responses than Phosphorus and Potassium when applied as foliar spray. The current field experiment was conducted to know the effect of organics and INM method of nutrition, shade pattern and irrigation schedule on the leaf carbohydrate status and yield of genotype S.274. The carbohydrate economy of the plant is usually regarded as an integrated system of sources and sinks. Present experiment shows that, both organic and INM methods of nutrition had a significant effect on leaf carbohydrates and product. Mineral nutrients are elements acquired by the plants primarily in the form of inorganic ions from the soil. After being absorbed by the roots, the mineral elements are translocated into various parts of the plant, where they are utilized in numerous biological and metabolic functions. Macro and micro nutrients are involved in numerous plant metabolic processes; foliar analysis has proven useful in establishing fertilizer schedules that sustain yields and ensure the food quality of many crops. Consequently, the current field experiment is conducted to know the influence of organic and integrated nutrient management practices (INM), on nutrient status of leaf major nutrient composition and yield of Robusta coffee. The results indicated that two flush periods could be discerned. Studies were carried out on the extension growth of primary, secondary and tertiary branches, since topping arrests the growth of the main stem. A period of slow growth from blossom showers up to July is followed by a period of rapid growth from August to October. ‘The vegetative growth slows down with the advent of dry period from November. The growth will be minimum from December to February (dormant period), and is resumed in March after the drought period. The role of environmental and edaphic factors like light, temperature, rainfall and soil moisture on growth is discussed (Vasudeva and Ramaiah, 1979).

title: Physiological studies on flowering in coffee under South Indian conditions: Changes in water content, growth rate, respiration and
text: carbohydrate metabolism of flower buds during bud enlargement and anthesis A comparative study has been made on the progressive changes in the water content, growth rate, respiration and carbohydrate metabolism in mature flower buds (just before blossom showers); during the enlargement of flower buds (after blossom showers) and in the fully opened flowers on the blossom day, in Arabica and Robusta coffee plants grown under field conditions at Central Coffee Research Institute. The results are described and discussed in detail. The data indicate that among the two species, Robusta coffee appear to be physiologically more efficient not only with respect to absorption of more quantities of water from soil by the roots (after blossom showers) and its supply to the flower buds for their renewed growth, ——s 197) F } i Lad but also the flower buds took up more oxygen with lesser availability of respirable substrate (reducing sugars) in the initial days of flower bud enlargement with the advent of blossom showers, as compared to the flower buds of Arabica coffee. This physiological efficiency in Robusta coffee plant offers an intriguing possibility to the plant breeder for its continuous use in breeding programmes. to evolve new cultivars with these advantageous features (Gopal et al., 1975).

title: Physiological studies on flowering in coffer under South Indian conditions: Flowering in relation to foliage and wood starch

The physiological condition of plants prior to blossom showers determines to a great extent the percentage of ‘normal flowering. Measures to be adopted in S.795 Arabica coffee plantations to obtain resumption of active growth in flower buds and maximum percentage of normal flowering are indicated (Gopal et al., 1975).

title: Studies on Ascorbic acid in coffee plants:
text: Distribution in ripe fruits and its relationship with coffee quality Ascorbicacid content was estimated in different components of ripe fruits of Coffea arabica L. (S.795, S.1934 and Kents). Coffea canephora Pierre Ex Froenher var. $.274 and Coffea dewevrei var. excelsa. Among the five plant types there were no significant differences in the Ascorbic acid content in the fruit wall and seed, but there were significant differences in the Ascorbic acid content of the mucilage. The content of Ascorbic acid was in the following order in the various fruit components: seed > fruit wall > mucilage (Vasudeva and Gopal, 1974).

title: Studies on Ascorbic acid in coffee plants:
text: Distribution in pulp and pulp water of ripe fruits The present study relates to the distribution of Ascorbic acid in mucilage and fruit wall of selected ripe fruit of S.795 Arabica and in the pulp and pulp water of bulk ripe fruits of Arabica. Two experiments were conducted one with ripe fruits and another with pulp and pulp water and Ascorbic acid was EEE 211 Pr ee determined. In both the experiments the Ascorbic acid content was significantly more (at 1% level) in fruit wall or pulp than in mucilage or pulp water. In the present study, Ascorbic acid content was lower in fruit wall as well as in mucilage of the ripe fruits in both the experiments as compared to that fund previously (Vasudeva and Gopal, 1973). This was mainly due to the time between the two samplin (fruits for the earlier experiment were aires! during November first week, while the fruits used for the present study were sampled during the last week of December). These studies indicate that the pulp of ripe Arabica coffee fruit contains considerable quantity of Ascorbic acid, which is of much nutritive value (Gopal and Vasudeva, 1974).

title: Transpirational studies on coffee
text: Experiments to evaluate transpirational loss from species and varieties of coffee, in case of Arabica, it was observed that 34% of water lost by transpiration in 24 hours period occurred from upper surface of leaves. Seedlings affected by leaf disease and brown eye spot transpired 154.4% and 124.3% respectively more than healthy Arabica seedlings though the area of fungal infection was <10% to the total leaf area. C. liberica transpired more than canephora, arabica and excelsa in the order stated. Out of 2 commercial species tested canephora and Arabica, the former registered higher transpirational loss than the latter. Spraying both surfaces of leaf of arabica with 2:2:40, Bordeaux mixture checked the rate of transpiration effectively than other treatments including control (Gopalakrishnan and Ananth, 1960).

title: Significance of plant water defic; and yield: A review eficits to growth
text: The intensive m Crop requires rational] irrigation, Plog anes Sich “ag : parameters closure or freezing point depression of cellular Sap are early indicators of plant water deficits. Conversely, the transpiration rate is a very insensitive indicator and cannot be used to determine irrigation requirements. Net photosynthesis is severely affected by small water deficits, a decrease of about 50% being expected from a 92-80% drop in relative turgidity of the leaves. The ratio T/P expresses the relative effect of water stress on transpiration and photosynthesis and therefore is a valuable selective parameter for drought resistance and has a great value under the perspective of agricultural economy. Other effects of plant water deficits on respiration, flowering and fruiting processes as well as some of the more important points which deserve further investigation are also discussed (Nunes, 1976).

Mctabolism of P was greater in root system of Robusta than in Arabica as indicated by more phosphate accumulation between 2 types of coffee species, Robusta absorbed more phosphate with both types of phosphate application than Arabica. The economic way of single Superphosphate application to both the species of coffee appears to be by foliar spray. It is safe to spray Superphosphate solution in a pH range of about 6.5 to 7.0 since too acidic solution may injure the plants and more insoluble phosphate may form at alkaline pH of the spray solution. It is advisable that Superphosphate may be sprayed at a time when the plants are physically more active since plants usually require more quantity of P during this period (Gopal et al., 1977).

title: Respiration in the mature embryos of coffee
text: Oxygen consumption and_ Respiratory Quotient (RQ) values in the embryos of 15 coffee types were studied. The RQ values showed an inverse relation to their weights. Higher RQ values recorded might be due to the involvement of TCA cycle intermediates as respiratory substrates. The data obtained rule out fermentation as a natural event in the embryo respiration (Sudhakara et al., 1977).

title: Changes in the respiratory quotient (RQ) of embryos of Coffea canephora ‘S.274’ with time
text: The linear increase of RQ with time in embryos of Coffea canephora ‘S.274 has been explained on the grounds that the material might respire on low to highly oxidized TCA cycle intermediates in a sequential fashion (Sudhakar, et. al., 1977).

title: Variability among the sibmated progenies of theree arabica selections for resistance to coffee leaf rust
text: Coffee leaf rust incidence was recorded from an experimental plot of sib-mated progenies of arabica coffee cultivars viz., Sln.5B. Sln.7.3 and SIn.10 for a period of five years from 1999 to 2003. The maximum mean percentage of rust incidence recorded was 79.73 in SIn.10 (Sib. 3), 41.75 in SIn.5B (Sib. 3) and 31.96 in SiIn.7.3 (Sib. 4). Variability in terms of rust incidence from 0.95% to 79.73% was found among the sib-mated progenies, indicating the wide variation of the genotypes for resistance to coffee rust pathogen. Of the three arabica selections studied, siblings of Sln.10 had highest rust incidence (79.73%) whereas the progenies of SIn.5B and Sln.7.3 showed certain level of resistance as indicated by low disease index. A rust incidence level of less than 10% was recorded in the sib-mated progenies of SIn.5B (SIn.1, 2 and 4) and SIn.7.3 (SIn.1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and 11). These siblings, with low rust scale could be exploited further in the breeding programme for coffee leaf rust disease resistance. Yield data indicated a variation in yield ranging from 398 to 927 kg/ha (clean coffee) among the sib-mated progenies. Among the siblings and within the selection, the yield varied from 476 to 912 kg/ha in SIn.5B; from 398 to 927 kg/ha in SIn.7.3 and from 580 to 862 kg/ha (clean coffee) in SIn.10 (Daivasikamani et al.,2005). ___ Rainfall during March/April, number 007 UU meee f it (Oia taco j j it at ti

title: Charncterization of virolent rust —_ ot Hemileia vastatrix from traditional coffee regions of India
text: Clones of thirty five rust race differentials ar indicator plants and twenty-four “A type” plant materials (Sarchimor, Cavimor, Catimor, Catimor * Catuaii and HDT accession lines), introduced from CIFC Portugal, were multiplied and established at eight different locations for trapping specific rust race/races. All the indicator clones were monitored regularly for rust incidence for nearly eight years. Around four hundred rust spore samples collected from the differentials, A type” plants and coffee fields from diverse locations in the traditional coffee growing areas of South India were differentiated from 2004 onwards. The rust race trapping strategy adopted in the present study proved to be very effective and it is of interest that as many as thirty-four rust races could be differentiated within a short period of eight years, among which fifteen were new races. The most significant finding in the present study is that two HDT lines (CIFC 832/1 and 832/2) which remained resistant to all the known races at CIFC and in the field for over 60 years were found susceptible to leaf rust in Kodagu. region of Karnataka and Pulney hills of Tamil Nadu. Rust races with virulent genes V2,5,6,7,8,9,? and V2,4,5,6,7,8,9,? were isolated from 832/1 and 832/2 respectively. Both these HDT lines were used as resistance source for evolving the most popular cultivars such as Catimor, Sarchimor and Cavimor which are widely cultivated in most of the coffee growing countries throughout the world. Hence, the rust pathogen is likely to overcome the resistance of Sarchimor and Cavimor in the near future (Sudhakar et al., 2013)

text: Coffee being a perennial crop, harbours pathogens on all parts of the plant continuously and the intensity of diseases increase under favourable conditions. Coffee Leaf Rust (CLR) caused by the fungus Hemileia vastatrix Berk. & Br. is one among the most important diseases affecting coffee all over the world. Coffea arabica L. is well known to be highly susceptible to leaf rust (Wellman, 1953; Waller, 1982). The infection leads to foliage and berries loss up to up to 50 and 70% respectively (Sudhakar et al., 2014). Under favourable conditions, the disease appears after the blossom showers in March/April. Foliage present at that period is mostly of the previous season and the fungus remains dormant on these infected leaves during the dry weather from December to February and sporulates to form fresh uredospores after the blossom showers (Muthappa et al., 1989). The season-II (post-monsoon period) recorded less disease reduction compared to season-I (pre-monsoon period) (Daivasikamani and Rajanaika, 2009). 2.4.4, Efficacy of biological agent Lecanicillium lecanii for the management of coffee leaf rust in India Coffee leaf rust (CLR), caused by Hemileia vastatrix, is a major disease affecting Coffea arabica worldwide, including India. While CLR management relies on fungicide use and resistant cultivars, biological control remains underexplored. Field studies identified a hyperparasite, Lecanicillium lecanii, colonizing CLR lesions and inactivating uredospores. In vitro studies showed that L. lecanii culture filtrate (CF) significantly (P < 0.01) inhibited uredospore germination. In vivo, uredospore discoloration (white) occurred within a week in treatments where L. lecanii was applied 24 - 48 hours before CLR inoculation. Among 11 Arabica cultivars, SIn.3 (S.795) showed the highest hyperparasitization (63%), followed by Sln.12 (51%). These findings suggest L. lecanii could be used as a prophylactic biological control for CLR, particularly in moderately tolerant or susceptible varieties (Divya et al., 2024).

title: Screening of coffee for resistance against brown eye spot
text: Six commercially important cultivars of C. arabica and 3 of C. canephora were screened in the nursery against brown eye spot caused by Cercospora coffeicola. It is clear from the result that no cultivar is resistant to disease and all of them were equally susceptible. Difference in the degree of susceptibility noticed was 2 in the 13 observations recorded for 2 years. The incidence recorded in Sln.11 & 8 of Arabica and 10 & 11 of Robusta in 2 observations during 2 years of trial was significantly lower. Inspite of some disease build up, there was less defoliation and the plants were fit for transplanting in the field. Growing plants under filtered shade did not considerably reduce the vigour of the plant (Nataraj, 1986).

title: Viability of Rhizoctonia solani
text: Rhizoctonia solani, coffee strain, which causes collar rot or damping off of coffee seedlings in the nursery stage, is a soil inhabitant. The outcome of the result indicates that the sclerotia of R. solani burried in the soil survive for more than one year in the seed beds. The survived sclerotia act as the primary inoculum for the next season and this leads to the perpetuation of the pathogen in the soil. Therefore, it is suggested to use the fresh soil every year to prepare the seed beds after removing the old soil completely (Venkatasubbaiah and Safeeulla, 1983). tts

title: Importance of inoculum density of
text: Rhizoctonia solani An attempt was made to relate the inoculum density and disease expression in collar rot infection of coffee seedlings. Results reveal that there was a linear relationship between inoculum density and disease expression up to inoculum densities of 25% and there after a gradual decline in infection was observed in both sterilized and unsterilized soils. While maximum infection (100%) was apparent from 5-25% inoculum density in sterilized soil, whereas between 25- 50% inoculum densities in unsterilized soil maximum infection was observed. The disease incidence was less in unsterilized soil than in sterilized soil. The decrease in disease incidence at higher inoculum densities might be a reflection of the operation of auto-inhibition by the propagules. Based on the fact that 5% inoculum density in sterilized soil would suffice to achieve 100% infection, it can be speculated that this represents the threshold value (Venkatasubbaiah and Safeeulla, 1983).

title: In vitro screening of Trichoderma spp.
text: against collar rot pathogen The success of establishing new plantations of a perennial crop like coffee mainly depends on the use of healthy seedlings with good vigour for planting. For this purpose, it is most essential to protect the seedlings in the primary and secondary nursery beds from attacks of pest and diseases. Coffee seedlings at the nursery stage are susceptible to fungal diseases. In the present study four Trichoderma spp. were tested for their ability to inhibit soil borne pathogen Rhizoctonia solani Kuhn. causing collar rot in coffee seedlings. Dual culture technique revealed that T: hamatum (75.68%) highly inhibited mycelial growth of pathogen followed by T: koningii (65.92), T: viride (57.90%) and T. harzianum (52.71%) respectively. title: Histopathological and histochemical changes due to Rhizoctonia solani in coffee seedlings
text: Rhizoctonia solani, the collar rot pathogen of coffee seedlings, penetrated the host tissue forming infection cushion and infection pegs. The fungal spread was both inter and intra cellular. Among various tissues, epidermis and cortex were more vulnerable to fungal invasion. The establishment of pathogen lead to the formation of sclerotia in the cortex. Distortion of the collar tissue and formation of cavities in the cortex was the common anomaly. The histochemical analysis of the infected collar tissue indicated reduction in insoluble polysaccharides, starch, protein and nucleic acid content (Venkatasubbaiah et al., 1984).

title: Red root rot of coffee
text: Gradual declining of plants resulted in periodical removal of several dead plants. It was observed that the declining plants were infected by red root disease fungus, Poria hypolateritia Berk. It was reported that, this fungus is causing red root disease of Tea in Sri Lanka which is a a nOOoT DISEASES serious problem. This constitutes the first record of Poeria causing red root rot of Arabica. Yellowing of leaves, defoliation and die-back of twigs leading to thinness are the first aerial symptoms seen on affected plants. The roots are seen with red, ribbon like strands of the fungal mycelium. Isolation of the diseased plant or the affected area by trenching will be a necessary step to contain the infection in case more effective control measures through soil fumigation are not possible (Venkataram and Muthappa, 1975).

title: Red root disease in coffee

Among the four root diseases, brown root disease caused by Phellinus noxius is predominantly observed and affects both Arabica and Robusta cultivars. Presently, brown root disease is managed by adopting integrated disease management practices which also includes drenching of the fungicide carbendazim 50 WP. Of late, it has been observed that the ineffectiveness of the fungicide may be due to the acquired resistance by the pathogen against the fungicide. In addition, most importantly carbendazim is included in draft order of banned pesticides list. Hence, exploring an alternative fungicide is need of the hour. In this context, laboratory bioassays were carried out to find an alternative fungicide for the management of brown root disease of coffee. Eight fungicide molecules with three concentrations viz., 1000, 2000 and 3000 ppm were tested by following poison food technique. Results indicated that, Propiconazole 25% EC, Tebuconazole 25.9% EC, Difenoconazole 25% EC, Propiconazole 13.9% + Difenoconazole 13.9% EC, Trifloxystrobin 25% + Tebuconazole 50% WG and Fluxapyroxad 167 g/L + Pyraclostrobin 333 g/L were highly effective and recorded 100 % mycelial inhibition. Whereas, Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC recorded inhibition of 99.38% followed by — azoxystrobin 23% SC (72.10%). title: Air-spora of coffee plantations
text: The qualitative and quantitative changes in the air-spora of coffee field at CCRI was studied continuously from 1* January to 31* December, 1988 using Burkard volumetric spore trap kept at a height of 1.98 m above the ground level. About 22 types of fungal spores along with ascospores, basidiospores, conidiospores, fern spores, hyphal fragments, insects, insect hairs and scales, pollen grains, plant hairs, trichomes and xylem elements, smut spores, uredospores and dust particles caught in the trap were considered under group classified and others not included in the above categories were considered under group unclassified to estimate the quantum of total air-spora. Spore concentration was maximum during the months of September and October and minimum in April and May corresponding to wet and dry conditions respectively. Diurnal periodicity of the total airspora exhibited peak concentration between 0 and 6.00 hours. Cladosporium, ascospores and basidiospores constituted 83% of the total air-spora. However, it may be concluded that there is no spore free season in coffee plantation (Hanumantha et al., 1991).

text: , Arabica coffee grafted on to Robusta root stock Coffee, both Arabica and Robusta can be rejuvenated by collar pruning the old and unproductive plants and allowing new shoots to develop from the stump. For this, the old plants are stumped at a height of nine inches from the ground on receipt of first summer showers and when the new suckers develop, two or three sturdy ones are retained for further training one into a healthy plant. The advantage here is that the root system is already well developed and so the new shoot comes to bearing earlier than if a plant had been raised from a seed. While doing such type of rejuvenation pruning, it is also possible to graft shoot material from high yielding disease resistant varieties by wedge cleft grating method (Anonymous, 2000). For this, the healthiest among the suckers, of about pencil thickness, that develop during the summer period is selected and a horizontal cut is made just below the first node. On this a straight downward cut to a depth of 1 to 1.5 cm is made, which acts as the cleft. The scion that is to be grafted, of the same thickness as the scion, is selected and a single node cutting is made. The lower tip of this is cut into the shape of a wedge and then inserted into the cleft and the union is tied into place using strips of polythene. After the union is firm, in about 45 to 60 days, the strips of polythene are removed. Normally, from this single node cutting that is grafted, only each leaf axil. title: Studies on the flight periods of coffee white stem borer
text: Maximum number of adults was recorded in the months of April to June and October to December on Pulney hills and in May and October to January on Shevaroy hills. No flight of the adults was recorded in September on Pulneys and July to September on Shevaroys. Small number of adults was recorded in other months also both in Pulneys and Shevaroys. The flight periods of the adults in respect of North East monsoon areas were not dissimilar from South West monsoon areas. A few beetles which emerged other than during April to May and October to January were due to weather conditions like temperature, rainfall and prolonged cloudy weather (Bhaskara and Bhat, 1987).

text: Coffee stem borer adults were Provided with different materials to check the Oviposition. In first set of experiment, three methods compared are as follows; Providing stem powder coated Paper cards to the beetles, Providing cut stems wrapped with strips of polyethylene to the beetles, Confining beetles in plastic containers with the mouth covered with cloth and inverting the container either with a lid containing stem powder or on to a paper sheet. In second set of experiments the container method was tried but with stem powder made from Arabica, Robusta, Cedrela toona and Dalbergia latifolia stems individually was used. This was to check if the material in the lid had any role in determining the oviposition capacity. The data presented shows that the mean number eggs collected was always more in the container method with plain paper (93.75 eggs/paper/25 females) whereas it was very low when stems with polyethylene wrapping (09.37 eggs/stem/25 females) or nylon mesh was provided (7.75 eggs/stem/25 females). Possibly the beetles that emerged during the summer flight lay eggs and develop into adults and emerge in the winter flight season and vice versa. title: Biology of Apenesiasahyadrica, a parasitoid of the coffee white stem borer
text: The parasitoid, Apenesia sahyadrica was multiplied in the laboratory on white stem borer larvae for the first time in India. Males were smaller in size compared to females, winged and black in color with 6.24 + 0.19 mm length, whereas females were wingless, dark brown in color with a length of 6.53 + 0.18 mm. The gravid female searched for the host larvae and paralyzed it before egg laying. More numbers of eggs were laid on the posterior lateral side of the host larvae. The average number of eggs laid was 8.03 + 0.49 eggs/day with a range of 1 to 15 eggs. The mated female could lay on an average of 17.52 +1.11 eggs in one single clutch. A female during her life span, laid 53.64 + 3.06 eggs. The eggs were elongate, oval, translucent, pale white in color, measuring 0.78 + 0.01 mm in length and 0.300.004 mm in width. Incubation period was less than 5 days. There were four larval instars with a total larval period of 10 to 12 days. The larval instars could be differentiated by the size and number of dentates. Pupation was inside the cocoon and pupal period lasted for 17.83 + 1.91days. The total duration of life cycle was 31.36 + 0.67 days. The sex ratio was generally one male to five females. Longevity of female wasps was 66.48 + 3.66 days and that of males was 7.96 + 0.3 days (Seetharama et al., 2007). fre

title: Varietal preference of Coffee Berry Borer
text: The present study was conducted in the laboratory and field to know the preference of berry borer of different coffee varieties like C. canephora, C. arabica, C. liberica and C. eugenioides. The laboratory experiment was replicated eight times, and each replication contained 80 seeds, a mixture of 20 parchment seeds painted with different colours. The preference to the seeds of C. arabica was significantly higher, followed by C. canephora, E eau e baie: 7 C. racemosa and Instly C. liberica in the laboratory condition. However, the fecundity of the beetle was higher in © cancphora followed by C. arabica. In C. liberica and C. racemosa the fecundity was very low. The observations on the field showed a significant preference of beetles for C. arabica followed by C. cancphora, C. liberica and C. eugenioides. However, there was no significant difference in fecundity between C. canephora and C. arabica. The fecundity in C. canephora and C. arabica was significantly higher than C. eugenioides and C. liberica. Thus, the above studies indicated that there is no significant difference in the susceptibility of C. arabica and C. canephora to the berry borer. However, among the species screened C. arabica and C. canephora are more prone to borer attack than other species. It has been well documented that the insect fecundity is greatly influenced by host species differences (Vijayalakshmi et. al., 1999).

title: Observations on the position of attack of the berry borer
text: To study the mode of attack of the coffee berry borer, an observational trial was conducted at the Kalyanamandiram estate, Puliyarmala, Kalpetta, Kerala. Twenty five plants in the infested estate were observed, dividing their height into upper, middle and lower tiers. One branch each’ from each tier was examined for infestation, counting the total number of fruits and infested fruits. Likewise, the infestation percentages, at the top of the branches, middle of the branch and base of the branch were calculated by counting the infested fruits, selecting two clusters at the top, middle and two nodes adjacent to the main stem. Similarly, plants were observed to find out, whether the position of the plant in the estate, affected infestation. Every 5" plant at the road side i.e., to the periphery of the plantation was examined for infestation. Plant infestation and fruit infestation were recorded. Likewise, leaving 10 plants in a row to the interior of the plantation, similar observations were recorded. Observations showed the plants positioned at the periphery of the plantation are more to pest attack as evident from both plant and fruit infestation (Vijayalakshmi et. al., 2000).

Ladybird _ beetle, Biology of the A predator Cryptolaemus montrouzieri, of mealy bugs The biology of the ladybird beetle, Cryptolaemus montrouzieri (Coleoptera, Coccinellidae), which is a predator of mealy bugs was studied under laboratory conditions. The incubation period was 5-6 days. The durations of the first, second, third and fourth instar larvae were 3 to 4, 4 to 5 and 7 to 8 days respectively. Prepupal and pupal periods ranged from 3 to 4 and 7 to 8 days respectively. Studies on longevity, fecundity and sex ratio were carried out. title: Biological control with exotic as well as indigenous natural enemies
text: os While defining the biological control, which is the regulation of an organism's population density by natural enemies, the paper elaborates further the overall phenomenon of natural control. Additional control by introducing natural enemies or by manipulating available natural enemies or the environment is also brought about. The author groups the natural enemies into parasites, predators and pathogens. How biological control in coffee mealy bug has been brought about is discussed in the paper (Chacko, 1987).

title: Mealy bugs of coffee and their control measure
text: Mealy bugs are major sucking pests of coffee. They occur both on Arabica and Robusta, se if gas i but a major pest of Robusta. Among a number of species of mealy bugs that attack coffee, the ae common ones include Planococcus citri (Risso) anc P. lilacinus (Cockerell). The biology of the mealy bug has been described and the ecological a that help the pest attack and the damage to coffee have been narrated. Apart from different control measures against the mealy bug, bio-control with the help of exotic predator i.¢., Australian ladybird beetle, Cryptolaemus montrouzieri and Leptomastix dactylopii the parasitoid are dealt with in this paper. Further indigenous natural enemies although are noticed are unable to exert desired control over the mealy bugs (Venkataramaiah and Ramaiah, 1988).

title: Bio-efficacy of neem formulations alone and in combination with synthetic insecticide against mealybug, Planococcus citri (Risso) on Coffea
text: Bioefficacy of some neem formulations viz, Econeem 0.3%, Gronim 0.15%, Neem Limnoids EC and Azadirachtin 1500 ppm alone at the dosages of 15 ml and 25 ml/litre, the same neem formulations at the dosage of 10 ml/litre in combination with half the recommended dose of Quinalphos 20 AF (0.75 ml/litre) and full dose of Quinalphos 20 AF (1.5 ml/litre) was evaluated against coffee mealy bug, P citri (Risso) (Homoptera: Pseudococcidae) on three-year old Coffea arabica plants at the Coffee Research Station, Chikkamangaluru. The results revealed that spraying of neem formulations alone at 15 ml or 25 ml/litre resulted in a significant reduction of 86.56 to 88.33% of the mealybug population as against 83.55% at the recommended dose of Quinalphos 20 AF (1.5 ml) alone during the post-treatment period up to 20 days. title: Attendant ants and activity of Spalgis epius
text: The mealy bug, Pcitri is always found in attendance with different species of ants, simple tests revealed the interference of the ants with the activity of Spalgis epius. The aggressiveness of the ants and S. epius population appeared to have a negative relationship. The base data on the activity of S. epius on mealy bug infested branches of the coffee plants attended by three different species of ants indicated that the ant species belonging to the genus Crematogaster interfered more with the predetor activity than the ant Oececophylla smaragdina. ‘The caterpillar number was much more on mealy bugs attended by non-aggressive ant, Anoplolepis longipes. There was an immediate improvement in the activity of S. epius and the mealy bug population was reduced considerably when ant movement was restricted. The onisci form nature of the caterpillars give them total protection from the ants because the head, legs and the soft ventral surface are completely covered by the bulging dorsal surface (Vinod Kumar et al., 2008).

title: Effect of augmentation of Spalgis epius on mealybug population
text: Release of known number of S epius caterpillars on the mealybug population on coffee plants indicated that ten to twenty caterpillars per plant were able to reduce the mealy bug population in a very short time even in the presence of attendant ants. Small numbers of the caterpillar are less likely to bring about appreciable control. The pre-release infestation of coffee plants in the selected 0.5 hectare plot was reasonably high and a random survey of the infested nodes indicated very less activity of the caterpillars of S. epius. Two releases of 450 pupae of S. epius, one at the end of February and the other during March end in the first year increased the average number of caterpillars slightly and the percentage of infested nodes decreased to some extent. Restriction of ant movement and subsequent release during the second year increased the number of caterpillars. 317 Ee a Even the pre-release estimate in the second year indicated that there was a slight improvement in the activity of S. epius than the previous year. By the month of April the predatory activity of S. epius caterpillars was much more noticeable and the percentage of infested nodes reduced considerably. This reduced level was maintained till the onset of monsoon. Overall there was a better predatory performance by S. epius due to repeated release (Vinod Kumar, et. al., 2009).

title: Survival of Leptomastix dactylopii (how) during winter season
text: The survival of L. dactylopii during the winter season in Wayanad district is reported in this paper. The parasitoids were multiplied in glass house on mealy bug infested pumpkins and field releases were made in seven Robusta coffee estates of Wayanad district in Kerala. About 25,000 parasitoids were released in a hectare plot of each estate during October 2005. The infestation level was medium (6-20 mealy bugs per node). Follow up observations were made during January 2006. The percentage parasitism of mealy bugs by L. dactylopii during winter season of Wayanad ranged from 25.34 + 5.94 to 39.68 + 3.33 with a mean of 33.63 + 4.87. It is noteworthy that L. dactylopii was able to survive the winter season and to bring about substantial control of mealy bugs. This may be due to the non severity of winter in Wayanad compared to other countries (Abdul Rahiman, et. al., 2009).

title: Studies on the control of coffee mealy bug,
text: Planococcus lilacinus Results of the tests with Dimecron, Telodrin and Folidol on the coffee mealy bug, Planococcus lilacinus are reported. Folidol supplemented with BHC 5% dust is significantly superior to the rest in almost all the observational periods at 0.01% and 0.02% a.i. Dimecron (plus BHC 5% dust) presents enhanced potency in 21 days. Telodrin (0.02% a.i.) is appreciably effective in 10 days but gradual build up of bug population is noticed in 21 days.
