title: Effect of insecticides on Spalgis epius
text: Three insecticides namely Ekalux 25 EC (quinalphos). Curacron 50 EC (profenofos) and Actara 25 WG (thiamethoxam) were tested for their toxicity on the coffee mealy bug P. citri and the indigenous Lycaenid predator S. epius. The LC,, dose for the mealy bugs was estimated to be 0.01875% a.i. for Ekalux 25 EC, 0.01 % a.i. for r ; Curacron 80 EC and 0.01125% a.i. for Actara 25 WG. Based on this it was concluded that among the three insecticides tested, Curacron 50 EC was more potent against the mealy bugs. Direct spray of the insecticides, at three dosages, on eggs of S. epius prevented the eggs from hatching; higher doses of the insecticides caused more mortality of the eggs. With the third instar caterpillar stage, which is the most active feeding stage of the butterfly predator, the effect was similar. In the residue film method, the insecticides proved to be toxic with the effect persisting beyond 21 days for both the caterpillar and adult stage. When tested in the field using III instar caterpillars, the effect of the insecticides was acute during the first few weeks and then gradually declined, but slight effect of the insecticide could be detected even up to the 56" day after spraying, indicating the longer residual effect. Spraying of the three insecticides on mealy bug infested plants showed that on the first few days both the pest i.e. Mealy bug P citriand its natural enemy S. epius were totally eliminated from the plants. But the mealy bug population started increasing gradually by the third week of spray. There was no sign of activity of any natural enemies during this period and later. Only by about 45 days after spray a few natural enemies like the encyrtid Leptomastix dactylopii and the common coccinellid Pullus pallidicollis made their appearance on the mealy bug colony. Only after another week a few caterpillars of S. epius were noticed. This indicated that the predator S. epius was extremely sensitive to the insecticide sprays (Vinod Kumar et al., 2010).

text: Green bug is a common pest of Arabica all over South India. It is however endemic to the Shevaroys, mainly because of the availability of green flush during the entire year. title: Biological contro] of coffee green scale
text: During cooler months 3 i fungi attack the scale and check the buildup a Population under natural conditions, High relative humidity and low temperature are essential for the epizootics of the fungi. Of the three, Verticillium lecanii is the most effective and it causes 30-95% mortality. The fungus is also compatible with most of the insecticides even though germination of fungal spores is inhibited by insecticide. 8x10° spores/ml and Fenthion 0.1% combination is better. A surfactant may be added @ 0.5 ml/L to increase the effectiveness. During summer a humectant (Glycerol 0.1%) can be added. Addition of wetting agent during summer will increase the pathogenicity of the fungus. Use of these biological agents on coffee green scales effectively controls the pest with least disruption to the ecosystem (Rajavel et al., 1989).

The infections of pathogen commencing in June reaches its peak September affecting majority of the scale population and peak incidence of parasitism of scales occurs in May. The natural enemies of green scale in the field are quite active and either the pathogen or the parasitoid is continuously operating upon the pest, depending on the weather conditions. Hence any pesticide application aimed at reducing the pest should be judicious and limited only to spot application so as to have least effect on the biotic agents in the field (Bhaskara and Bhat, 1989).

text: Nuvacron 40 EC and Rogor 30 EC were more effective and gave consistently effective control against green bug at 2 concentrations tried, 0.025% and 0.05% than other chemicals. title: Control of hairy caterpillars on coffee estates in South India
text: A few control measures suggested such as; (1) Set up light traps in June July to catch the adult moths during break in monsoon. (2) During July lop branches of shade trees and destroy egg masses. (3) Collect and destroy clusters of caterpillars or dust them with Folidol 1.5% dust or Metacid combi 2% dust. (4) Most effective and cheapest control measures is to collect and destroy all the pupae. (5) Digging and liming during the month of February and March. (6) Coffee and Dadap may be sprayed with Metacid combi 40 EC @ 8 Ozs/barrel of water + 1 lb. Fish-oil- resin soap or DDT + Parathion compound or BHC 50 WP at 2 Kg + 1 Ib. Fish- oilresin soap/barrel of water (Bhat, 1972).

title: Laboratory evaluation of some insecticides for the control of hairy caterpillar

title: Preliminary screening with antifeedants against hairy caterpillar attacking coffec
text: The present study on hairy caterpillar, Eupterote canaraica’ Moore _ (Lepidoptera, Eupterotidea), was “undertaken to assess the efficacy of two antifeedants, viz., Brestan 60 (Fentin acetate) and Du-Ter 20 WP (Fentin hydroxide). In the first trial, the antifeedants were sprayed at 0.06% a.i. Both Brestan and Du-Ter showed some promise. Only little feeding was noticed in both the treatments. In control, the caterpillars fed well. However, no death of caterpillar was observed. In the second and third trials, the chemicals were sprayed at 0.2 and 0.4% a.i. respectively (Bhat and Chacko, 1976).

title: Control of Eupterote canaraica attacking coffee
text: Life history and bionomics of hairy caterpillar are studied. Adults are attracted to ordinary electric light and petromax, but not to coloured lights. They are not attracted to chemicals like Trichloro ethylene, Furfurol etc. Metacid 50EC, Dipterex 95SP and Metacid combi 40 EC at 0.05% in the laboratory and Thiodan 35EC and Dipterex 95SP at 0.015% (using low volume spray) in the field gave effective control of caterpillar (Bhat and Ananda, 1978).

title: Insecticidal control trials against Eupterote canaraica infesting coffee
text: Laboratory and field trials were conducted to evaluate effectiveness of Metacid 50EC and Sumithion 50EC on Eupterote canaraica. In the field both the insecticides gave effective control at 0.02, 0.04 and 0.06% a.i. In the laboratory Metacid gave effective kill at all the three concentrations but Sumithion only at 0.06% a.i (Chacko and Bhat, 1981).

title: Record of Metarhizium cylindrosporum
text: (Hypocreales: Clavicipitaceae) on Terpnosia psecas from India During a survey for entomopathogens in the coffee ecosystem, a light green fungus infecting adults of the cicada Terpnosia psecas Walker was encountered in the farm of the Central Coffee Research Institute in Chikmagalur district. Karnataka, India (13° 22M N, 750 28 E and 850 m). The cadavers of three males and one female with fungal growth were found attached to the trunks of certain shade trees during August-October 2011. Microscopic examination of the fungus revealed two types of conidia. The microconidia were ellipsoidal (3.4-6.9 x 2.3 mm) and macroconidia banana shaped (11.6-23.1 x 2.8 mm). The fungus was identified as Metarhizium cylindrosporum based on the light green colour of the conidial mass and the conidial measurements (Balakrishnan et al., 2012).

Canephora Pierte ex Fr) coffee plants reacted differently to the five Pratylenchus spp. P brachyurus, P. coffeae, P. flakkensis, P vulnus and P zeae. The commonly occurring nematode species in the coffee tracts of South India P brachyurus and P. coffeae readily infested and multiplied fast on both the coffees. P zeae however, did not multiply on Robusta. Based on the results obtained, a pathogencity study involving P brachyurus and P. coffeae and the two coflee species were conducted in the laboratory and found that P brachyurus and was highly pathogenic to both the coffee species while Robusta showed tolerance to P. coffeae. In another study existence of four biological races in P. coffeae i.e., coflee, cardamom, pavetta and bamboo races was confirmed. Possibility of existence of ‘Robusta race, which is more virulent to Robusta, in Kodagu District of Karnataka was discussed. As a result of these two factors i.e., highly pathogenic nature of P brachyurus to Robusta and existence of a Robusta race, the departmental recommendation to manage nematode problem which hitherto included the replacement of arabica with Robusta or arabicaRobusta grafted plants, however, has to be recasted (Kumar, 1988).

text: Eight insecticides and two fungicides used in coffee pest and disease management were tested at recommended dosages in a simple preliminary trial in the laboratory, to find out their relative toxicity on the emergence of the parasitoid, L. dactylopii How. title: Impact of drying surface and raking frequencies on mould incidence, ochratoxin
text: A contamination and cup quality during preparation of Arabica and Robusta cherries at the farm level The aim of this study was to evaluate the impact and contribution of various drying surfaces (soil, cement, and tarpaulin) and raking frequencies (1 and 4/day) on the incidence of toxigenic molds, ochratoxin A (OTA) production, and on the overall cup quality during preparation of arabica and robusta coffee cherry in India. Two individual experimental batches (run 1 at the begin of harvest and run 2 at the end of harvest) were set up for the study. Results showed high incidence of molds in coffee dried on soil surface compared with that on cement and tarpaulin surfaces. In both arabica and robusta, OTA could be detected in Aspergillus ochraceus contaminated samples at the end of harvest. Raking of the cherries 4 times/day showed lower fungal incidence with no OTA levels detected. Overall, coffee cherry prepared by drying on tarpaulin surface with 4 rakings/day showed lower OTA and fungal incidence with good and acceptable cup quality and this is recommended to be practiced at the farm level (Velmourougane et al., 2010).

title: Relationship between sensory perceived acidity and instrumentally measured acidity in Indian coffee samples
text: A study was taken up to evaluate the relationship between the sensory perceived acidity and instrumentally measured acidity in thirteen coffee samples representing the two major commercially cultivated coffee varieties viz., Coffea arabica (arabica coffee) and C. canephora (Robusta coffee) in India. The acidity level in these coffee samples was assessed by three ways viz., organoleptic (sensory perceived) scoring, pH meter and titratable acidity. The results of this study revealed that acidity level assessed by the organoleptic scoring matched with the acidity level measured by pH meter and titratable assay method. Statistical analysis of these results indicated there was close correlation between sensory perceived acidity and instrumentally measured acidity as evidenced by the correlation coefficient (r2) value ranging from 0.86 to 0.99 (Basavaraj et al., 2014). text: The normal practice of coffee planters for cleaning dried cherry is time consuming, laborious, and totally depends on natural wind conditions. A low-cost power-operated dry cherry winnower was, therefore, developed at Central Coffee Research Institute, Karnataka. The dry cherry winnower consisted of a hopper, blower unit (exhaust fan), cherry outlet, and frame with an overall of 1.28 (L) x 0.7 (W) x 1.6 arabica 1.) and ro dimension 3 (CH) m. Air velocity of 4 m/s was effective with lower percentage of blown cherry. Cleaning efficiency of arabica cherry was 99.85%, 99.73%, and 98.85% at 20, 25, and 30 kg.min"' feed rate, respectively. Similarly, the cleaning efficiency of robusta cherry was 99.74%, 99.1 1%, and 98.53% at 20, 25, and 30 kg/min feed rates. The output capacity ranged from 1,200 kg/h to 1,807 kg/h for arabica cherry, and 1,220 kg/h to 1,821 kg/h for robusta cherry. Higher cleaning efficiency of 99.85% and 99.74% were recorded for arabica and robusta cherry, respectively, at 20 kg/min feed rate and 4 m/s air velocity. The average power consumption was 0.375 kwh. The cost of operation of the winnower was Rs. 105/hour. The estimated cost of the winnower was Rs. 16,000 per unit. title: Post-harvest evaluation of arabica and robusta coffee for physical, mechanical and aerodynamic properties
text: Knowledge about physicomechanical and aerodynamic properties is indispensable for any crop that undergoes post-harvest processing; coffee is no exception. These properties are the most crucial parameters for designing and developing processing machinery and storage structure. As far as coffee is concerned, these properties are imperative for designing dryers, hullers, peelercum-polisher and size graders. Though coffee is one of the leading plantation crops in India, published reports on physical, mechanical and aerodynamic properties are rather limited. In this direction, a study was attempted to generate data cod in respect of physical (length, width, thickness, volume, surface area, thousand seed weight, bulk density, true density and porosity), mechanical (angle of repose and co-efficient of friction) and aerodynamic (terminal velocity) property in different coffee types (parchment, cherry and clean coffees of both Arabica and Robusta varieties). At the prescribed moisture content of 11%, the length, width, thickness, volume and _ surface area were significantly higher (p=0.05) in cherry coffee, followed by parchment and clean coffees. The porosity, bulk density and true density were found in the order of 45 to 58%, 395 to 466 kg/m? and 856 to 944 kg/m? for cherry, 56 to 57%, 400 to 410 kg/m, 950 to 966 kg/m’ for parchment and 37.5 to 44%, 691 to 780 kg/m? and 1,106 to 1,401 kg/m? for clean coffee, respectively. There were no significant differences between coffee types in respect of angle of repose, co-efficient of friction and terminal velocity. title: Incidence of toxigenic moulds in cured & uncured coffee samples
text: The presence of mycotoxins particularly Ochratoxin-A (OTA) in coffee is drawing attention of the consumers as it causes health hazard. OTA is a nephrotoxic mycotoxin classified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) as a possible carcinogen. This toxin is known to be produced by Aspergillus ochraceus and Penicillium sp. Studies have been initiated to know the extent contamination particularly toxigenic fungi in the final product of both Arabica and Robusta coffee. As a part of the study, a survey on contamination of mould in cured and uncured samples of coffee at different curing works in Chikkamagaluru and Hassan zones was conducted. The results of the survey revealed that Aspergillus sp. was found to be predominant in all the samples (18-89%), followed by Fusarium sp. (15-43%) and yeast (17-37%). The moulds like Penicillium sp., Rhizopus sp, Mucor sp. and Cladosporium sp. were also observed in most of the samples from both the zones. The presence of toxin producing mould like A. ochraceus was found to be more in Arabica and Robusta cherry than in parchment. However, its presence was noticed in cuts, bits and black beans of both Arabica and Robusta processed by wet and dry method. In general, the frequency of A. ochraceus and Penicillium sp. recorded was high in dry processed coffee than in wet processed coffee (Panneerselvam et al., 2000).

title: Coffee husk - A _ potential source of ochratoxin- A contamination
text: Solid wastes from coffee processing, e.g. parchment and cherry husks of ‘Arabica’ and ‘Robusta’ varieties were tested for the presence of ochratoxin A (OTA), a mycotoxin produced by aii Aspergillus ochraccus and Penicillium verrucosut. The cherry husk of ‘Robusta’ had relatively higher level of OTA, ranging from 7.9 to 53.0 ppb compared to 3.6 to 18.0 ppb in ‘Arabica cherry husk. In the parchment of ‘Robusta’ and ‘Arabica there was no significant difference in the OTA. The results indicated that the coffee husk can be a potential source of OTA; hence, effective separation and immediate disposal of these wastes are of paramount importance to minimize the OTA contamination in coffee products (Gopinandhan et al., 2006).

title: The occurrence of ochratoxin-A in green and commercial coffee samples
text: A total of 148 coffee samples were tested for the natural occurrence of ochratoxin-A (OT-A). Among these, 100 (68%) and 19 (13%) samples had OT-A contamination of 0.1-1.0 ppb, and 1.1-5.0 ppb, respectively and 3 samples had> 5 ppb. The highest level of OT-A contamination was 11.7 ppb in a ‘Robusta’ cherry. The results indicated that majority of the Indian coffee samples analyzed that contained insignificant level of OT-A (Gopinandhan et al., 2007).

title: Effect of roasting and brewing on stability of ochratoxin A in coffee k
text: Effect of roasting and filter brewing on the stability of ochratoxin A (OTA) was studied using 3 naturally contaminated and 2 artificially infected coffee bean (Coffea canephora) samples. The OTA contaminated coffee samples were subjected to roasting temperatures of 180, 200 and 220°C, roasting levels of light, medium and dark, brewing times of 7, 15 and 20 min and analyzed for OTA content following immuno affinity column cleanup procedure coupled with high performance liquid chromatography. Naturally contaminated coffee samples showed OTA reduction from 4 to 36.8% with an average of 22%. Artificially infected coffee sample showed OTA reduction from 7 to 28.3% with an average of 16.6%. The filter method of coffee brewing reduced OTA content by 14% (Gopinandhan et al., 2009). In the present study, field trials were undertaken consecutively for 3 years to evaluate the impact of CBB on the microbial contamination of Arabica and Robusta coflee bean varieties, with emphasis laid toward ochratoxin-A (OTA) producing fungi. Results revealed higher microbial contamination in CBBinfested beans in both the varieties of coffee with the presence of toxigenic molds (such as Aspergillus niger, Aspergillus ochraceus). The “timely harvested” coftee, which was infested with CBB, was found to possess comparatively lesser OTA levels than those berries left in soil or on coffee plants. Studies carried out on coftee beans collected from nine curing factories indicated the presence of OTA in almost all the CBB-infested coffee beans, irrespective of the variety. Results of the present study provide sufficient baseline information and evidence to understand and correlate the role of CBB with various OTA-producing molds in coffee beans. Understanding the role of CBB might be useful and applicable in the coffee-growing regions of the world, especially in plantations for production of quality coffee (Velmourougane et al., 2010).

Evaluation of a new method for treating coffee effluent Coffee fruits are processed by either wet method or dry method at the estate level to obtain the coffee bean. Of these two methods, coffee processing by wet method requires large amount of water and thus generates enormous amount of effluent which needs to be treated extensively before discharge. Currently, the effluent treatment plant (ETP) module developed by Central Coffee Research Institute (CCRI) in collaboration with National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI) during 1980 is employed for treating the coffee effluent. The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) has recommended CCRINEERI ETP module for adoption at the estate level to treat the coffee effluent. In the present investigation, a new method viz., AcidificationNeutralization-Sedimentation-Filtration (ANSF) developed recently by CCRI was evaluated for treating the coffee effluent for four consecutive seasons (2017-2018 to 2020-2021) under field conditions. The results indicated that the BOD reduction by ANSF method is comparatively higher than the BOD reduction by CCRI-NEERI method. text: The new process is concerned only with the second step in the preparation of coffee for the market freeing the coffee bean from the pecticgel coat that surrounds it. Essentially, the new method calls merely for substituting the action of caustic soda for the natural bacterial action in the fermentation process. In the new chemical process, green-coffee weight losses are greatly reduced because of the rapidity of the process it takes less than an hour to free the coffee beans from their cover of gel. The seed does not have enough time to transform its solids into gases. During 195152 season, when > 430,000 pounds of coffee berries was chemically processed in El Salvador, yield gains ranged from 1 to 3%. It requires no elaborate equipment. Caustic soda costs little. text: This paper presents a simple, reproducible method for the determination of added flavours in roasted and ground coffee. The encapsulated flavours containing 4.5% cardamom oil and 5.4 % clove oil were incorporated into R&G coffee at 0.5% to 0.4% levels. title: Speciality coffees
text: Speciality coffees are high quality coffees and are different from that of normal coffees with reference to visual quality, in cup or in both. Speciality coffees are produced and processed with great care to preserve the intrinsic quality of the beans. Specialty coffees are growing in the world coffee market and they are fetching an attractive premium over that of normal coffees. Specialty coffees can be broadly classified into six categories based on their unique features. 1) Flavoured coffees, 2) Decaffeinated coffees, 3) Organic coffee, 4) Estate coffee, 5) Varietal coffee, 6) Indian Specialty coffee and 7) The monsooned coffee (Basavaraj et al., 1998).

title: Quality improvement of coffee through irradiation-prospects

Both low and high doses of gamma rays could be employed to improve the quality beans. While low doses of gamma rays help in controlling the coffee weevil proliferation, high doses of gamma rays might result in the enhancement of coffee aroma by activating aroma precursors. title: Coffee starter microbiome and in-silico approach to improve Arabica coffee
text: Arabica coffee is fermented to obtain intense flavor profile and finds elusive prospects in the coffee industry. The Arabica coffee mucilage constitute 2-5% of the fruit dry weight with 94% moisture, 4% sugar, 0.7% protein and 1-3% pectin. Inductive isolation and screening of functional attributes of microbial strains were examined. Fermentative vigor along with the enzymatic progression of the microbes was streamlined and the potential isolates of consortia were optimized. The In-silico docking studies on the fermentation mechanism evidenced minimal interaction between Pectin and pectinase at lower energy level. The 1CZF disclose the best interaction binding energy (—3.92 kJ/mol) with rapid enzymatic and desired fermentation. A CCRD was employed to study the interactive effect of isolates. The consortia of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Lactobacillus plantarum and Bacillus sphaericus (1:1:1) at 10% inoculum concentration found significant in demucilizatin of coffee beans with noticeable improvement in alcohol (70.26 mg/ ml), sugar (5.5 mg/ml) and pectinase (11.66 U/ml) compared to natural fermentation. The sensory TONAL, DEVERAGL, BREWING PHIST( profile of starter fermentation (G) scored 7.0 on 1-10 scale. text: §rowing regions of India The findings on cost of production of robusta coffee in major growing regions of India indicated that the average cost of production per hectare is Rs. 38.775 in Chikkamagaluru. Rs. 40.096 in Kodagu and Rs. 36,994 in Kerala. However, the cost per Kg was low in Kodagu (Rs. 21 per Kg) followed by Chikkamagaluru (Rs. 27 per Kg) and Kerala (Rs. 31 per Kg) because of varied yield realizations (1922 Kg/ha, 1435 Kg/ha and 1203 Kg/ha respectively). Further, the analysis revealed that an average yield gap of 830 Kg/ha in Chikkamagaluru. 631Kg/ha in Kodagu and 527 Kg/ha in Kerala were observed between irrigated and non-irrigated holdings. Thus, bridging the yield gaps either through irrigation or better management practices between the regions as well as irrigated and non-irrigated holdings of different regions to potential levels will boost the productivity levels of robusta, which reduces the cost of production per unit of output (Babu Reddy et al., 2001).

title: Estimation of cost of production of Arabica coffee in Chikkamagaluru region, Karnataka
text: A study was carried out to estimate the cost of production of Arabica coffee in Chikkamagaluru region covering 63 estates consisting of holdings with different sizes by adopting a multistage random sampling method. The results indicated that the average total cost of cultivation of Arabica (Abstracts of Research Pzpers) coffee in Chikkamagaluru region was Rs. 52,955 per ha which translated into a cost of production of Rs. 51 per kg with an average yield realization of 1040 kg/ha. Among the total cost, labour cost alone accounted for 54% followed by input cost (30%) and overhead expenditure (16%). While, across the holding size groups, the cost of cultivation was high in 4 to 10 hectare category with Rs. 55,450 per ha, followed by Rs. 54,790 (10-40 ha), Rs. 53,400 (> 40 ha) and Rs. 48.045 (4 ha) and per unit cost of production worked out to be Rs. 47 per kg (<4 ha.). Rs 51 per kg (410 ha). Rs. 49 per kg (10-40 ha and Rs, 53 per kg (> 40 ha), which was reflected mainly by varied yield realizations and the cost components. The yield realizations were 1020 kg/ ha (<4 ha), 1085 kg/ha (4-10 ha). 1125 kg/ha (1040 ha) and 1015 kg/ha (> 40 ha) indicating a yield gap of 110 kg/ha among the different size holding groups. Measures should focus on improving productivity by bridging the yield gaps and on reducing the cost of production by judicious use of farm resources, both labour and inputs, so that the cost per unit of output could be reduced so as to become more competitive in the market (Babu et. al., 2003).

title: Coffee certificntion in India: Awareness, practices, and sustainability perception of prowers
text: Certification programs have been employed in many apricultural products as a means to encourage and communicate compliance with standards associated with various attributes, such as organic, fair-trade, GMO free and eco-friendly among others. Such programs further seek to provide added value, through a price premium, to producers and supply chain actors associated with the label. In this paper, we review a number of global labeling and certification programs that could add value for coffee farms in India through the promotion of conservation and environmental protection. We provide results from a survey conducted ona sample of coflee farms in Coorg district, India, to assess their awareness and perceptions related toward certified coffee and environmental conservation in general. Survey results illustrate strong positive associations with the environment by coffee planters, particularly among certified and organic producers. However, price premiums for certified and organic coffee are relatively small. While the potential of conservation-oriented certification for coffee in Coorg could be relatively limited outside of a few individual-level niches, branding Coorg more generally as a conservation-oriented region could hold promise, leveraging and personalizing the uniqueness of the natural offerings from Coorg and tapping into burgeoning associations with place and region in India (Rich et al., 2018).

It is an interesting fact that the coffee drink is preferred by the people of developed countries and crop is grown in developing countries. Therefore, it is the developing countries who are the major producers and exporters of coffee to the world. Brazil is the largest producer and exporter of coffee in the world and India is the seventh largest producer and 8" largest exporter of coffee. The study attempts to analyze the trends, growth and instability in the area, production and productivity of coffee in major coffee producing countries and India. The production and yield of coffee had increased in all the major coffee producing countries from pre-liberalization to post liberalization period. The area had decreased in Brazil and Colombia but in other countries including India the area had increased in both the periods. The stability of the area, production and productivity remains unstable (>20%) over the years in the countries including India however the instability started to decline (15-20%) in the postliberalization period. The export competitiveness of Indian coffee in the international market has been analyzed using the Trade Intensity Index. The results showed that India had competitive advantage in exporting coffee to Italy, Belgium and Russia which are the major importers of coffee in the world (Soujanya et al., 2023).
